answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in the figure.

answer.text:
The device is an NMOS whose bulk is tied to its source,
so that there is no body effect. The input is applied to the
source, the output is taken at the drain, and the gate is not
at a fixed bias. Instead a fraction of the output is fed back
to the gate.

$$
V_F=\frac{R_2}{R_1+R_2}V_{out}\equiv \beta V_{out},
\qquad 
\beta =\frac{R_2}{R_1+R_2}<1
$$

It is a common-gate stage with drain-to-gate voltage feedback.

### DC operation

With $V_{IN}$ the dc level at the input,

$$\begin{aligned}
V_{F,Q}&=\beta V_{OUT,Q}\\
V_{GSQ}&=V_{F,Q}-V_{IN,Q}\\
I_{DQ}&=\frac12\mu_nC_{ox}\frac WL\,
\bigl(V_{GSQ}-V_{TH}\bigr)^2\bigl(1+\lambda V_{DSQ}\bigr)
\end{aligned}$$

and, at the output node,

$$
\frac{V_{DD}-V_{OUT,Q}}{R_D}=I_{DQ}+\frac{V_{OUT,Q}}{R_1+R_2}\; .
$$

The feedback is negative at dc as well: $I_D\uparrow\Rightarrow
V_{out}\downarrow\Rightarrow V_F\downarrow\Rightarrow V_{GS}\downarrow
\Rightarrow I_D\downarrow$.  Hence to first order

$$
V_{OUT,Q}\approx\frac{V_{IN,Q}+V_{GSQ}}{\beta},
$$

i.e. the output is a stepped-up replica of the input level.
Saturation, $V_{out}\ge V_F-V_{TH}$, is easily satisfied since
$\beta<1$.

### Small-signal gain

Let lower-case letters denote increments. The gate draws
no current, so

$$
v_f=\beta v_{out},\qquad 
v_{gs}=v_f-v_{in}= \beta v_{out}-v_{in}.
$$

The loading at the output by the divider is

$$
R_L' = R_D\;\Big\|\;(R_1+R_2).
$$

KCL at the drain, with $i_d$ flowing from drain to source,

$$
\frac{v_{out}}{R_L'}+i_d=0,\qquad
i_d=g_m v_{gs}+\frac{v_{out}-v_{in}}{r_o}.
$$

Hence

$$
-\frac{v_{out}}{R_L'}
   =g_m\bigl(\beta v_{out}-v_{in}\bigr)+\frac{v_{out}-v_{in}}{r_o},
$$

$$
\,A_v\equiv\frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}}
      =\frac{g_m+1/r_o}{\,g_m\beta+1/r_o+1/R_L'\,}
      =\frac{g_mr_o+1}{1+g_mr_o\beta+r_o/R_L'}\,  .
$$

Intuitively: $v_{in}\uparrow\to v_{gs}\downarrow\to i_d\downarrow\to
v_{out}\uparrow$, so the gain is positive; the rise in $v_{out}$
raises $v_f$ and partly restores $v_{gs}$ - negative feedback.

For $g_mr_o\gg1$,

$$
A_v\approx \frac{1}{\displaystyle \beta+\frac{1}{g_mR_L'}} 
        =\frac{1/\beta}{1+1/(g_m\beta R_L')}.
$$

Defining the loop gain (approximately)

$$
T \approx g_m\beta\,\bigl(R_L'\|r_o\bigr),
$$

if $T\gg1$,

$$
\,A_v\approx\frac1\beta = 1+\frac{R_1}{R_2}\,
$$

a non-inverting gain set by a resistor ratio, largely
independent of $g_m$, $R_D$ and device parameters. The maximum
attainable gain is of course limited to the open-loop
common-gate gain $\approx g_m(R_L'\|r_o)$, reached when
$\beta$ is made so small that $T\not\gg1$.

### Input resistance

The (downward) source current equals $i_d=-v_{out}/R_L'$,
so the current entering the source port is $v_{out}/R_L'$ and

$$
R_{in}=\frac{v_{in}}{i_{in}}=\frac{R_L'}{A_v}
      =\frac{1+R_L'\bigl(g_m\beta+1/r_o\bigr)}{g_m+1/r_o}
      \;\approx\;\frac{1+g_m\beta R_L'}{g_m}
      =\frac1{g_m}+\beta R_L'.
$$

For $\beta=0$ this reduces to the familiar $\approx1/g_m$ of
a common-gate stage. The series mixing of the feedback
raises $R_{in}$ by roughly $(1+T)$, to $\approx\beta R_L'$ for
$T\gg1$. With a source resistance $R_S$, $v_{out}/v_s=
A_vR_{in}/(R_{in}+R_S)$.

### Output resistance

With $v_{in}$ shorted for ac ($R_S=0$), applying a test
voltage at the output gives $v_{gs}=\beta v_x$, whence the
total resistance at the output terminal, including $R_D$
and $R_1+R_2$, is

$$
\,R_{out}
   =\frac{1}{\,g_m\beta+1/r_o+1/R_L'\,}
   =R_L'\;\big\|\;r_o\;\Big\|\;\frac{1}{g_m\beta}
   \;\approx\;\frac{1}{g_m\beta}\quad (T\gg1)\,  .
$$

Voltage (shunt) sampling at the output reduces $R_{out}$
by $\approx(1+T)$ from $R_D\|(R_1+R_2)\|r_o$. 
In general, for input source resistance $R_S$,
$R_{out}=\Bigl[1/R_L'+
\bigl(g_m\beta+1/r_o\bigr)/\bigl(1+(g_m+1/r_o)R_S\bigr)\Bigr]^{-1}$.

### Feedback interpretation

 sampled quantity: $v_{out}$; returned quantity: $v_f=\beta v_{out}$,
subtracted in series from $v_{in}$ in $v_{gs}$: a series-shunt
(voltage-voltage) feedback amplifier. Feedback thus
stabilises the gain to $1/\beta$, raises $R_{in}$, lowers
$R_{out}$, reduces distortion and sensitivity to $g_m$,
at the price of reduced gain.

In practice $R_1+R_2$ loads the output and dissipates power;
making it large raises the gate-node pole
$\sim\bigl[(R_1\|R_2)(C_{gs}+C_{gd})\bigr]^{-1}$, which lies inside
the loop together with the output pole and must be kept
high enough for phase margin. The pull-up at the output is
only through $R_D$, so sinking capability (via $M_1$) is much
stronger than sourcing capability.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in the figure.

answer.text:
Both transistors are NMOS. The arrowed terminal is the
source, with the body shorted to the source, as drawn.
Hence to first order there is no body effect in either
device.

* $M_{1}$: drain to $V_{DD}$, gate $=$ input, source $=$ output.
  It is a common-drain device.
* $M_{2}$: gate at a fixed bias $V_{b}$, source to ground,
  drain $=$ output. It is a saturated NMOS current source.

This is a source follower with an active, constant current,
load - a class A voltage buffer and d-c level shifter.

### 1. D-C bias

Gate currents are zero, so with no d-c load at the output

$$I_{D1}=I_{D2}\equiv I_{D}$$

$M_{2}$ fixes, to first order neglecting $\lambda$,

$$ 
I_{D}= \frac12\mu_{n}C_{ox}\left(\frac WL\right)_{2}
      \left(V_{b}-V_{TH}\right)^{2}
      =\frac12\mu_{n}C_{ox}\left(\frac WL\right)_{2}V_{ov2}^{2}
$$

$M_{1}$ must carry the same current:

$$
I_{D}= \frac12\mu_{n}C_{ox}\left(\frac WL\right)_{1}
      \left(V_{in}-V_{out}-V_{TH}\right)^{2}
$$

i.e.

$$ V_{GS1}=V_{TH}+V_{ov1},\qquad 
V_{ov1}= \sqrt{\frac{2I_{D}}{\mu_{n}C_{ox}(W/L)_{1}}} $$

$$ V_{out}=V_{in}-V_{GS1}=V_{in}-V_{TH}-V_{ov1} $$

The output follows the input with an essentially constant
$V_{GS1}$ drop. With $\lambda\ne0$, $I_D$ varies slightly
with $V_{out}$ through $r_{o1},r_{o2}$, giving a slope
slightly $<1$.

Saturation requires

$$\begin{aligned}
M_{2}:&\;V_{DS2}=V_{out}\ge V_{GS2}-V_{TH}=V_{ov2}\\
M_{1}:&\;V_{DS1}=V_{DD}-V_{out}\ge V_{GS1}-V_{TH}
      \;\Longleftrightarrow\;V_{in}\le V_{DD}+V_{TH}
\end{aligned}$$

usually satisfied for $V_{in}\le V_{DD}$.

Hence, approximately,

$$V_{out,min}\approx V_{ov2},\qquad 
  V_{out,max}\approx V_{DD}-V_{TH}-V_{ov1}\;\;{\rm for}\;V_{in,max}=V_{DD} $$

The follower cannot reach the positive rail; it loses
at least $V_{GS1}$. It can go to within $V_{ov2}$ of ground.

### 2. Small signal model

$V_{DD}$ and $V_b$ are a-c ground. $M_1$: $v_{gs1}=v_{in}-v_{out}$,
$v_{ds1}=-v_{out}$. $M_2$: $v_{gs2}=0$, so it is simply $r_{o2}$
to ground. With an external $R_L$, KCL at the output,

$$g_{m1}(v_{in}-v_{out})-\frac{v_{out}}{r_{o1}}
      =\frac{v_{out}}{r_{o2}}+\frac{v_{out}}{R_{L}}$$

$$ A_v\equiv\frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}}
      =\frac{g_{m1}}
             {g_{m1}+g_{o1}+g_{o2}+G_{L}} $$

$$ g_{mi}=\sqrt{2\mu_nC_{ox}(W/L)_iI_D}= \frac{2I_D}{V_{ovi}},\qquad
   r_{oi}= \frac1{\lambda_i I_D}$$

In ordinary form, $R_L' = r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2}\parallel R_L$,

$$ A_v = \frac{R_L'}{R_L'+1/g_{m1}} <1 $$

no phase inversion, $\approx 1$ for $g_{m1}r_o\gg1$.
With a resistive load the larger current in $M_1$ required
by $R_L$ makes $V_{GS1}$ $V_{out}$ dependent, and $A_v$ falls.

Input resistance, low frequency,

$$ R_{in}= \frac{v_{in}}{i_{in}}\approx\infty $$

gate current being zero. The effective input capacitance is
small, $C_{in}\approx C_{gd1}+C_{gs1}(1-A_v)$, because $C_{gs1}$
is bootstrapped.

Output resistance, $v_{in}=0$,

$$ R_{out}= r_{o2}\;\Big\|\; \left(\frac{r_{o1}}{1+g_{m1}r_{o1}}\right)
        = r_{o2}\parallel r_{o1}\parallel\frac1{g_{m1}}
        \approx \frac1{g_{m1}} $$

in parallel with any $R_L$. Increasing $I_D$ or $(W/L)_1$
increases $g_{m1}$, makes $A_v\to1$, lowers $R_{out}$ and
increases bandwidth $\approx [2\pi R_{out}C_L]^{-1}$ at the
expense of static power $P\approx V_{DD}I_D$.

### 3. Large signal behaviour, merits and limits

Ideally $I_{D1}$ is constant, $V_{GS1}$ is constant, so the
transfer $V_{out}=V_{in}-{\rm const}$ is very linear. Non-
linearity comes from $\lambda$ and, in a normal $p$-substrate
process where the body of $M_1$ cannot be tied to its source,
from body effect: then $g_{m1}\to g_{m1}+g_{mb1}$ in $A_v$ and
$R_{out}$, and $V_{TH1}$ becomes $V_{out}$ dependent.

Current drive is asymmetric. $M_1$ can supply a large
current to a load on a rising output, $v_{gs1}$ increasing
transiently. On a falling output, or sinking current, the
maximum available current is the bias current $I_D$ set by
$M_2$. The negative slew rate into $C_L$ is $\approx I_D/C_L$.

In short:

| $A_v$ | $R_{in}$ | $R_{out}$ | Phase |
|---|---|---|---|
| $\dfrac{g_{m1}}{g_{m1}+g_{o1}+g_{o2}+G_L}\lesssim1$ | $\approx\infty$ | $\approx1/g_{m1}$ | $0^\circ$ |

It is used where high input impedance, low output
impedance, near-unity gain and a $V_{GS}$ level shift are
wanted, e.g. as an output buffer, at the cost of headroom
$V_{TH}+V_{ov1}$ at the top, static class-A power, and
limited current sinking.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly identifies M1 as a source follower and M2 as its NMOS current-source load, and gives a positive gain below but near unity. The ideal no-body-effect model is consistent with the full-credit rule.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in the figure.

answer.text:
The two devices are NMOS devices.
$M_{1}$ has its drain at the a.c. ground $V_{DD}$, its gate
is the input and its source is the output. $M_{2}$ has a
fixed gate voltage $V_{b}$. It is not a signal device.

It is a common drain stage, a source follower, with an
active current source load.

$$M_{1}: {\rm input\; device}\qquad 
  M_{2}: {\rm bias\; current\; source}$$

The current source gives a much larger incremental
resistance than a resistor, $r_{o2}$, with much less voltage
drop.

### D.C. bias

With no d.c. load at the output the gate currents are zero,
hence, apart from channel length modulation,

$$ I_{D1}=I_{D2}\equiv I_{B} $$

$M_{2}$ in saturation fixes, to first order,

$$ I_{B}\approx 
\frac12\mu_{n}C_{ox}\Bigl(\frac WL\Bigr)_{2}
\bigl(V_{b}-V_{TH2}\bigr)^{2}
      =\frac12\mu_{n}C_{ox}\Bigl(\frac WL\Bigr)_{2}V_{ov2}^{2} $$

and $M_{1}$ must develop the $V_{GS1}$ necessary to carry
$I_{B}$ :

$$ I_{B}\approx 
\frac12\mu_{n}C_{ox}\Bigl(\frac WL\Bigr)_{1}
\bigl(V_{in}-V_{out}-V_{TH1}\bigr)^{2}  $$

i.e.

$$ V_{out}=V_{in}-V_{GS1}
       =V_{in}-V_{TH1}-V_{ov1} $$

$$ V_{ov1}= \sqrt{\frac{2I_{B}}
{\mu_{n}C_{ox}(W/L)_{1}}}\;, \qquad 
g_{m1}= \frac{2I_{B}}{V_{ov1}}=
\sqrt{2\mu_{n}C_{ox}(W/L)_{1}I_{B}}  .$$

To first order $I_{B}$ and hence $V_{GS1}$ are constant.
The output follows the input with an essentially constant
level shift $V_{GS1}$ downward, with unity slope.  In a
common $p$--substrate process the bulk of $M_{1}$ is at
ground, $V_{BS1}=-V_{out}$, so $V_{TH1}$ increases with
$V_{out}$ and the shift is not quite constant.  This is
the body effect, represented below by $g_{mb1}$.  For a
bulk-to-source strapped device $g_{mb1}\to0$.

For both devices to stay in saturation

* $M_{2}$: $\;V_{DS2}\ge V_{GS2}-V_{TH2}$ i.e. 
  $$V_{out}\ge V_{b}-V_{TH2}=V_{ov2}$$
* $M_{1}$: $\;V_{DD}-V_{out}\ge V_{in}-V_{out}-V_{TH1}$ i.e.
  $$V_{in}\le V_{DD}+V_{TH1}$$

in practice satisfied for $V_{in}\le V_{DD}$.  Hence the
useful output range is approximately

$$ V_{ov2}\;\lesssim\;V_{out}\;\lesssim\;V_{DD}-V_{GS1} $$

The output cannot reach $V_{DD}$; it is $V_{GS1}$ below
the maximum input.  For very low $V_{in}$, $M_{1}$ cuts off
and $M_{2}$ pulls $V_{out}$ to ground.

Static power is $P\approx V_{DD}I_{B}$, class-A.

### Small signal behaviour

$V_{DD}$ and $V_{b}$ are a.c. ground. $M_{2}$ appears at the
output simply as $r_{o2}$ to ground.  KCL at the output,
with $v_{gs1}=v_{in}-v_{out}$, $v_{bs1}=-v_{out}$,

$$ g_{m1}(v_{in}-v_{out})-g_{mb1}v_{out}
      -\frac{v_{out}}{r_{o1}}=\frac{v_{out}}{r_{o2}} $$

i.e.

$$ A_{v}\equiv\frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}}
      =\frac{g_{m1}}
             {g_{m1}+g_{mb1}+g_{o1}+g_{o2}}
      =\frac{g_{m1}\,(r_{o1}\!\parallel\! r_{o2})}
             {1+(g_{m1}+g_{mb1})(r_{o1}\!\parallel\! r_{o2})}
      \;<\;1 $$

positive, non-inverting.  With $g_{m}r_{o}\gg1$,
$A_{v}\approx g_{m1}/(g_{m1}+g_{mb1})$, typically
$0.7$--$0.95$.  With bulk tied to source $g_{mb1}=0$ and
$A_{v}\to1$ for $r_{o}\to\infty$.  With a load $R_{L}$ add
$1/R_{L}$ to the denominator.

Input resistance at low frequency is the gate resistance,

$$ R_{in}\approx \infty $$

apart from $C_{gd1}+C_{gs1}(1-A_{v})$, the latter being
small because $A_{v}\approx1$.

Resistance looking into the source of $M_{1}$, in parallel
with $r_{o2}$,

$$ R_{out}= \frac{1}{g_{m1}+g_{mb1}+g_{o1}+g_{o2}}
        =\frac{1}{g_{m1}+g_{mb1}}\;\Big\|\;r_{o1}\;\Big\|\;r_{o2}
        \;\approx\;\frac1{g_{m1}} $$

normally a few hundred ohms to a few k$\Omega$.  Hence
the dominant pole with a capacitive load $C_{L}$ is at
the output,

$$ f_{p,out}\approx\frac{1}{2\pi R_{out}C_{L}} $$

which is high because $R_{out}$ is low.

### Use and limitations

It is a voltage buffer and d.c. level shifter: very
high $R_{in}$, low $R_{out}$, voltage gain close to, but
less than, unity, wide bandwidth, able to drive resistive
and capacitive loads.

Limitations are the $V_{GS1}$ loss of headroom,
$g_{mb}$ and finite $r_{o}$ reducing the gain below 1
and making it somewhat $V_{out}$ dependent, and
class-A sinking: $M_{1}$ can source a large current, but
the current that can be sunk from a load is limited to
$I_{B}$.  The negative slew rate with $C_{L}$ is
$\approx I_{B}/C_{L}$.  Increasing $I_{B}$ or $(W/L)_{1}$
increases $g_{m1}$, makes $A_{v}$ closer to 1, lowers
$R_{out}$ and improves slew and distortion, at the cost
of power and of $V_{ov2}$ headroom.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in the figure.

answer.text:
The two devices are NMOS, $M_{1}$ on top of $M_{2}$.
$M_{1}$ has its drain at a-c ground, $V_{DD}$, its gate is the
input and its source is the output. $M_{2}$ has a fixed gate
bias $V_{b}$, its drain is the output and its source is ground.
It is a common drain, i.e. source follower, stage biased by
an active current source load.

$M_{1}$ is the follower, $M_{2}$ in saturation is to first order
a constant current $I_{B}$ with a large incremental resistance
$r_{o2}$ to ground. No d-c gate current flows.

### D-C bias

With no d-c load at the output

$$I_{D1}=I_{D2}\equiv I_{B}$$

$$ 
I_{B}\approx \frac12\mu_{n}C_{ox}\Bigl(\frac WL\Bigr)_{2}
      \bigl(V_{b}-V_{th2}\bigr)^{2}\bigl(1+\lambda_{2}V_{out}\bigr)
$$

$$ 
I_{B}\approx \frac12\mu_{n}C_{ox}\Bigl(\frac WL\Bigr)_{1}
      \bigl(V_{in}-V_{out}-V_{th1}\bigr)^{2}
      \bigl(1+\lambda_{1}(V_{DD}-V_{out})\bigr)
$$

i.e. to first order

$$ V_{out}=V_{in}-V_{GS1},\qquad 
V_{GS1}=V_{th1}+\sqrt{\frac{2I_{B}}
{\mu_{n}C_{ox}(W/L)_{1}}}\equiv V_{th1}+V_{ov1} $$

The output follows the input, level shifted down by one
$V_{GS}$. $I_{B}$, hence $g_{m1}$, is set by $V_{b}$ and $M_{2}$,
essentially independent of $V_{in}$. Static dissipation is
$V_{DD}I_{B}$.

Saturation: for $M_{2}$

$$V_{DS2}=V_{out}\ge V_{GS2}-V_{th2}=V_{ov2}$$

for $M_{1}$

$$V_{DS1}=V_{DD}-V_{out}\ge V_{GS1}-V_{th1}\iff V_{in}\lesssim V_{DD}+V_{th1}$$

normally always satisfied.  Hence in the useful range

$$ V_{in,min}\approx V_{GS1}+V_{ov2},\qquad 
   V_{out,min}\approx V_{ov2},\qquad 
   V_{out,max}\approx V_{DD}-V_{GS1}\;\;{\rm for}\;V_{in,max}=V_{DD}. $$

Below this $M_{2}$ goes triode and $V_{out}\to0$; $M_{1}$ cuts off
for very low $V_{in}$. With $\lambda\ne0$, $I_{B}$ varies
slightly with $V_{out}$, so $V_{GS1}$ varies slightly with
$V_{out}$ - the source of the gain error below.

As drawn the bulk is tied to the source, so $V_{BS}=0$ for
both devices. In a common $p$-substrate process the bulk of
$M_{1}$ is at ground; then $V_{th1}$ increases with $V_{out}$
and a $g_{mb1}$ term appears below.

### Small signal behaviour

$g_{m1}=\sqrt{2\mu_{n}C_{ox}(W/L)_{1}I_{B}}=2I_{B}/V_{ov1}$,
$r_{oi}=1/\lambda_{i}I_{B}$. $M_{2}$ has $v_{gs2}=0$; incrementally
it is simply $r_{o2}$ from output to ground. KCL at the output,

$$g_{m1}(v_{in}-v_{out})-g_{mb1}v_{out}
      -\frac{v_{out}}{r_{o1}}-\frac{v_{out}}{r_{o2}}=0$$

with $g_{mb1}=0$ for bulk-source tie as drawn. Hence

$$\;
\frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}}=
\frac{g_{m1}\,(r_{o1}\!\parallel\! r_{o2})}
     {1+(g_{m1}+g_{mb1})(r_{o1}\!\parallel\! r_{o2})}
=
\frac{r_{o1}\!\parallel\! r_{o2}}
     {1/(g_{m1})+r_{o1}\!\parallel\! r_{o2}}\;\;{\rm approx.}
$$

non-inverting, $<1$, typically $0.8$--$0.95$. With an external
$R_{L}$, replace $r_{o2}$ by $r_{o2}\!\parallel\! R_{L}$. The
active load gives a much larger $r_{o1}\!\parallel\! r_{o2}$,
hence gain much closer to unity and much more constant
$I_{B}$, than a resistive or diode load.

Input resistance is the gate resistance,

$$R_{in}\approx \infty\qquad\text{d-c}$$

with input capacitance $C_{in}\approx C_{gd1}+C_{gs1}(1-A_{v})$,
small because $1-A_{v}\ll1$; there is essentially no Miller
multiplication.

Output resistance, $v_{in}=0$,

$$\;
R_{out}=r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2}\parallel\frac{1}{g_{m1}+g_{mb1}}
      \approx \frac{1}{g_{m1}+g_{mb1}}\;
$$

low, set by the bias current through $g_{m1}$. This is the
purpose of the circuit: a voltage buffer / level shifter
with high $R_{in}$, low $R_{out}$, gain $\approx1$.

The dominant high frequency poles are approximately
$1/R_{out}C_{L}$ at the output, large because $R_{out}$ is
small, and $1/R_{sig}C_{in}$ at the input.

### Large signal, limitations

$M_{1}$ can source $\gg I_{B}$ on a positive excursion, but
it can sink at most $I_{B}$, the current in $M_{2}$. Negative
slew into $C_{L}$ is limited to $I_{B}/C_{L}$, and a d-c $R_{L}$
steals current from $M_{1}$, making $V_{GS1}$ and $A_{v}$
signal dependent. Headroom is lost at the top by $V_{GS1}$
and at the bottom by $V_{ov2}$ of the current source.
Increasing $I_{B}$ raises $g_{m1}$, lowers $R_{out}$, improves
gain and speed, at the cost of power and of larger $V_{GS1}$
and device sizes. Lower $V_{ov2}$ improves swing but lowers
$r_{o2}$.

In short: an NMOS source follower with NMOS current-source
load, $A_{v}\lesssim1$, $R_{in}\approx\infty$, 
$R_{out}\approx1/g_{m1}$, used as a buffer and d-c level shift
between a high impedance gain stage and a low impedance load.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in the figure.

answer.text:
The circuit is the static CMOS inverter, a NOT gate.

$M_{1}$ is the NMOS pull-down device, its source and body
to ground. $M_{2}$ is the PMOS pull-up device, its source and
body to $V_{DD}$. Hence there is no body effect. The gates
are the common input, the drains the common output.

$$\begin{aligned}
V_{GS1}&=V_{in}, & V_{DS1}&=V_{out}\\
V_{SG2}&=V_{DD}-V_{in}, & V_{SD2}&=V_{DD}-V_{out}
\end{aligned}$$

Put 
$\beta_{n}=\mu_{n}C_{ox}(W/L)_{1}$, $\beta_{p}=\mu_{p}C_{ox}(W/L)_{2}$,
$V_{tn}>0$, $V_{tp}<0$.

### Static operation

| $V_{in}$ | $M_{1}$ | $M_{2}$ | $V_{out}$ |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| $0$, logic 0 | OFF | ON | $V_{DD}$, logic 1 |
| $V_{DD}$, logic 1 | ON | OFF | $0$, logic 0 |

In either steady state one device is off, so (apart from
leakage) there is no d-c path $V_{DD}\to$ GND and no
static power. The output swings rail to rail,
$V_{OH}=V_{DD}$, $V_{OL}=0$.

### Voltage transfer characteristic

With no d-c load $I_{D1}=I_{D2}$. As $V_{in}$ rises from 0 to
$V_{DD}$, $V_{out}$ falls monotonically from $V_{DD}$ to 0.

1. $V_{in}<V_{tn}$: $M_{1}$ off, $M_{2}$ in triode with
$I_D=0$, so $V_{SD2}=0$, $V_{out}=V_{DD}$.

2. $V_{in}$ just $>V_{tn}$, $V_{out}$ still high: $M_{1}$
saturated, $V_{out}\ge V_{in}-V_{tn}$; $M_{2}$ in triode,
$V_{out}>V_{in}+|V_{tp}|$.
$$\frac{\beta_n}{2}(V_{in}-V_{tn})^{2}
 =\beta_p\!\left[(V_{DD}-V_{in}-|V_{tp}|)(V_{DD}-V_{out})
 -\frac{(V_{DD}-V_{out})^{2}}{2}\right]$$
$V_{out}$ falls slowly.

3. Intermediate $V_{in}$: both saturated,
$V_{in}-V_{tn}\le V_{out}\le V_{in}+|V_{tp}|$. $V_{out}$
falls very rapidly, and a substantial "crowbar" current
flows from $V_{DD}$ to ground.

4. $V_{in}$ large, $V_{out}$ low: $M_{1}$ in triode, $M_{2}$
saturated, the mirror image of 2.

5. $V_{in}>V_{DD}-|V_{tp}|$: $M_{2}$ off, $M_{1}$ in triode
with $I_D=0$, $V_{out}=0$.

```
Vout
VDD |------\
    |       \
    |        \     <- very steep, both saturated
  0 |         ------
    +-------------- Vin
              VM
```

### Switching threshold

Define $V_M$ by $V_{in}=V_{out}=V_M$. Both devices are in
saturation there, so, neglecting $\lambda$,
$$\frac{\beta_n}{2}(V_M-V_{tn})^2=
 \frac{\beta_p}{2}(V_{DD}-V_M-|V_{tp}|)^2$$
$$\;V_M=
\frac{V_{tn}+r\,(V_{DD}-|V_{tp}|)}{1+r}\;,
\qquad 
r=\sqrt{\frac{\beta_p}{\beta_n}}$$

For $\beta_n=\beta_p$ and $V_{tn}=|V_{tp}|$, $V_M=V_{DD}/2$.
Since $\mu_n\approx 2$–$3\,\mu_p$, a symmetric inverter
normally makes $(W/L)_2\approx(\mu_n/\mu_p)(W/L)_1$, at
the cost of area and input capacitance.

$V_{IL}$ and $V_{IH}$ are the $dV_{out}/dV_{in}=-1$ points.
With $V_{OL}=0$, $V_{OH}=V_{DD}$,
$NM_L=V_{IL}-V_{OL}$, $NM_H=V_{OH}-V_{IH}$, both typically
$\sim 0.4V_{DD}$, i.e. excellent noise immunity.

Biased at $V_M$ the circuit is also a high-gain inverting
amplifier: both transistors act as common-source devices
in parallel,
$$A_v=-(g_{m1}+g_{m2})\,(r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2})$$
which explains the steep VTC. Finite $\lambda$ makes the
slope finite but large.

### Dynamic behaviour and power

The output sees a load capacitance $C_L$ (next gate,
parasitics, wiring). $M_{2}$ charges $C_L$ to $V_{DD}$,
$M_{1}$ discharges it to ground. To first order,
$$t_{pHL}\sim \frac{C_LV_{DD}}{\beta_n(V_{DD}-V_{tn})^2},
\qquad
t_{pLH}\sim \frac{C_LV_{DD}}{\beta_p(V_{DD}-|V_{tp}|)^2}$$
or $t_p\approx0.69R_{eq}C_L$. Equal rise and fall times
again require $\beta_n\approx\beta_p$.

Static power is $\approx V_{DD}I_{leak}$ only. On a
$0\to1$ output transition $C_LV_{DD}^{2}$ is drawn from
the supply, half dissipated in $M_{2}$, half stored on
$C_L$ and later dissipated in $M_{1}$. For activity
factor $\alpha$ and frequency $f$,
$$P_{dyn}= \alpha f C_L V_{DD}^{2}$$
plus a smaller short-circuit term from the interval in
region 3 when both devices conduct.

In summary: a complementary, rail-to-rail, inverting
stage with infinite d-c input resistance, low output
resistance, essentially zero static power, large noise
margins, and speed/power dominated by $C_LV_{DD}^{2}f$ —
the basic building block of static CMOS logic.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in the figure.

answer.text:
The circuit is the CMOS inverter. $M_{1}$ is an
NMOS device, its body tied to ground, its source to ground
and its drain to the output. $M_{2}$ is a PMOS device, its
body tied to $V_{DD}$, its source to $V_{DD}$ and its drain
to the output. The gates are tied together.

$$V_{out}=\overline{V_{in}}$$

Since the source of each device is tied to its body,
$V_{BS}=0$ for both devices and there is no body effect.

### Steady state operation

Let $V_{TN}>0$ be the NMOS threshold and $V_{TP}<0$
the PMOS threshold.

$V_{in}=0$:
$$V_{GS1}=0<V_{TN}\qquad V_{SG2}=V_{DD}>|V_{TP}|$$
$M_{1}$ is off, $M_{2}$ is on. There is no dc path from
$V_{DD}$ to ground, and $M_{2}$ pulls the output to

$$V_{out}=V_{DD}\qquad \text{logic 1}$$

$V_{in}=V_{DD}$:
$$V_{GS1}=V_{DD}>V_{TN}\qquad V_{SG2}=0<|V_{TP}|$$
$M_{2}$ is off, $M_{1}$ is on. $M_{1}$ pulls the output to

$$V_{out}=0\qquad \text{logic 0}$$

Hence the output swings rail-to-rail,
$V_{OH}=V_{DD}$, $V_{OL}=0$. In either steady state one
transistor is off, so ideally

$$I_{DD,static}=0,\qquad P_{static}\approx 0$$

except for leakage. The input draws no dc current,
the static output resistance is low, because the
on transistor is in the triode region with $V_{DS}\approx 0$.

### Voltage transfer characteristic

As $V_{in}$ is raised from $0$ to $V_{DD}$, five regions occur.

| $V_{in}$ | $M_{1}$ NMOS | $M_{2}$ PMOS | $V_{out}$ |
|---|---|---|---|
| $V_{in}<V_{TN}$ | off | triode | $V_{DD}$ |
| low | saturation | triode | $\approx V_{DD}$, falling slowly |
| $V_{in}\approx V_{M}$ | saturation | saturation | falls steeply |
| high | triode | saturation | $\approx 0$, falling slowly |
| $V_{in}>V_{DD}-|V_{TP}|$ | triode | off | $0$ |

In the middle region both devices are saturated, so the
small signal voltage gain is large. With both gates driven
and both drains at the output,

$$A_{v}=-(g_{m1}+g_{m2})\,(r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2}) ,\qquad |A_{v}|\gg 1$$

so the VTC is very steep around its switching point.

### Switching threshold

Define $V_{M}$ by $V_{in}=V_{out}=V_{M}$. There both devices
are saturated and $I_{D1}=I_{D2}$. Neglecting $\lambda$,

$$\frac{\beta_n}{2}(V_{M}-V_{TN})^{2}
 =\frac{\beta_p}{2}\bigl(V_{DD}-V_{M}-|V_{TP}|\bigr)^{2}$$

where $\beta_{n,p}=\mu_{n,p}C_{ox}(W/L)_{n,p}$. Hence

$$V_{M}=
\frac{V_{TN}+\sqrt{\beta_p/\beta_n}\,\bigl(V_{DD}-|V_{TP}|\bigr)}
     {1+\sqrt{\beta_p/\beta_n}} .$$

If $\beta_n=\beta_p$ and $V_{TN}=|V_{TP}|$,

$$V_{M}= \frac{V_{DD}}{2}$$

at the centre of the supply range. Since $\mu_n\approx 2$--$3\,\mu_p$,
this usually requires

$$\left(\frac{W}{L}\right)_p \approx \frac{\mu_n}{\mu_p}
\left(\frac{W}{L}\right)_n $$

i.e. the PMOS is made wider than the NMOS. This also
equalises the rise and fall times.

Noise margins are defined from the points where
$dV_{out}/dV_{in}=-1$, $V_{IL}$ and $V_{IH}$:

$$NM_L=V_{IL}-V_{OL}=V_{IL},\qquad 
  NM_H=V_{OH}-V_{IH}=V_{DD}-V_{IH}.$$

For a balanced inverter they are each close to $V_{DD}/2$,
so the inverter has excellent noise immunity and restores
logic levels at every stage.

### Switching, power and speed

During a transition, for $V_{TN}<V_{in}<V_{DD}-|V_{TP}|$,
both transistors are on briefly, producing a short
``crowbar'' current from $V_{DD}$ to ground. This is the
main short-circuit power component.

With a load capacitance $C_L$ at the output, a $0\to1$
transition draws $C_LV_{DD}^{2}$ of energy from the supply,
half stored on $C_L$ and half dissipated in $M_{2}$; the
stored energy is dissipated in $M_{1}$ on the $1\to0$
transition. For switching activity $\alpha$ at frequency $f$,

$$P_{dyn}\approx \alpha C_L V_{DD}^{2} f .$$

The propagation delays are approximately set by charging
$C_L$ through the on resistance of $M_{2}$ and discharging
it through $M_{1}$:

$$t_{PLH}\approx 0.69\,R_{eq,p}C_L,\qquad
  t_{PHL}\approx 0.69\,R_{eq,n}C_L,$$
$$t_p=\frac{t_{PLH}+t_{PHL}}{2}.$$

In summary, the circuit is a NOT gate with rail-to-rail
swing, very high input impedance, low static output
impedance, essentially zero static power, large noise
margins, and speed/power determined mainly by the load
capacitance and the transistor sizes.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in the figure.

answer.text:
The two devices form the complementary pair of a
CMOS NOT gate.

$M_{1}$ is n-channel, source and body to ground.
$M_{2}$ is p-channel, source and body to $V_{DD}$.
The two gates are the input, the two drains are the output.
Hence $V_{SB1}=V_{SB2}=0$; there is no body effect in the
ideal analysis.  Put

$$
 \beta_{n,p}= \mu_{n,p}C_{ox}\Bigl({W\over L}\Bigr)_{n,p}\qquad 
V_{Tn}>0,\;\;V_{Tp}<0 .
$$

### Logic operation

* $V_{in}\approx 0$:  $V_{GS1}=0<V_{Tn}$, $M_{1}$ off;
$V_{SG2}=V_{DD}>|V_{Tp}|$, $M_{2}$ on. $M_{2}$ pulls the
output, and any load capacitance, to $V_{DD}$,
$$
V_{out}=V_{DD},\qquad I_{D}=0 .
$$

* $V_{in}\approx V_{DD}$: $M_{2}$ off, $M_{1}$ on. $M_{1}$ pulls
the output to ground,
$$
V_{out}=0,\qquad I_{D}=0 .
$$

i.e. in the logic sense

$$
V_{out}=\overline{V_{in}},\qquad 
\begin{array}{c|c} V_{in}&V_{out}\\ \hline 0&V_{DD}\\ V_{DD}&0\end{array}
$$

rail to rail swing, essentially no static current,
and, the gates being insulated, essentially no d-c
input current.  Static power is, apart from leakage, zero.

### Voltage transfer characteristic

For $0<V_{in}<V_{DD}$ the drain currents must be equal,
$I_{D1}=I_{D2}$, the series current from $V_{DD}$ to ground.
In the long channel approximation, $\lambda =0$ except
where noted,

1. $V_{in}<V_{Tn}$: $M_{1}$ off, $M_{2}$ in triode with
$I_{D2}\approx0$, $V_{out}=V_{DD}$.

2. $V_{Tn}<V_{in}\lesssim V_{M}$: $M_{1}$ saturated,
$M_{2}$ in triode,
$${\beta_n\over2}(V_{in}-V_{Tn})^2=
\beta_p\Bigl[(V_{DD}-V_{in}-|V_{Tp}|)(V_{DD}-V_{out})
-{(V_{DD}-V_{out})^{2}\over2}\Bigr]$$
$V_{out}$ stays close to $V_{DD}$.

3. $V_{in}\approx V_{M}$: both devices saturated.
$V_{out}$ falls very rapidly with $V_{in}$.

4. $V_{in}\gtrsim V_{M}$: $M_{1}$ in triode, $M_{2}$ saturated,
$V_{out}$ close to $0$.

5. $V_{in}>V_{DD}-|V_{Tp}|$: $M_{2}$ off, $M_{1}$ in triode
with $I_{D1}\approx0$, $V_{out}=0$.

$M$, the switching threshold, defined by $V_{in}=V_{out}=V_M$
with both devices saturated, follows from $I_{D1}=I_{D2}$:

$$
\sqrt{\beta_n}\,(V_M-V_{Tn})=
\sqrt{\beta_p}\,\bigl(V_{DD}-V_M-|V_{Tp}|\bigr)
$$

$$
\,V_M=
{V_{Tn}+r\,(V_{DD}-|V_{Tp}|)\over 1+r}\,,\qquad 
r=\sqrt{\beta_p/\beta_n}\;  .
$$

For $\beta_n=\beta_p$ and $V_{Tn}=|V_{Tp}|$, $V_M=V_{DD}/2$,
the VTC is symmetric and the (ideal) noise margins are
$\approx V_{DD}/2$.  Since $\mu_n\approx2\!-\!3\,\mu_p$,
$\beta_n=\beta_p$ normally requires
$(W/L)_p\approx2\!-\!3\,(W/L)_n$.
Increasing $\beta_p/\beta_n$ moves $V_M$ up, and vice versa.

Biased at $V_M$ the circuit is a high gain amplifier.
Both transconductances aid,

$$
A_v=\left.{{dV_{out}}\over{dV_{in}}}\right|_{V_M}
=-(g_{m1}+g_{m2})\,(r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2})
=-{(g_{m1}+g_{m2})\over I_D(\lambda_n+\lambda_p)}\;,
$$

large in magnitude; with $\lambda\to0$ the transition
in 3. becomes vertical.  The current through the pair
is zero at the two logic levels and peaks near $V_M$,
the familiar short-circuit current during switching.

### Dynamic behaviour

$M_1$ discharges a load $C_L$ to ground and $M_2$ charges
it to $V_{DD}$, with on resistances roughly
$R_n\approx[\beta_n(V_{DD}-V_{Tn})]^{-1}$,
$R_p\approx[\beta_p(V_{DD}-|V_{Tp}|)]^{-1}$. Hence,
to first order,

$$
t_{pHL}\approx0.69\,R_nC_L,\qquad 
t_{pLH}\approx0.69\,R_pC_L .
$$

The d-c input resistance is infinite; the input
capacitance is essentially $C_{ox}(W_1L_1+W_2L_2)$.
The output resistance in a logic state is the $R_{on}$
of the device that is on.  Mean power at switching
frequency $f$ with activity $\alpha$ is dominated by

$$
P \approx \alpha C_LV_{DD}^{2}f
$$

plus a small short-circuit term.  In short: a rail-to-rail,
high-noise-margin, essentially zero-static-power inverter,
the basic CMOS logic gate, and, biased at $V_M$, a
high-gain inverting amplifier.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in the figure.

answer.text:
This is not, at first sight, what it looks like.
It looks like a complementary inverter, but look at the
terminals which carry the arrow, i.e. at the sources.

* $M_{1}$ : drain to $V_{DD}$, source to the output node.
  The arrow is at the output side.  $M_{1}$ is $n$--channel.
* $M_{2}$ : source to the output node, drain to ground.
  The arrow is at the output side, reversed. $M_{2}$ is
  $p$--channel.

The drains go to the supplies and the sources meet at
$V_{out}$.  The gates are in common.  It is the complementary
common drain, i.e. push-pull source follower, the MOS
class-B output stage.  It is in phase with the input, it
has no voltage gain, and it cannot swing to the rails.

Let $V_{TN}>0$, $V_{TP}<0$, $|V_{TP}|$ for the $p$ device.
In a monolithic version the $n$ body is to ground and the
$p$ body is to $V_{DD}$, so in general $V_{TN}$ and
$|V_{TP}| $ are $V_{out}$ dependent through the body effect.
To first order take them constant.

### Large signal behaviour

The current in $M_{1}$ flows $V_{DD}\to V_{out}$, the
current in $M_{2}$ flows $V_{out}\to {\rm GND}$.  With no
d-c load current the (first order) d-c current in a device
that is on must go to zero.

$M_{1}$ on, $M_{2}$ off.
$M_{2}$ is off for
$$V_{SG2}=V_{out}-V_{in}<|V_{TP}|\;.$$
$M_{1}$ is a source follower.  With $I_{D1}\approx0$

$$V_{GS1}\approx V_{TN},\qquad 
V_{out}\approx V_{in}-V_{TN}(V_{out})\qquad {\rm upper\;branch}$$

$M_{1}$ supplies any load current that flows out of the
output node,
$V_{out}=V_{in}-V_{TN}-\sqrt{2I_{L}/\beta_{n1}}$ to second
order.  $M_{1}$ is in saturation for $V_{in}\lesssim V_{DD}$.

$M_{2}$ on, $M_{1}$ off.
$M_{1}$ is off for
$$V_{GS1}=V_{in}-V_{out}<V_{TN}\;.$$
$M_{2}$ is a $p$ source follower pulling the output down.
With $I_{D2}\approx0$

$$V_{SG2}\approx |V_{TP}|,\qquad 
V_{out}\approx V_{in}+|V_{TP}(V_{out})|\qquad{\rm lower\;branch}$$

$M_{2}$ sinks any load current that flows into the output
node. 

Both off.  Both are off for

$$V_{in}-V_{TN}\;<\;V_{out}\;<\;V_{in}+|V_{TP}|\;.$$

In that window no device drives the output.  With a
capacitive load $V_{out}$ simply stays where it was.
On a slow sweep the $V_{out}(V_{in})$ characteristic follows
the lower branch up, stays essentially constant over a
dead band of about

$$\Delta V\;\approx\;V_{TN}+|V_{TP}|$$

in $V_{in}-V_{out}$, and then follows the upper branch.
This is the familiar class-B cross-over distortion.
Body effect, $V_{TN}=V_{TN}(V_{out})$, 
$|V_{TP}|=|V_{TP}(V_{out})|$, widens the dead band and
makes the shift $V_{in}-V_{out}$ grow toward the rails.

In particular even with no load

$$\begin{aligned}
V_{in}=V_{DD}&:&V_{out,\max}&\approx V_{DD}-V_{TN,eff}<V_{DD}\\
V_{in}=0&:&V_{out,\min}&\approx |V_{TP,eff}|>0
\end{aligned}$$

no full rail-to-rail swing, no inversion, and no
$\gg1$ voltage gain to make a logic threshold.  It is
useless as a NOT gate.

### Small signal behaviour

Bias, say, on the upper branch, $M_{2}$ off.  It is the
ordinary source follower

$$ 
A_{v}=\frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}}=
\frac{g_{m1}}{g_{m1}+g_{mb1}+g_{ds1}+G_{L}}\;<\;1,
\qquad 
R_{out}\approx\frac{1}{\,g_{m1}+g_{mb1}+g_{ds1}\,}\;\Big\|\;R_{L},
\qquad R_{in}\approx\infty 
$$

with $g_{mb1}=0$ if the body is tied to the source.
On the lower branch the same formulas hold with
$M_{2}$ in place of $M_{1}$.  Close to the cross-over
both $g_{m}$'s can appear in parallel,
$A_{v}\approx (g_{m1}+g_{m2})/
(g_{m1}+g_{mb1}+g_{m2}+g_{mb2}+g_{ds1}+g_{ds2}+G_{L})$,
still $<1$.

The quiescent current with a common gate is essentially
zero - class B.  Supply current is drawn, by $M_{1}$ from
$V_{DD}$ on positive demand and by $M_{2}$ to ground on
negative demand, essentially only to supply the load.

In short: a non-inverting buffer of voltage gain
slightly less than unity, low output resistance, very
high input resistance, reduced output swing
$|V_{TP}|\lesssim V_{out}\lesssim V_{DD}-V_{TN}$, and a
$V_{TN}+|V_{TP}|$ dead zone about cross-over.  It is used
as a power output / load driving stage, with cross-over
distortion unless separately biased into class AB,
not as an inverter.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in the figure.

answer.text:
Both transistors are NMOS. The arrow is on the
source, at the bottom of both devices. $M_{1}$ is a source
follower, drain to $V_{DD}$, source to $V_{out}$, and $M_{2}$ is
a device from $V_{out}$ to ground whose gate is not a fixed
bias but the input itself. It is not a CMOS inverter, and it
is not inverting.

Let, to first order, $\lambda =\gamma =0$,
$\beta_i=\mu_nC_{ox}(W/L)_i$, a common $V_T$, and no d-c load
at the output, so that $I_{D1}=I_{D2}$.

### Large signal behaviour

For $V_{in}<V_T$ both devices are off in the square law model.
$V_{out}$ is then undefined - a capacitive output simply holds
its charge, in practice leaking slowly to $\approx 0$ through
$M_{2}$.

For $V_{in}>V_T$ both are on. $M_{1}$ can be on only for

$$
V_{GS1}=V_{in}-V_{out}>V_T\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad 
V_{out}<V_{in}-V_T .
$$

Hence for $M_{2}$

$$
V_{DS2}=V_{out}<V_{in}-V_T=V_{GS2}-V_T ,
$$

i.e. $M_{2}$ is in the triode region. The assumption that both
are saturated is self-contradictory. For $M_{1}$, with
$V_{in}\le V_{DD}$,

$$
V_{DS1}=V_{DD}-V_{out}\ge V_{GS1}-V_T
\iff V_{DD}\ge V_{in}-V_T ,
$$

so $M_{1}$ is in saturation. Thus: $M_{1}$ saturated source
follower, $M_{2}$ triode pull-down, in series. There is a
static $V_{DD}$-to-ground current for $V_{in}>V_T$.

Equating currents,
$$
\frac12\beta_1\big(V_{in}-V_{out}-V_T\big)^2
=
\beta_2\Big[(V_{in}-V_T)V_{out}-\frac{V_{out}^{2}}2\Big].
$$
Put $x=V_{in}-V_T$, $y=V_{out}$. The equation reduces to
$(\beta_1+\beta_2)(x-y)^2=\beta_2x^2$, whence

$$
\,V_{out}=(V_{in}-V_T)
\left[\,1-\sqrt{\frac{\beta_2}{\beta_1+\beta_2}}\,\right]\,,\qquad V_{in}>V_T .
$$

To first order the transfer curve is a straight line of slope
$<1$, offset by $V_T$. The common current and static power are

$$
I_D=\frac12\,\frac{\beta_1\beta_2}{\beta_1+\beta_2}\,(V_{in}-V_T)^2,
\qquad P\simeq V_{DD}I_D .
$$

In particular
$$
V_{out,max}\approx 
\left[1-\sqrt{\frac{\beta_2}{\beta_1+\beta_2}}\right](V_{DD}-V_T)<V_{DD}-V_T ,
$$
so the output is neither rail-to-rail nor able to reach
$V_{DD}$. In an integrated version $M_{1}$ has $V_{SB}=V_{out}$,
so its $V_T$ is raised by body effect and the result is
compressed and somewhat nonlinear; $M_{2}$ has $V_{SB}=0$.

### Small signal gain

The subtlety is that $M_{2}$ is in triode. Its incremental
parameters at the bias point are not the saturation values, but

$$
g_{m2}^{(tr)}=\left.\frac{\partial I_{D2}}{\partial V_{GS}}\right|_{V_{DS}}
=\beta_2V_{out},\qquad
g_{ds2}=\beta_2\big(V_{in}-V_T-V_{out}\big),
$$
while
$$
g_{m1}=\beta_1\big(V_{in}-V_{out}-V_T\big),\qquad 
g_{ds1}=\lambda_1 I_D .
$$

KCL at the output, including body effect of $M_{1}$ ($g_{mb1}$),
$$
g_{m1}(v_{in}-v_{out})-g_{mb1}v_{out}-g_{ds1}v_{out}
= g_{m2}^{(tr)}v_{in}+g_{ds2}v_{out},
$$
gives

$$
A_v=\frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}}
=\frac{\,g_{m1}-g_{m2}^{(tr)}\,}
       {\,g_{m1}+g_{mb1}+g_{ds1}+g_{ds2}\,}>0 .
$$

The $-g_{m2}^{(tr)}$ term is the physics of the circuit: a rise
in $V_{in}$ turns $M_{1}$ on harder, pushing $V_{out}$ up, but
simultaneously turns the triode pull-down $M_{2}$ on harder,
pulling $V_{out}$ down. The two actions partly cancel.

With $\lambda=\gamma=0$ this reduces to the slope of the
large-signal curve,

$$
A_v = 1-\sqrt{\frac{\beta_2}{\beta_1+\beta_2}}
     = 1-\frac{1}{\sqrt{1+\beta_1/\beta_2}}\;<\;1 .
$$

For $(W/L)_1=(W/L)_2$, $A_v=1-1/\sqrt2\approx0.29$. $A_v\to1$
only for $\beta_1\gg\beta_2$, and $A_v\to0$ for $\beta_1\ll\beta_2$.
Body effect and $\lambda$ lower it further.

The (low) resistance at the output, with $v_{in}=0$, is that of
a source follower in parallel with the triode resistance of
$M_2$,
$$
R_{out}=\frac{1}{g_{m1}+g_{mb1}+g_{ds1}+g_{ds2}},
$$
the input resistance is essentially the gate capacitance of
$M_1+M_2$, and the dominant pole with load $C_L$ is
$\approx (g_{m1}+g_{mb1}+g_{ds1}+g_{ds2})/C_L$.

In short, it is a non-inverting, gain-less-than-unity buffer:
a saturated source follower loaded by an input-controlled
triode NMOS. It suffers a $V_T$ drop, ratio-dependent gain,
static power dissipation for $V_{in}>V_T$, an undefined low
state, and is a poor substitute for either a CMOS inverter or
a properly biased source follower.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in the figure.

answer.text:
Both devices are NMOS. The body terminal of each is
tied to the lower terminal, i.e. to its source, so that
there is no body effect in the idealised schematic.

$$\begin{array}{lll}
M_{1}:& D=V_{DD},& G=V_{in},\qquad S=V_{out}\\
M_{2}:& D=V_{out},& G=V_{in},\qquad S=0
\end{array}\qquad 
\begin{aligned}
V_{GS1}&=V_{in}-V_{out}, & V_{DS1}&=V_{DD}-V_{out}\\
V_{GS2}&=V_{in}, & V_{DS2}&=V_{out}
\end{aligned}$$

It looks like a CMOS inverter, but the two transistors
turn on and turn off together.  Let $\beta_i=\mu_nC_{ox}(W/L)_i$
and $V_t$ be common, $\lambda=0$, and let the output be
unloaded except for a capacitance.  In dc

$$I_{D1}=I_{D2}\equiv I_D\tag{1}$$

### 1.  $V_{in}<V_t$: no dc output

Both transistors are off in the square law model,
$I_D=0$, and $V_{out}$ is a high impedance node.  A charge
previously stored on the load capacitance is simply held,
and in practice leaks away, essentially through the
subthreshold current of $M_2$ to ground.  There is no
actively driven state for low input.

### 2.  $V_{in}>V_t$: $M_1$ saturated, $M_2$ in triode

For $V_{in}\le V_{DD}$

$$V_{DS1}-(V_{GS1}-V_t)=V_{DD}-V_{in}+V_t>0$$

so $M_1$, when on, is saturated.
$M_2$ cannot be saturated in steady state: saturation
would require $V_{out}\ge V_{in}-V_t$, i.e. $V_{GS1}\le V_t$,
so $I_{D1}=0$.

Hence from (1)

$$ \frac{\beta_1}{2}\bigl(V_{in}-V_{out}-V_t\bigr)^2
      =\beta_2\Bigl[(V_{in}-V_t)V_{out}-\frac{V_{out}^{2}}{2}\Bigr]
      \qquad V_{in}>V_t \tag{2}$$

Put $u=V_{in}-V_t$, $v=V_{out}$.  (2) is
$\beta_1(u-v)^2=\beta_2\bigl[u^{2}-(u-v)^2\bigr]$, whence

$$\,u-v=u\sqrt{\frac{\beta_2}{\beta_1+\beta_2}}\,$$

$$\;V_{out}= 
\Biggl[1-\sqrt{\frac{\beta_2}{\beta_1+\beta_2}}\;\Biggr]
\bigl(V_{in}-V_t\bigr)\equiv c\,(V_{in}-V_t),\qquad 
0<c<1\; \tag{3}$$

i.e. the (ideal) transfer characteristic for $V_{in}>V_t$
is a straight line of slope $c<1$ starting at $(V_t,0)$.
$M_1$ is a source follower and $M_2$, in the triode region,
is a gate controlled non-linear resistor to ground; the
output is the ratioed division between them.  In small
signal form, $\lambda$ included,

$$ \frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}}=
\frac{g_{m1}-g_{m2}}{g_{m1}+g_{ds1}+g_{ds2}},\qquad
R_{out}\approx\frac1{g_{m1}+g_{ds1}+g_{ds2}} ,$$
which reduces to $c$ for $\lambda=0$.

For identical transistors $c=1-1/\sqrt2\approx0.29$.
E.g. $V_{DD}=V_{in}=5\,{\rm V}$, $V_t=1\,{\rm V}$ gives
$V_{out}\approx1.2\,{\rm V}$, neither a good ``1'' nor
a good ``0''.  In general the largest attainable output,
at $V_{in}=V_{DD}$, is only

$$V_{out,max}=c\,(V_{DD}-V_t)<V_{DD}-V_t .$$

Making $\beta_2\gg\beta_1$ makes $c$ small, $V_{out}$ lower
for high $V_{in}$, at the expense of ratioed operation;
making $\beta_1\gg\beta_2$ makes $c\to1$, $V_{out}\approx
V_{in}-V_t$, a poor source follower.

Whenever $V_{in}>V_t$ a dc current flows from $V_{DD}$
to ground,

$$I_D=\frac{\beta_1}{2}\bigl(V_{in}-V_{out}-V_t\bigr)^2
     =\frac{\beta_1}{2}(V_{in}-V_t)^2\,
       \frac{\beta_2}{\beta_1+\beta_2},\qquad 
P_{stat}=V_{DD}I_D\neq0,$$

even with no load.  Transitorily, if $V_{out}$ starts
above the value (3), $M_1$ is off and $M_2$ discharges
$C_L$ until (3) is reached; if it starts below, $M_1$
charges $C_L$ up to (3).

### Conclusion

The circuit is not an inverter at all.  It is
non-inverting, with voltage gain $c<1$, no rail-to-rail
swing, a floating output for $V_{in}<V_t$, a level that
depends on $\beta_1/\beta_2$, and static power
dissipation for $V_{in}>V_t$.  It is merely an NMOS
source follower $M_1$ loaded by a triode NMOS $M_2$
whose gate is tied, unfortunately, to the same input.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in the figure.

answer.text:
The upper device is a pMOS with its bulk tied to its
source, $V_{DD}$, and the lower device is an nMOS with its
bulk tied to its source, ground. There is no body effect.
$M_{1}$ is the driver, $M_{2}$ is connected gate-to-drain,
i.e. as a diode, between $V_{DD}$ and the output. In the
d-c steady state, with no d-c load,

$$ I_{D1}=I_{D2}\equiv I_D $$

Let
$$ \beta_1=\mu_nC_{ox}\Bigl({W\over L}\Bigr)_1 ,\qquad 
   \beta_2=\mu_pC_{ox}\Bigl({W\over L}\Bigr)_2 $$
and neglect $\lambda$ at first.

For $M_{2}$

$$ V_{SG2}=V_{DD}-V_{G2}=V_{DD}-V_{out}=V_{SD2} .$$

Hence, when it is on,
$V_{SD2}=V_{SG2}>V_{SG2}-|V_{TP}|$; a gate-drain connected
device is always in saturation (or off). Its current is

$$ I_D={\beta_2\over 2}
        \bigl(V_{DD}-V_{out}-|V_{TP}|\bigr)^{2}\qquad M_{2}\;{\rm sat} \tag{1}$$

For $M_1$, $V_{GS1}=V_{in}$, $V_{DS1}=V_{out}$.

### Voltage transfer characteristic

1. $V_{in}<V_{TN}$ : $M_1$ off. 

$I_D=0$. $M_2$ charges the output capacitance up until it
itself turns off, $V_{SG2}=|V_{TP}|$, i.e.

$$ V_{out,max}=V_{DD}-|V_{TP}| $$

The high output level is degraded by a pMOS threshold.

2. $V_{in}>V_{TN}$, $M_1$ saturated.

$$ I_D={\beta_1\over 2}\bigl(V_{in}-V_{TN}\bigr)^{2}
     ={\beta_2\over 2}\bigl(V_{DD}-V_{out}-|V_{TP}|\bigr)^{2} \tag{2}$$

whence, with 
$$ S\equiv\sqrt{\beta_1\over \beta_2}
      =\sqrt{\,{\mu_n (W/L)_1\over \mu_p (W/L)_2}} $$

$$\,V_{out}=V_{DD}-|V_{TP}|-S\,\bigl(V_{in}-V_{TN}\bigr)\, \tag{3}$$

a straight line of slope $-S$. This is the useful
amplifying region. $M_1$ saturation, $V_{out}\ge V_{in}-V_{TN}$,
requires

$$ V_{in}\le V_{TN}+
      {V_{DD}-|V_{TP}|-V_{TN}\over 1+S}\; . $$

The ``switching'' voltage $V_{in}=V_{out}=V_M$ from (3) is

$$ V_M={V_{DD}-|V_{TP}|+S V_{TN}\over 1+S} $$

tending to $V_{TN}$ for $S\gg1$ and to $V_{DD}-|V_{TP}|$ for
$S\ll1$. It is a ratioed circuit.

3. Large $V_{in}$ : $M_1$ in triode, $M_2$ still saturated.

$$ \beta_1\Bigl[(V_{in}-V_{TN})V_{out}-{V_{out}^{2}\over2}\Bigr]
   ={\beta_2\over2}\bigl(V_{DD}-V_{out}-|V_{TP}|\bigr)^{2} \tag{4}$$

$V_{out}$ falls slowly toward a non-zero $V_{OL}$. For
$V_{in}=V_{DD}$, $V_{OL}\ll V_{DD}$,

$$V_{OL}\approx 
{\beta_2\over2\beta_1}\,
{(V_{DD}-|V_{TP}|)^{2}\over V_{DD}-V_{TN}}\; ,$$

small only for $\beta_1\gg\beta_2$. There is static current,
$P\approx V_{DD}I_D$, whenever $V_{in}>V_{TN}$. 

Thus as a logic gate it is an inverter with reduced swing
$V_{OL}$ to $V_{DD}-|V_{TP}|$, static power dissipation and
levels set by the $\beta_1/\beta_2$ ratio - much inferior to a
complementary CMOS inverter. It needs $V_{DD}>V_{TN}+|V_{TP}|$
to operate at all.

### Small signal behaviour

Bias in region 2. At the output node, $M_2$ with
$v_g=v_d=v_{out}$, $v_s=0$ a-c, presents the diode impedance,
with $\lambda$ restored,

$$ R_{2}={1\over g_{m2}+g_{ds2}}\approx{1\over g_{m2}}\qquad 
\bigl(g_{mb2}=0\bigr) $$

in parallel with $r_{o1}$ of $M_1$. Hence

$$ R_{out}=r_{o1}\;\Big\|\;{1\over g_{m2}+g_{ds2}}
        \approx {1\over g_{m2}} $$

and from KCL at the output, $g_{m1}v_{in}+(g_{m2}+g_{ds1}+
g_{ds2})v_{out}=0$,

$$ A_v\equiv{v_{out}\over v_{in}}
     =-\,{g_{m1}\over g_{m2}+g_{ds1}+g_{ds2}}
     =-g_{m1}\bigl(r_{o1}\|r_{o2}\|1/g_{m2}\bigr)
     \;\approx\;-\,{g_{m1}\over g_{m2}}  $$

Since the same $I_D$ flows in the two devices,
$g_m=\sqrt{\beta I_D}$ (up to constants), so to first order

$$ |A_v|\approx\sqrt{\beta_1\over\beta_2}
   =\sqrt{{\mu_n (W/L)_1\over \mu_p (W/L)_2}}\;, $$

set by geometry, essentially independent of bias current
and of $V_{DD}$. The input resistance is (ideally) infinite.

Large $|A_v|$ demands $(W/L)_1\gg (W/L)_2$; e.g. $|A_v|=10$
needs a $\beta$ ratio of $100$, $\mu_n/\mu_p\approx2$--$3$
notwithstanding. Gains of a few to $\sim10$ are typical.
The dominant pole at the output is
$\omega_p\approx (g_{m2})/C_{L,tot}$, i.e. the low diode
resistance gives a comparatively wide bandwidth for the
gain obtained, at the expense of limited output swing:
$V_{out}$ cannot exceed $V_{DD}-|V_{TP}|$ and cannot fall
below the $M_1$ saturation edge $V_{in}-V_{TN}$ in linear
operation. In short, a common-source nMOS stage with a
diode-connected pMOS active load, usable as a low-gain,
geometry-controlled amplifier stage.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in the figure.

answer.text:
The circuit is a common-source stage $M_{1}$ with a
diode-connected pMOS active load $M_{2}$.

$M_{1}$ is nMOS, source and body to ground, gate $=V_{in}$,
drain $=V_{out}$. $M_{2}$ is pMOS, source and body to $V_{DD}$,
drain $=V_{out}$, and gate tied to its own drain. Hence

$$V_{BS1}=V_{BS2}=0$$

so there is no body effect in either device. No dc gate
current flows, so, with no external dc load,

$$I_{D1}=I_{D2}\equiv I_D $$

and $R_{in}=\infty$ at low frequencies.

### The load device

For $M_{2}$, gate $=$ drain, so

$$V_{SD2}=V_{DD}-V_{out}=V_{SG2}$$

The saturation condition for a pMOS,
$V_{SD}\ge V_{SG}-|V_{tp}|$, is therefore always satisfied
when $M_{2}$ is on. A gate-drain tied transistor is always
in saturation, and acts as a non-linear resistor whose
small-signal resistance, looking into its drain with its
source at ac ground, is

$$ R_{2}= \frac{1}{g_{m2}+g_{mb2}+g_{ds2}}
      =\frac{1}{g_{m2}+g_{ds2}}\approx\frac1{g_{m2}} $$

since $g_{mb2}=0$. Looking into the output node, $M_{2}$
conducts more when $V_{out}$ falls and less when $V_{out}$
rises: it is local shunt feedback at the output.

### DC transfer characteristic

Neglect $\lambda$ for the large-signal characteristic,
$\beta_n=\mu_nC_{ox}(W/L)_1$, $\beta_p=\mu_pC_{ox}(W/L)_2$.

$M_2$ in saturation:
$$ I_D=\frac{\beta_p}{2}\,
\bigl(V_{DD}-V_{out}-|V_{tp}|\bigr)^{2}\qquad 
V_{out}<V_{DD}-|V_{tp}|  \tag{1}$$

1. $V_{in}<V_{tn}$: $M_1$ off, $I_D\approx0$.  $M_2$ charges
$V_{out}$ up until it turns off,
$$V_{out,max}\approx V_{DD}-|V_{tp}|$$
not $V_{DD}$. The output is not rail-to-rail.

2. $M_1$ and $M_2$ in saturation: $V_{out}\ge V_{in}-V_{tn}$,
$$ \frac{\beta_n}{2}(V_{in}-V_{tn})^{2}
   =\frac{\beta_p}{2}\bigl(V_{DD}-V_{out}-|V_{tp}|\bigr)^{2} $$
i.e.
$$\,V_{out}=V_{DD}-|V_{tp}|
      -\sqrt{\frac{\beta_n}{\beta_p}}\;(V_{in}-V_{tn})\,  \tag{2}$$
Remarkably, in ideal square law the $V_{out}$-$V_{in}$
characteristic is *linear* in this region, although $I_D$
is quadratic in $V_{in}$.

3. Large $V_{in}$: $V_{out}$ falls to $V_{in}-V_{tn}$ and
$M_1$ enters the triode region, $M_2$ remaining saturated:
$$ \beta_n\!\left[(V_{in}-V_{tn})V_{out}-\tfrac12V_{out}^{2}\right]
 =\frac{\beta_p}{2}\bigl(V_{DD}-V_{out}-|V_{tp}|\bigr)^{2} $$
$V_{out}$ bends over toward $0$, never quite reaching it
for finite $V_{in}$, and $|dV_{out}/dV_{in}|$ collapses.
Used as a logic inverter it therefore has poor noise
margins and dissipates static power for $V_{out}$ low.

For amplifier use, $V_{in}$ is biased at a $Q$-point in
region 2.

### Small-signal gain and output resistance

Small signal, $M_1$ is a $g_{m1}v_{in}$ source in parallel
with $r_{o1}$ from $V_{out}$ to ground; $M_2$ is
$1/g_{m2}\parallel r_{o2}$ from $V_{out}$ to $V_{DD}$ (ac ground).
Hence

$$ R_{out}=r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2}\parallel\frac1{g_{m2}}
        \approx \frac1{g_{m2}}\quad\text{usually} $$

$$ A_v=\frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}}=
 -\,g_{m1}R_{out}
 =-\,\frac{g_{m1}}{\,g_{m2}+g_{ds1}+g_{ds2}\,}
 \;\xrightarrow[\lambda\to0]{}\;-\frac{g_{m1}}{g_{m2}} $$

Since $M_1$ and $M_2$ carry the same bias current, in
square law

$$ A_v\approx -\sqrt{\frac{\mu_n (W/L)_1}{\mu_p (W/L)_2}}
      =-\frac{V_{ov2}}{V_{ov1}}  $$

The gain is set essentially by a device-geometry ratio,
is to first order independent of $I_D$ and $V_{DD}$, and
is modest in practice — obtaining $|A_v|>10$ requires a
very large $(W/L)_1/(W/L)_2$, especially as $\mu_n\approx
2\!-\!3\,\mu_p$. $\lambda\neq0$ makes $|A_v|$ somewhat
smaller and bias dependent.

### Consequences

* **Bandwidth:** $R_{out}\approx1/g_{m2}$ is low, so the
output pole $1/(R_{out}C_{L,eff})$ is high; gain is traded
for bandwidth, with $GBW\approx g_{m1}/2\pi C_L$.
$C_{L,eff}$ includes $C_{db1},C_{db2},C_{gs2}$ and the next stage.
* **Linearity:** good in saturation, by (2), apart from
$\lambda$, mobility degradation and the triode knee.
* **Swing:** limited above by $V_{DD}-|V_{tp}|$ and below
by $M_1$ entering triode, $V_{out}\gtrsim V_{in}-V_{tn}$.
* **PSRR:** poor. With $I_D$ fixed by $M_1$, $V_{SG2}$ is
fixed, so $V_{out}\approx V_{DD}-V_{SG2}$ follows $V_{DD}$
almost 1:1.
* **Power:** $P=V_{DD}I_{DQ}$ at the bias point,
$I_{DQ}=\tfrac{\beta_n}{2}(V_{inQ}-V_{tn})^2$; zero
(ideal) when $M_1$ is off.

In short: a low-to-moderate gain, wideband, fairly linear
integrated gain stage that needs no resistor, at the price
of limited output swing, limited gain, static power and
poor supply rejection.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in the figure.

answer.text:
$M_{1}$ is the n-channel driver and $M_{2}$ is the p-channel
load.  The body of $M_{1}$ is its source, the body of $M_{2}$ is
its source, so there is no body effect. The gate of $M_{2}$ is
tied to its drain,

$$ V_{G2}=V_{D2}=V_{out}\qquad V_{S2}=V_{DD}$$

i.e. $M_{2}$ is a diode connected p-device between $V_{DD}$ and the
output.  $M_{1}$ is a common source device. With no d-c load at
the output

$$I_{D1}=I_{D2}=I_D $$

$\beta_{n,p}=\mu_{n,p}C_{ox}(W/L)_{1,2}$.

For the p-device
$$V_{SG2}=V_{DD}-V_{out}=V_{SD2}$$
hence, when it is on,
$$V_{SD2}=V_{SG2}>V_{SG2}-|V_{TP}|$$
$M_{2}$ is always in saturation when it conducts. Its current,
$\lambda$ neglected for the moment, is

$$ I_{D2}= \frac{\beta_p}{2}\,
\bigl(V_{DD}-V_{out}-|V_{TP}|\bigr)^{2}\qquad 
V_{DD}-V_{out}>|V_{TP}| $$

For $M_{1}$

$$ I_{D1}= \frac{\beta_n}{2}\,(V_{in}-V_{TN})^{2} \quad{\rm sat.}$$
$$ I_{D1}= \beta_n\Bigl[(V_{in}-V_{TN})V_{out}-\tfrac12V_{out}^{2}\Bigr]
\quad{\rm triode.}$$

### Voltage transfer characteristic

1. $V_{in}<V_{TN}$: $M_{1}$ off. $I_D=0$. $M_{2}$ conducts only
until $V_{SG2}=|V_{TP}|$.  In the square law model

$$ V_{OH}=V_{DD}-|V_{TP}| $$

The output cannot pull all the way to $V_{DD}$. The node is
in fact floating at this level.

2. $V_{in}$ just above $V_{TN}$: $M_{1}$ and $M_{2}$ in saturation.
$I_{D1}=I_{D2}$ gives

$$ \beta_n (V_{in}-V_{TN})^{2}
      =\beta_p\bigl(V_{DD}-V_{out}-|V_{TP}|\bigr)^{2} $$

$$\,V_{out}=V_{DD}-|V_{TP}|
      -\sqrt{\frac{\beta_n}{\beta_p}}\;(V_{in}-V_{TN})\,  $$

The square law of $M_{1}$ is cancelled by the square law of the
diode load: the $V_{out}-V_{in}$ characteristic is, to first
order, a straight line. 

$M_{1}$ stays in saturation for $V_{out}\ge V_{in}-V_{TN}$.
The end of the saturated region is at

$$ V_{in}-V_{TN}= \frac{V_{DD}-|V_{TP}|}
{1+\sqrt{\beta_n/\beta_p}},\qquad
V_{out}= \frac{V_{DD}-|V_{TP}|}
{1+\sqrt{\beta_n/\beta_p}} .$$

3. Larger $V_{in}$: $M_{1}$ in the triode region, $M_{2}$ still
saturated,

$$ \beta_n\Bigl[(V_{in}-V_{TN})V_{out}-\tfrac12V_{out}^{2}\Bigr]
 =\frac{\beta_p}{2}\bigl(V_{DD}-V_{out}-|V_{TP}|\bigr)^{2} $$

$V_{out}$ falls slowly toward a non-zero $V_{OL}$, for
$V_{in}=V_{DD}$ approximately

$$ V_{OL}\approx 
\frac{\beta_p\,(V_{DD}-|V_{TP}|)^{2}}
     {2\beta_n\,(V_{DD}-V_{TN})}\ll V_{DD}\;\;{\rm if}\;\;
\beta_n\gg\beta_p . $$

It is ratioed logic: $V_{OL}$, the switching point and the gain
depend on $\beta_n/\beta_p$. The logic switching voltage,
$V_{in}=V_{out}=V_M$, from (2),

$$ V_M=
\frac{\,V_{DD}-|V_{TP}|+\sqrt{\beta_n/\beta_p}\;V_{TN}\,}
     {\,1+\sqrt{\beta_n/\beta_p}\,} .$$

With $V_{in}$ high there is a direct d-c current
$I_D\approx \tfrac{\beta_p}{2}(V_{DD}-|V_{TP}|)^{2}$ from
$V_{DD}$ to ground: static power dissipation in the low state.
In the high state, ideally, there is none.

### Small signal behaviour in saturation

For $M_{2}$, $v_{sg2}=-v_{out}$.  A diode connected MOS is, to
small signals, a resistance $1/g_{m2}$ in parallel with $r_{o2}$
to a-c ground.  Hence at the output node

$$ R_{out}= r_{o1}\;\Big\|\;r_{o2}\;\Big\|\;\frac1{g_{m2}}
        =\frac{1}{g_{m2}+g_{ds1}+g_{ds2}}
        \approx \frac1{g_{m2}} $$

and

$$\,A_v=\frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}}=-g_{m1}R_{out}
      =-\,\frac{g_{m1}}{g_{m2}+g_{ds1}+g_{ds2}}\, $$

With $\lambda=0$, at the same bias current
$g_m=\sqrt{2\beta I_D}$,

$$ A_v\approx -\frac{g_{m1}}{g_{m2}}
      =-\sqrt{\frac{\beta_n}{\beta_p}}
      =-\sqrt{\,
        \frac{\mu_n (W/L)_1}{\mu_p (W/L)_2}}\; $$

in agreement with $dV_{out}/dV_{in}$ from the large signal
expression.  With $\lambda\ne0$ $|A_v|$ is slightly smaller and
the transfer curve is slightly bent.

The gain is to first order independent of $I_D$ and of $V_{DD}$,
set only by the device ratio. To get $|A_v|>1$, let alone
$5$--$10$, $\beta_n\gg\beta_p$ is required. $R_{out}\approx
1/g_{m2}$ is low, so the output pole $ \approx
(g_{m2}+g_{ds1}+g_{ds2})/C_L$ is high: low gain but wide
bandwidth and good capability to drive a capacitive load on
the pull-down. Pull up is weak and becomes progressively
weaker as $V_{out}\to V_{DD}-|V_{TP}|$.

In short: a common-source nMOS with a diode-connected pMOS
load, usable as a low-gain, fairly linear amplifier, or as a
ratioed inverter with $V_{OH}=V_{DD}-|V_{TP}|$, non-zero
$V_{OL}$, static power in the low state, and gain,
swing and noise margins fixed by $(W/L)_1/(W/L)_2$.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in the figure.

answer.text:
Both devices are $p$-channel. The arrow is the
source terminal, shorted to the $n$-body.
For $M_{2}$ the source is tied to $V_{DD}$, for $M_{1}$ the
source is tied to the output node. Hence there is no body
effect in either device. Put $|V_{tp}|=V_{t}>0$,
$\beta_i=\mu_pC_{ox}(W/L)_i$.

$$\begin{aligned}
M_{2}:&\qquad V_{SG2}=V_{DD}-V_{in}, &&V_{SD2}=V_{DD}-V_{out}\\
M_{1}:&\qquad V_{SG1}=V_{out}-0=V_{out}, &&V_{SD1}=V_{out}-0=V_{out}
\end{aligned}$$

$M_{2}$ is a common source $p$-device with source at a.c.
ground. $M_{1}$ has gate and drain both at ground: it is a
diode connected $p$-device between $V_{out}$ and ground,
source at $V_{out}$, gate-drain at ground. It is the load.

For $M_{1}$, when it is on,
$$
V_{SD1}=V_{SG1}>V_{SG1}-V_{t}
$$
so $M_{1}$ is always in saturation, or off.  Neglecting
$\lambda$ for the d.c. characteristic,

$$
I_{1}= \begin{cases}
0 & V_{out}\le V_{t}\\[2pt]
\dfrac{\beta_{1}}{2}\,(V_{out}-V_{t})^{2} & V_{out}>V_{t}\quad{\rm sat.}
\end{cases}
$$

i.e. a non linear load whose current grows as
$(V_{out}-V_{t})^{2}$. $M_{2}$ may be off, saturated or linear,
with $I_{2}=I_{1}\equiv I$ in the series branch.

### Voltage transfer characteristic

$V_{in}=V_{DD}$: $M_{2}$ is off, $I=0$, hence $I_{1}=0$ and

$$
V_{out}\approx V_{t}\qquad V_{in}>V_{DD}-V_{t}.
$$

The output can never be pulled to ground. Below $V_{t}$,
$M_{1}$ turns off and in the ideal model the node is floating.
In practice subthreshold leakage settles it near $V_{t}$.
This is the ``low'' output level.

For $V_{in}<V_{DD}-V_{t}$, $M_{2}$ first saturates,
$V_{DD}-V_{out}>V_{DD}-V_{in}-V_{t}$. With $I_{1}=I_{2}$,

$$
\frac{\beta_{1}}{2}(V_{out}-V_{t})^{2}
   =\frac{\beta_{2}}{2}(V_{DD}-V_{in}-V_{t})^{2}
$$

$$
\,V_{out}=V_{t}+\sqrt{\frac{\beta_{2}}{\beta_{1}}}\,
\bigl(V_{DD}-V_{t}-V_{in}\bigr)\,
\qquad\text{both saturated}
$$

an inverting, essentially linear, characteristic of slope
$-\sqrt{\beta_{2}/\beta_{1}}$.

$M_{2}$ enters the triode region when
$V_{SD2}=V_{SG2}-V_{t}$, i.e. $V_{out}=V_{in}+V_{t}$, at

$$
V_{in,tr}= \frac{\sqrt{\beta_{2}/\beta_{1}}}{1+\sqrt{\beta_{2}/\beta_{1}}}
\,(V_{DD}-V_{t}) .
$$

For $V_{in}<V_{in,tr}$, $M_{2}$ is linear, $M_{1}$ saturated,

$$
\frac{\beta_{1}}{2}(V_{out}-V_{t})^{2}
 =\beta_{2}\Bigl[(V_{DD}-V_{in}-V_{t})(V_{DD}-V_{out})
      -\frac{(V_{DD}-V_{out})^{2}}{2}\Bigr],
$$

and $V_{out}$ bends over toward a maximum $V_{OH}<V_{DD}$,
obtained at e.g. $V_{in}=0$. With $x=V_{DD}-V_{OH}$ small,
$x\approx \dfrac{\beta_{1}}{2\beta_{2}}(V_{DD}-V_{t})$.
The output can never quite reach $V_{DD}$, because at
$V_{out}=V_{DD}$ $M_{1}$ would demand a large current which
$M_{2}$ in triode with $V_{SD2}\to0$ cannot supply.

The switching voltage $V_{in}=V_{out}=V_{M}$, in saturation,
is
$$
V_{M}= \frac{\sqrt{\beta_{2}}\,V_{DD}+(\sqrt{\beta_{1}}-\sqrt{\beta_{2}})V_{t}}
{\sqrt{\beta_{1}}+\sqrt{\beta_{2}}},\qquad 
V_{M}=V_{DD}/2\;\;{\rm if}\;\;\beta_{1}=\beta_{2}.
$$
It is a ratioed characteristic: levels and $V_{M}$ depend
on $\beta_{2}/\beta_{1}$, unlike a CMOS inverter.

Except at $V_{in}\approx V_{DD}$ there is a direct d.c. path
$V_{DD}\to M_{2}\to M_{1}\to{\rm GND}$ and a static current
$I$ above, $P_{stat}\approx V_{DD}I$, largest for $V_{in}$ low.

### Small signal behaviour

Bias in the both-saturated region. $M_{1}$, diode connected
with gate-drain at a.c. ground and body to source, presents
at its source

$$
R_{1}= \frac{1}{g_{m1}+g_{mb1}+g_{ds1}}=\frac{1}{g_{m1}+g_{ds1}}\approx\frac1{g_{m1}} .
$$

Hence at the output

$$
R_{out}= r_{o2}\Big\|\frac{1}{g_{m1}+g_{ds1}}\approx\frac1{g_{m1}},
\qquad 
A_{v}= \frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}} = -g_{m2}R_{out}
      =-\,\frac{g_{m2}}{g_{m1}+g_{ds1}+g_{ds2}} .
$$

For $g_mr_o\gg1$, with the same current in the two devices,

$$
A_{v}\approx -\frac{g_{m2}}{g_{m1}}
      =-\sqrt{\frac{(W/L)_{2}}{(W/L)_{1}}}\;,
$$

in particular $|A_{v}|\approx1$ for equal devices. In the
triode region for $M_{2}$, $|A_{v}|$ is even smaller.
Input resistance is that of a gate, essentially infinite.

In short it is a $p$-channel common-source stage with a
saturated diode-connected $p$-load to ground, i.e. a ratioed
$p$MOS inverter. It inverts, but with

* incomplete swing, $V_{t}\lesssim V_{out}\lesssim V_{DD}$,
  never $0$ or $V_{DD}$;
* static power dissipation in essentially every state except
  $V_{in}=V_{DD}$;
* low, size-ratio determined gain $\approx
  -\sqrt{(W/L)_{2}/(W/L)_{1}}$, and considerable non-linearity
  outside the both-saturated window;
* slow, incomplete discharge of a capacitive load: $M_{1}$
  current $\propto (V_{out}-V_{t})^{2}$ vanishes at $V_{out}=V_{t}$.

Large gain requires $(W/L)_{2}\gg (W/L)_{1}$, at the expense
of swing, bias range and static current. It is therefore a
poor logic gate and a low-gain, limited-swing amplifier.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in the figure.

answer.text:
Both transistors have their body terminal tied to the
terminal with the arrow, i.e. to their source, and the arrow
points from source to body. Both are PMOS.

* $M_{2}$ : source to $V_{DD}$, drain to $V_{out}$, gate $=V_{in}$
* $M_{1}$ : source to $V_{out}$, drain to ground, gate to ground

Hence for both devices $V_{SB}=0$; there is no body effect and
$|V_{Tp}|$ is constant. $M_{1}$ has gate tied to drain, both at
ground. It is a diode connected PMOS load. The stage is the
PMOS analogue of a saturated-load inverter: an inverting
common-source $M_{2}$ with a diode connected load $M_{1}$.
It is a ratioed, not a complementary, stage.

Let currents be taken as magnitudes, $\beta_i=\mu_pC_{ox}(W/L)_i$,
$\lambda =0$ for the moment, no d.c. load at the output, so
$I_{D1}=I_{D2}$.

For $M_{1}$
$$
V_{SG1}=V_{out},\qquad V_{SD1}=V_{out}
$$
so $M_{1}$ is on only for $V_{out}>|V_{Tp}|$, and
$$
V_{SD1}=V_{SG1}>V_{SG1}-|V_{Tp}|
$$
i.e. a diode connected $M_{1}$ is always in saturation when on:
$$
 I_{D1}= \frac{\beta_1}{2}\bigl(V_{out}-|V_{Tp}|\bigr)^{2}\tag{1}
$$
For $M_{2}$
$$
V_{SG2}=V_{DD}-V_{in},\qquad V_{SD2}=V_{DD}-V_{out} \tag{2}
$$
on for $V_{in}<V_{DD}-|V_{Tp}|$, saturated for
$V_{SD2}\ge V_{SG2}-|V_{Tp}|$, i.e. for $V_{out}\le V_{in}+|V_{Tp}|$.

### D.C. transfer characteristic

1. $V_{in}>V_{DD}-|V_{Tp}|$ : $M_{2}$ off.

$I_D=0$, hence from (1) $M_{1}$ can only discharge an output
capacitance down to
$$
V_{out}\;\approx\;|V_{Tp}|
$$
and then it cuts off. The low level is not $0$.

2. $M_{2}$ and $M_{1}$ saturated.
From (1) and $I_{D2}= \tfrac{\beta_2}{2}(V_{DD}-V_{in}-|V_{Tp}|)^2$,
$I_{D1}=I_{D2}$ gives
$$
\,V_{out}=|V_{Tp}|+
\sqrt{\frac{\beta_2}{\beta_1}}\,
\bigl(V_{DD}-|V_{Tp}|-V_{in}\bigr)\, \tag{3}
$$
a straight line of slope $-\sqrt{\beta_2/\beta_1}$.
It is valid for $V_{out}\le V_{in}+|V_{Tp}|$, i.e. down to
$$
V_{in,tr}= \frac{V_{DD}-|V_{Tp}|}{1+\sqrt{\beta_1/\beta_2}}\; .
$$

3. $V_{in}<V_{in,tr}$ : $M_{2}$ in triode, $M_{1}$ saturated.
$$
\beta_2\!\left[(V_{DD}-V_{in}-|V_{Tp}|)(V_{DD}-V_{out})
-\tfrac12(V_{DD}-V_{out})^{2}\right]
=\frac{\beta_1}{2}\bigl(V_{out}-|V_{Tp}|\bigr)^{2} \tag{4}
$$
$V_{out}$ bends over toward $V_{DD}$.  At $V_{in}=0$
$V_{OH}<V_{DD}$ is given by (4); for $\beta_2\gg\beta_1$
$$
V_{OH}\approx V_{DD}-\frac{\beta_1}{2\beta_2}\,(V_{DD}-|V_{Tp}|).
$$

In words, $V_{out}$ is $\approx |V_{Tp}|$ for large $V_{in}$, rises
with slope $-\sqrt{\beta_2/\beta_1}$ in the middle, and flattens
at $V_{OH}<V_{DD}$ for small $V_{in}$. It inverts, but with
severely reduced swing, $|V_{Tp}|$ to $V_{OH}$.

### Small signal behaviour, region 2

$M_{1}$ with gate a.c. ground and $v_{s}=v_{out}$ presents at
the output
$$
R_{1}= \frac{v_{out}}{i_{out}}=
\frac{1}{g_{m1}+g_{ds1}}\approx\frac1{g_{m1}}\qquad (g_{mb1}=0).
$$
Hence, with $\lambda\ne0$,
$$
 A_v=\frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}}
      =-g_{m2}\Bigl(r_{o2}\parallel r_{o1}\parallel\frac1{g_{m1}}\Bigr)
      =-\,\frac{g_{m2}}{\,g_{m1}+g_{ds1}+g_{ds2}\,}
      \;\approx\;-\frac{g_{m2}}{g_{m1}}
      =-\sqrt{\frac{\beta_2}{\beta_1}}
      =-\sqrt{\frac{(W/L)_2}{(W/L)_1}}\;,
$$
$$
R_{out}\approx r_{o2}\parallel \frac1{g_{m1}}\approx\frac1{g_{m1}} .
$$
The gain is set only by the size ratio. A gain of even
$3$--$5$ requires a very large $(W/L)_2/(W/L)_1$. In the
triode region $|A_v|$ falls to zero.

### As a logic gate

* $V_{OL}\approx |V_{Tp}|\ne0$, $V_{OH}<V_{DD}$: poor noise margins.
* For $V_{in}$ low, output high, both devices are on and a
static current
$I\approx \tfrac{\beta_1}{2}(V_{OH}-|V_{Tp}|)^2$ flows from
$V_{DD}$ to ground: static power $V_{DD}I$. For $V_{in}$ high
the current is ideally zero.
* Pull-up is by $M_{2}$ fighting the on $M_{1}$; pull-down is
by $M_{1}$ alone, and it stops at $|V_{Tp}|$.

Small $\beta_1$ improves $V_{OH}$, gain and static power, but
slows the discharge and makes $R_{out}\approx1/g_{m1}$ large.
In short, a low-gain inverting amplifier / ratioed PMOS
inverter with diode-connected saturated load, limited swing,
static dissipation in one state, and gain $\approx
-\sqrt{(W/L)_2/(W/L)_1}$.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in the figure.

answer.text:
Both devices are PMOS, with the body tied to the
source, so that there is no body effect in either device.
$M_{2}$ is the input device and $M_{1}$ is the load.
For $M_{1}$ the gate is tied to the drain, both at ground:
it is a diode connected PMOS between $V_{out}$ and ground.

Let, in magnitude,
$$ \beta_i=\mu_pC_{ox}\left({W\over L}\right)_i\qquad 
|V_{TP}|>0\qquad S=\sqrt{\beta_2\over \beta_1}\; .$$
The same d-c current $I_D$ flows in $M_1$ and $M_2$ from
$V_{DD}$ to ground.

### Large signal behaviour

For $M_{1}$
$$ V_{SG1}=V_{SD1}=V_{out} $$
so that, whenever it is on,
$$ V_{SD1}=V_{SG1}\ge V_{SG1}-|V_{TP}| $$
i.e. the diode connected load is always in saturation,
$$ I_{D}= {\beta_1\over 2}\,
\bigl(V_{out}-|V_{TP}|\bigr)^{2}\qquad V_{out}>|V_{TP}| \tag{1}$$
neglecting $\lambda$ for the moment.  For $M_{2}$
$$ V_{SG2}=V_{DD}-V_{in},\qquad V_{SD2}=V_{DD}-V_{out} $$
$$ I_D={\beta_2\over 2}
\bigl(V_{DD}-V_{in}-|V_{TP}|\bigr)^{2}\quad{\rm in\; saturation} \tag{2}$$
$M_{2}$ is in saturation for
$$V_{SD2}\ge V_{SG2}-|V_{TP}|\iff V_{out}\le V_{in}+|V_{TP}| .$$

$M_{2}$ off:  $V_{in}\ge V_{DD}-|V_{TP}|$.  Then $I_D=0$ and
from (1) 
$$ V_{out}\;\to\;|V_{TP}| \equiv V_{OL} $$
in the ideal square law model.  The output cannot be pulled
to ground.

$M_{1},M_{2}$ saturated: equating (1) and (2),
$$ \sqrt{\beta_{2}}\,
\bigl(V_{DD}-V_{in}-|V_{TP}|\bigr)=
\sqrt{\beta_{1}}\,
\bigl(V_{out}-|V_{TP}|\bigr) $$
i.e.
$$\,V_{out}=|V_{TP}|+S\,
\bigl(V_{DD}-|V_{TP}|-V_{in}\bigr)\,,\qquad 
S=\sqrt{\frac{(W/L)_{2}}{(W/L)_{1}} }  \tag{3}$$
a straight line of slope $-S$.  This holds for 
$V_{in}\le V_{DD}-|V_{TP}|$ and $V_{out}\le V_{in}+|V_{TP}|$,
i.e. down to
$$ V_{in,b}={S\over 1+S}\bigl(V_{DD}-|V_{TP}|\bigr),\qquad
   V_{out,b}=|V_{TP}|+{S\over 1+S}\bigl(V_{DD}-|V_{TP}|\bigr). $$

$M_{2}$ in triode, $M_{1}$ saturated, for $V_{in}$ still lower:
$$ \beta_{2}\!\left[(V_{DD}-V_{in}-|V_{TP}|)(V_{DD}-V_{out})
-{(V_{DD}-V_{out})^{2}\over2}\right]
={\beta_{1}\over2}\bigl(V_{out}-|V_{TP}|\bigr)^{2} $$
$V_{out}$ approaches, but does not reach, $V_{DD}$.
For $V_{in}=0$, e.g., $V_{DD}-V_{OH}\approx
(V_{DD}-|V_{TP}|)/2S^{2}$ for $S\gg1$.

Hence an inverting, ratioed, transfer characteristic,
$|V_{TP}|\lesssim V_{out}\lesssim V_{DD}$, with static current
$I_D=\tfrac12\beta_{1}(V_{out}-|V_{TP}|)^{2}$ except when
$M_{2}$ is off.  Biased in the both-saturated region it is a
PMOS common-source amplifier with a saturated diode load.
With $\lambda\ne0$ (3) is only approximate.

### Small signal behaviour

In the both-saturated region, with $I_{DQ}$ the bias current,
$$g_{mi}= \beta_i\bigl(V_{SGi}-|V_{TP}|\bigr)=\sqrt{2\beta_i I_{DQ}}\;, 
\qquad r_{oi}=1/g_{dsi}\; .$$
For $M_{1}$, $v_g=0$ and $v_{sg}=v_{sd}=v_{out}$, and
$v_{bs}=0$ (body tied to its source).  Hence the current
pulled to ground by $M_{1}$ changes by
$(g_{m1}+g_{ds1})v_{out}$: $M_{1}$ looks from the output like
$$ R_{1}={1\over g_{m1}+g_{ds1}}={1\over g_{m1}}\;\Big\|\;r_{o1}
\approx {1\over g_{m1}} $$
to ground.  For $M_{2}$, $v_{sg2}=-v_{in}$, so that at the output
$$ -g_{m2}v_{in}=(g_{m1}+g_{ds1}+g_{ds2})v_{out} $$
$$\,A_v={v_{out}\over v_{in}}=
-{g_{m2}\over g_{m1}+g_{ds1}+g_{ds2}}
= -g_{m2}R_{out}\,  $$
with
$$\,R_{out}= {1\over g_{m1}+g_{ds1}+g_{ds2}}
      = r_{o2}\;\Big\|\;{1\over g_{m1}+g_{ds1}}\approx{1\over g_{m1}}\,,\qquad R_{in}\approx\infty  $$
at low frequencies.  At the same $I_{DQ}$,
$g_{m2}/g_{m1}=\sqrt{\beta_{2}/\beta_{1}}$, so for $\lambda\to0$
$$ A_{v}\;\approx\;-\sqrt{\beta_{2}\over\beta_{1}}
      =-\sqrt{\frac{(W/L)_{2}}{(W/L)_{1}}}\;, $$
independent, to first order, of the bias point, in agreement
with (3).  Channel length modulation reduces $|A_v|$ somewhat.

Thus useful gain requires $(W/L)_{2}\gg(W/L)_{1}$, at the
expense of the allowable $V_{in},V_{out}$ swing in the
saturated region, $\,V_{out,b}-|V_{TP}|=
\frac{S}{1+S}(V_{DD}-|V_{TP}|)$, and of speed, $R_{out}\approx
1/g_{m1}$ being large for a small load device.  It is a low
to moderate gain inverting stage, or a PMOS ratioed inverter
with a degraded low level $ |V_{TP}|$ and static power
dissipation in the on state. ∎

answers.question: Find Rout in the figure.

answer.text:
In the small signal model $V_{DD},V_{b1},V_{b2}$ are a-c ground.
$M_{2}$ and $M_{1}$ are p-channel devices in series.  The
terminal at the bottom is the drain of $M_{1}$.  $M_{1}$ is the
common-gate device and $M_{2}$ is the device feeding its source
at $X$.

For both devices the body is tied to its own source, as drawn,
so that

$$V_{BS1}=V_{BS2}=0\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad g_{mb1}=g_{mb2}=0$$
in the small signal model.

Apply a test voltage $V_T$ at the output and let $I_T$ be the
current entering the drain of $M_{1}$.

The gate and source of $M_{2}$ are at a-c ground, so from $X$
to a-c ground $M_{2}$ looks simply as its output resistance
$r_{o2}$.  Hence the voltage at the source of $M_{1}$ is

$$V_X = I_T r_{o2}. $$

For $M_{1}$ the gate is at a-c ground, so

$$v_{gs1} = -V_X\qquad\text{(in magnitude }v_{sg1}=V_X\text{).}$$

The drop across $r_{o1}$ is due to $I_T$ and to the controlled
source $g_{m1}V_X$:

$$V_T = V_X + r_{o1}\bigl(I_T+g_{m1}V_X\bigr).$$

Substituting $V_X=I_T r_{o2}$,

$$\begin{aligned}
V_T &= I_T r_{o2}+r_{o1}I_T+g_{m1}r_{o1}I_T r_{o2} \\
    &= I_T\Bigl[\,r_{o1}+r_{o2}+g_{m1}r_{o1}r_{o2}\Bigr].
\end{aligned}$$

Hence

$$R_{\text{out}}=\frac{V_T}{I_T}=r_{o1}+r_{o2}+g_{m1}r_{o1}r_{o2}
      = r_{o1}+\bigl(1+g_{m1}r_{o1}\bigr)r_{o2}\;\approx\;g_{m1}r_{o1}r_{o2}$$

for $g_{m1}r_{o1}\gg1$, i.e. the resistance $r_{o2}$ boosted by the
intrinsic gain of the cascode device $M_{1}$.

answers.question: Find Rout in the figure.

answer.text:
$V_{b1},V_{b2}$ and $V_{DD}$ are a-c ground.  
As drawn the bulk of each device is tied to its own source,
so that, incrementally,

$$v_{bs1}=v_{bs2}=0$$

and there is no body effect. $M_{1}$ is the common-gate
device, $M_{2}$ is the device whose drain resistance
degenerates the source of $M_{1}$.

Apply a test voltage $V_{t}$ at the output and let $I_{t}$
be the current drawn into the drain of $M_{1}$. Let the
(incremental) voltage at the intermediate node be $V_{X}$.

For $M_{2}$ the source and the gate are at a-c ground, so
$v_{sg2}=0$ and the resistance from node $X$ to a-c ground
is simply $r_{o2}$.  The same (incremental) current flows
in $M_{1}$ and $M_{2}$, hence

$$V_{X}= I_{t}r_{o2}\tag{1}$$

For $M_{1}$, with current taken from source to drain,

$$-I_{t}=g_{m1}v_{sg1}+\frac{v_{sd1}}{r_{o1}} $$

$$v_{sg1}=V_{X}-0=V_{X},\qquad v_{sd1}=V_{X}-V_{t}$$

so that

$$-I_{t}=g_{m1}V_{X}+\frac{V_{X}-V_{t}}{r_{o1}} \tag{2}$$

Substituting (1) in (2),

$$-I_{t}=g_{m1}I_{t}r_{o2}+\frac{I_{t}r_{o2}-V_{t}}{r_{o1}}$$

$$\frac{V_{t}}{r_{o1}}=I_{t}\left(1+g_{m1}r_{o2}+\frac{r_{o2}}{r_{o1}}\right)$$

Hence the resistance looking into the drain of the
cascode device $M_{1}$ is

$$\boxed{\,R_{out}=\frac{V_{t}}{I_{t}}
      =r_{o1}+r_{o2}+g_{m1}r_{o1}r_{o2}
      =r_{o2}+\bigl(1+g_{m1}r_{o2}\bigr)r_{o1}
      \;\approx\; g_{m1}r_{o1}r_{o2}\,}$$

for $g_{m1}r_{o1},\,g_{m1}r_{o2}\gg1$.  $M_{2}$ contributes
only its $r_{o2}$ as source degeneration for the common-gate
device $M_{1}$, boosting $r_{o1}$ by about $g_{m1}r_{o2}$.

answer.text:
Both devices are in saturation with the same $I_D$.
$V_{b1},V_{b2}$ and $V_{DD}$ are a-c ground.

For $M_2$ the body is tied to $V_{DD}$, i.e. to its source.
For $M_1$ the body is tied at $X$ to its own source.
Hence for both devices

$$
V_{BS}=0\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad g_{mb}v_{bs}=0
$$

i.e. there is no body effect.

Apply a test voltage $V_t$ at the lower terminal and let
$I_t$ be the current drawn, $v_x$ being the small signal
voltage at $X$.

$M_2$ has $v_{sg2}=0$, gate and source at a-c ground, so
from the source of $M_1$ the impedance to a-c ground is
simply the output resistance of $M_2$,

$$
R_S = r_{o2}.
$$

$M_1$ is a common gate device with source degeneration
$R_S=r_{o2}$.  At node $X$

$$
-I_t=\;g_{m1}v_x+\frac{v_x-V_t}{r_{o1}},\qquad 
-I_t=-\frac{v_x}{r_{o2}}
$$

in magnitude, whence

$$
V_t = v_x\bigl(g_{m1}r_{o1}+1+r_{o1}/r_{o2}\bigr),\qquad 
I_t = \frac{v_x}{r_{o2}} .
$$

Therefore

$$
R_{out}= \frac{V_t}{I_t}
       = r_{o1}+r_{o2}+g_{m1}r_{o1}r_{o2}
$$

i.e. for $g_{m1}r_{o1}\gg1$

$$
\,R_{out}\approx g_{m1}r_{o1}r_{o2}\,
$$

the $r_{o2}$ of the lower cascode device boosted by
$g_{m1}r_{o1}$.

answers.question: How do we ensure that M2 is in saturation in the figure?

answer.text:
$M_{2}$ is the p-channel device at the top, $M_{1}$
the p-channel cascode device below it. The drain
voltage of $M_{2}$ is not free; it is the source voltage
of $M_{1}$,

$$V_{X}=V_{b1}+V_{SG1}
      =V_{b1}+|V_{THP1}|+V_{ov1}\qquad 
V_{ov1}= \sqrt{\frac{2I_D}{\mu_pC_{ox}(W/L)_1}} $$

the bodies being tied to the respective sources, so that
there is no body effect.  For a pMOS in saturation, with
$V_{THP}<0$,

$$ V_{SD}\ge V_{SG}-|V_{THP}|=V_{ov}\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad 
       V_{D}\le V_{G}+|V_{THP}| .$$

For $M_{2}$, $V_{D2}=V_X$, $V_{G2}=V_{b2}$, i.e.

$$ V_{SD2}=V_{DD}-V_X \;\ge\; V_{ov2}
\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad 
V_X \le V_{b2}+|V_{THP2}| . $$

Inserting $V_X$ from $M_{1}$,

$$\,V_{b1}+|V_{THP1}|+V_{ov1}\;\le\;V_{b2}+|V_{THP2}|\,$$

i.e. for $|V_{THP1}|\approx |V_{THP2}|$

$$ V_{b2}-V_{b1}\;\gtrsim\;V_{ov1}  $$

with a small safety margin in practice.  $V_{b1}$ and
$V_{b2}$ cannot be chosen independently; $I_D$ and
$(W/L)_2$ fix $V_{b2}=V_{DD}-|V_{THP2}|-V_{ov2}$, and
$V_{b1}$ must then be made low enough, $V_{b1}\lesssim V_{b2}-V_{ov1}$.
In practice $V_{b1},V_{b2}$ are generated by a replica
$M_{1}$-$M_{2}$ bias branch so the inequality tracks
$I_D$ and process.  Putting $M_{2}$ just at the edge of
saturation, $V_{b2}-V_{b1}\approx V_{ov1}$, also maximises
the voltage available at the drain of $M_{1}$.

answer.text:
$M_{2}$ is the current-setting pMOS and $M_{1}$ is the
common-gate cascode device below it.  For the
$R_{out}\approx g_{m1}r_{o1}r_{o2}$ result both must be
saturated.

For a pMOS, in magnitudes,

$$
V_{SD}\ge V_{SG}-|V_{Tp}|=V_{ov}\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad 
V_{D}\le V_{G}+|V_{Tp}| .
$$

For $M_{2}$, $V_{S}=V_{DD}$, $V_{G}=V_{b2}$ and $V_{D}=V_{X}$, so
$M_{2}$ is saturated iff

$$
V_{DD}-V_{X}\ge V_{ov2}\qquad\Longleftrightarrow\qquad 
V_{X}\le V_{b2}+|V_{Tp2}| \tag{1}
$$

The point is that $V_{X}$ is not free: it is fixed by the
cascode device $M_{1}$, whose source is $X$, gate is $V_{b1}$,
and whose well is tied to its source, as drawn, so there is
no body effect in $M_{1}$:

$$
V_{X}=V_{b1}+V_{SG1}=V_{b1}+|V_{Tp1}|+V_{ov1},
\qquad 
V_{ov1}= \sqrt{\frac{2I_D}{\mu_pC_{ox}(W/L)_1}} .
$$

Inserting this in (1),

$$
V_{b1}+|V_{Tp1}|+V_{ov1}\;\le\;V_{b2}+|V_{Tp2}|
$$

i.e. for $|V_{Tp1}|\approx |V_{Tp2}|$

$$
\,V_{b2}-V_{b1}\;\ge\;V_{ov1}\,
\qquad\text{or}\qquad 
V_{SD2}=V_{ov2}+\bigl(V_{b2}-V_{b1}-V_{ov1}\bigr)>V_{ov2}.
$$

So $V_{b1}$ and $V_{b2}$ cannot be chosen independently, and
in particular $V_{b1}=V_{b2}$ puts $M_{2}$ in the triode region.
The cascode gate bias $V_{b1}$ must be about one overdrive
*below* $V_{b2}$.  Making $V_{b1}$ much lower only wastes
headroom, since $M_{1}$ requires $V_{out}\le V_X-V_{ov1}$.

In practice $V_{b1},V_{b2}$ are generated by a replica bias
branch of the same pMOS devices at the same current density,
so that $V_{b2}-V_{b1}=V_{ov1}+$ margin tracks $V_{ov1}$ and
$|V_{Tp}|$ over process and temperature, keeping $M_{2}$
just in saturation with maximum output swing.

answers.question: How do we ensure that M2 is in saturation in the figure?

answer.text:
$M_{2}$ is the p-channel device next to $V_{DD}$ and $M_{1}$ is
the cascode device. Let

* source of $M_{2}$: $V_{DD}$, gate: $V_{b2}$, drain: $X$,
* source of $M_{1}$: $X$, gate: $V_{b1}$, drain: the output.

The voltage at $X$ is not set by $M_{2}$. To first order the
same current flows in $M_{1}$, so $|V_{GS1}|$ is fixed by that
current and by the size of $M_{1}$, and $M_{1}$, acting as a
source follower, clamps

$$
V_X = V_{b1}+|V_{GS1}|
     = V_{b1}+|V_{TH1}|+V_{ov1}\; ,
$$
with no body effect on $M_{1}$, since its n-well is tied to $X$.

For a PMOS device saturation requires, in magnitudes,

$$
|V_{DS}|\ge |V_{GS}|-|V_{TH}|\equiv V_{ov}.
$$

For $M_{2}$

$$
V_{SD2}=V_{DD}-V_X ,\qquad 
V_{SG2}=V_{DD}-V_{b2},
$$

so $M_{2}$ is in saturation iff

$$
V_{DD}-V_X \;\ge\; V_{DD}-V_{b2}-|V_{TH2}|
$$

i.e.

$$
\,V_X \le V_{b2}+|V_{TH2}|\,  .
$$

Substituting $V_X=V_{b1}+|V_{GS1}|$,

$$
V_{b1}\le V_{b2}+|V_{TH2}|-|V_{GS1}|
      = V_{b2}-V_{ov1}-\bigl(|V_{TH1}|-|V_{TH2}|\bigr)
      \;\approx\; V_{b2}-V_{ov1}\; .
$$

Thus $V_{b1}$ must be made sufficiently *low*, at least about
one $M_{1}$ overdrive below $V_{b2}$. In particular $V_{b1}=V_{b2}$
puts $M_{2}$ in the triode region.

The largest $V_{b1}$ that still saturates $M_{2}$, 
$V_X = V_{DD}-V_{ov2}$, gives the least headroom loss:

$$
V_{b1,\max}=V_{DD}-|V_{GS1}|-|V_{GS2}|+|V_{TH2}|\;,
$$

in practice generated with a replica stack of two diode-connected
PMOS devices, with a small extra margin for PVT and $\lambda$.
Lowering $V_{b1}$ further keeps $M_{2}$ safely saturated but lowers
$V_X$ and hence wastes headroom at the output.
