answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in the figure.

answer.text:
The stage is a telescopic NMOS cascode.

* $M_{1}$ is a common-source device.
* $M_{2}$ is a common-gate device, $V_{b1}$ being a dc bias and therefore
an ac ground.
* $I_{1}$ is the active load. Let its small-signal resistance be $R_{1}$;
for an ideal current source $R_{1}\to\infty$.
* The signal current is developed at node $X$ and taken out at the
drain of $M_{2}$.

Assume midband operation, i.e. neglect device capacitances, and
$M_{1},M_{2}$ in saturation. Put
$g_m'=g_{m2}+g_{mb2}$ for $M_{2}$, whose source is above ground.
If the body of $M_{2}$ is tied to its source, $g_{mb2}=0$.

### 1.  DC bias

The same current flows in $M_{1},M_{2}$ and $I_{1}$:

$$
I_{D1}=I_{D2}=I_{1}
      =\frac12\mu_nC_{ox}\left(\frac WL\right)_1V_{ov1}^{2}
      =\frac12\mu_nC_{ox}\left(\frac WL\right)_2V_{ov2}^{2}
$$
ignoring $\lambda$ for the bias calculation, with
$V_{ov i}=V_{GSi}-V_{THi}$, 
$$
g_{mi}=\frac{2I_{1}}{V_{ovi}},\qquad 
r_{oi}=\frac1{\lambda_i I_{1}} .
$$

The intermediate voltage is
$$
V_X = V_{b1}-V_{GS2}=V_{b1}-V_{TH2}-V_{ov2},
\qquad V_{DS1}=V_X,\;\; V_{DS2}=V_{out}-V_X .
$$
$V_{TH2}$ is increased by body effect if the substrate is grounded,
$V_{BS2}=-V_X$.
In saturation
$$
V_X\ge V_{ov1},\qquad V_{out}-V_X\ge V_{ov2}
\;\Longleftrightarrow\;
V_{out}\ge V_{b1}-V_{TH2}.
$$
The lowest useful $V_{b1}$, $V_{b1}\approx V_{ov1}+V_{TH2}+V_{ov2}$,
gives
$$
V_{out,\min}\approx V_{ov1}+V_{ov2},
$$
the usual headroom penalty of a cascode. At the top,
$V_{out,\max}\approx V_{DD}-V_{I1,\min}$, where $V_{I1,\min}$ is the
voltage $I_{1}$ needs to stay in saturation. The quiescent $V_{out}$ is
set by the realisation of $I_{1}$; an ideal $I_{1}$ in series with an
ideal gate-controlled stack leaves it indeterminate.

### 2.  Small-signal gain and resistances

Input resistance, at the gate of $M_{1}$,
$$
R_{in}\approx\infty\qquad\text{(low frequency).}
$$

Resistance looking into the drain of the cascode, with $v_{in}=0$,
is obtained by a test source at the output. The resistance seen
at $X$ is $r_{o1}$, and $M_{2}$ boosts it by its intrinsic gain:

$$
\,R_{down}=r_{o2}+\bigl[\,1+(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})r_{o2}\bigr]r_{o1}\,
      \approx (g_{m2}+g_{mb2})\,r_{o1}r_{o2}\quad (g_mr_o\gg1)
$$

Hence
$$
\,R_{out}=R_{down}\parallel R_{1}\,\qquad 
\bigl(R_{1}\!\to\!\infty:\;R_{out}\approx(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})r_{o1}r_{o2}\bigr)
$$
i.e. about $(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})r_{o2}$ times larger than $r_{o1}$ alone.
An external load $R_L$ is included by $R_1\to R_1\parallel R_L$.

The (exact, to first order) midband voltage gain is

$$
A_v=\frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}}
 =-\,g_{m1}\,
   \frac{\bigl[1+(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})r_{o2}\bigr]r_{o1}R_{1}}
        {R_{1}+R_{down}}
\;\approx\;
-\,g_{m1}\bigl(R_{down}\parallel R_{1}\bigr).
$$

For an ideal load,
$$
\,A_v\approx -g_{m1}(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})\,r_{o1}r_{o2}\,
$$
negative, i.e. inverting, of order $(g_mr_o)^2$ for matched devices.
The short-circuit transconductance remains $\approx g_{m1}$; the
cascode does not increase $G_m$, it increases the resistance into
which $G_m$ works.

The voltage at the internal node is
$$
\frac{v_x}{v_{in}}\approx -g_{m1}\Bigl(r_{o1}\parallel 
\frac{R_{1}+r_{o2}}{1+(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})r_{o2}}\Bigr),
\qquad 
\frac{v_{out}}{v_x}= \bigl[1+(g_{m2}+g_{mb2})r_{o2}\bigr]
\frac{R_{1}}{R_{1}+r_{o2}}>0 ,
$$
so $|v_x/v_{in}|\ll |A_v|$: the Miller multiplication of $C_{gd1}$
is set by the gain to $X$, not by the full gain.

### 3.  Remarks

* Dominant pole is normally at the output,
$\omega_{p,out}\approx1/(R_{out}C_L)$. The pole at $X$,
$\omega_{pX}\approx1/(R_XC_X)$ with $C_X$ the small capacitance at
$X$ ($C_{db1}+C_{gs2}+C_{sb2}+\cdots$), is much higher; the stage is
considerably faster, for a given gain, than a simple common-source
stage, and has good reverse isolation.
* Costs: an extra $V_{ov}$ of headroom and reduced output swing,
an extra bias $V_{b1}$, and the noise and finite $R_{1}$ of the
real current source $I_{1}$, which in practice limit the
$(g_mr_o)^2$ gain above. Large-signal rise of a capacitive load
is slew-limited by $I_{1}/C_L$.

In short: $M_{1}$ converts $v_{in}$ to a current $\approx g_{m1}v_{in}$,
$M_{2}$ passes that current to a load while raising the output
resistance from $r_o$ to $\sim g_mr_o^{2}$, giving a high-gain,
wideband, inverting telescopic cascode stage.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly identifies M1 as the common-source NMOS input and M2 as the common-gate NMOS cascode, and gives the equivalent ideal-load gain with the finite-load resistance relation.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in the figure.

answer.text:
The circuit is a **telescopic cascode common-source stage**. $M_1$ is the input common-source device, $M_2$ is a common-gate cascode device, $V_{b1}$ is a fixed bias (a.c. ground) and $I_1$ is an active load.

### 1. d.c. bias

Both devices carry the same current,

\[
I_{D1}=I_{D2}=I_1 .
\]

With $\beta_i=\mu_nC_{ox}(W/L)_i$ and ignoring $\lambda$,

\[
I_1=\tfrac12\beta_1V_{OV1}^{2}=\tfrac12\beta_2V_{OV2}^{2},
\qquad 
g_{mi}=\frac{2I_1}{V_{OVi}}, \qquad 
r_{oi}=\frac{1}{\lambda_iI_1}.
\]

The required input bias is

\[
V_{in,DC}=V_{TH1}+V_{OV1},
\]

and the voltage at the internal node $\,X$ is

\[
V_X = V_{b1}-V_{GS2}=V_{b1}-V_{TH2}-V_{OV2}=V_{DS1}.
\]

Note that $M_2$ suffers body effect if its bulk is the (grounded) substrate, since $V_{BS2}=-V_X$. Then $V_{TH2}$ is raised and the effective transconductance of $M_2$ is $g_{m2}'=g_{m2}+g_{mb2}$. (If the bulk is tied to its source, use just $g_{m2}$.)

For both devices to stay in saturation:

* $M_1$: $\;V_X\ge V_{OV1}$, i.e. $\;V_{b1}\ge V_{OV1}+V_{OV2}+V_{TH2}$,
* $M_2$: $\;V_{out}\ge V_{b1}-V_{TH2}$.

Hence the lowest permissible output voltage is $V_{b1}-V_{TH2}$, and the highest is set by the compliance of $I_1$, $V_{DD}-V_{I_1,\min}$. This extra stacked $V_{GS}$ is the headroom price paid for cascoding. The optimum (lowest) $V_{b1}$ is the value which just keeps $M_1$ saturated.

### 2. Small-signal gain and output resistance

With $V_{b1}$ at a.c. ground, $M_2$ presents a source-degenerated output looking into its drain. The resistance looking into the drain of the cascode is

\[
R_{out,N}=r_{o2}+\bigl[1+g_{m2}'r_{o2}\bigr]r_{o1}
\;\approx\;g_{m2}'\,r_{o1}r_{o2},
\qquad g_{m2}'=g_{m2}+g_{mb2}.
\]

$M_1$'s output resistance $r_{o1}$ is boosted by roughly $g_{m2}'r_{o2}$ — this is the main job of $M_2$. The short-circuit transconductance is essentially unchanged, $G_m\approx g_{m1}$, because the cascode is a near-unity-gain current buffer. Therefore

\[
\boxed{\,A_v=\frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}}\approx -g_{m1}\Bigl(R_{out,N}\,\big\|\,R_{I_1}\Bigr)\,}
\]

where $R_{I_1}$ is the finite output resistance of the current source $I_1$. For an ideal $I_1$ ($R_{I_1}\!\to\!\infty$) this reduces to $A_v\approx-g_{m1}g_{m2}'r_{o1}r_{o2}$: compared with a simple common-source stage ($-g_{m1}r_{o1}$), the gain is multiplied by $\approx g_{m2}'r_{o2}$, the intrinsic gain of $M_2$. In practice a real (e.g. PMOS) current source will limit $R_{out}$ to $R_{out,N}\|R_{I_1}$.

Other terminal properties:

* **Input resistance:** $R_{in}\approx\infty$ (gate of $M_1$); at high frequency it is capacitive.
* **Resistance at node $X$:** looking into the source of $M_2$,
  \[
  R_X=r_{o1}\;\Big\|\;\frac{R_{I_1}+r_{o2}}{1+g_{m2}'r_{o2}}\;\approx\;\frac{1}{g_{m2}'}
  \]
  for a practical (finite) load. $X$ is therefore a low-impedance node.

### 3. Why the cascode is used

* **High gain / high $R_{out}$**, as above, without a larger load resistor.
* **Suppressed Miller effect.** The gain from the input to $M_1$'s drain (node $X$) is only
  \[
  \frac{v_x}{v_{in}}\approx-\frac{g_{m1}}{g_{m2}'}\approx -1,
  \]
  instead of the full $|A_v|$. Hence $C_{gd1}$ is multiplied by $\approx(1+g_{m1}/g_{m2}')\approx2$, not by $(1+|A_v|)$, so $C_{in}\approx C_{gs1}+C_{gd1}(1+g_{m1}/g_{m2}')$ is small and the input pole stays high.
* **High-frequency pole at $X$:** $\omega_{pX}\approx g_{m2}'/C_X$ with $C_X\approx C_{db1}+C_{gs2}+C_{sb2}+C_{gd1}$. Since $R_X$ is small this pole is far out; the dominant pole is normally at the output, $\omega_{p,out}\approx1/(R_{out}C_L)$.
* **Noise:** the input-referred noise is dominated by $M_1$ (and by $I_1$, referred back through $g_{m1}$). $M_2$'s noise is source-degenerated by $r_{o1}$ and contributes negligibly.

### 4. Summary

| Property | Result |
|---|---|
| Topology | NMOS telescopic cascode CS stage, active load $I_1$ |
| Bias current | $I_1$ in both $M_1$, $M_2$ |
| Voltage gain | $-g_{m1}\bigl(g_{m2}'r_{o1}r_{o2}\;\|\;R_{I_1}\bigr)$ |
| Output resistance | $\approx g_{m2}'r_{o1}r_{o2}\;\|\;R_{I_1}$ |
| Input resistance | $\approx\infty$ (capacitive) |
| Min. output voltage | $V_{b1}-V_{TH2}$ |
| Main cost | Reduced swing/headroom, extra bias $V_{b1}$ |

In short: $M_1$ converts $v_{in}$ to a current, $M_2$ passes that current to the output while shielding $M_1$ from $v_{out}$ and boosting the output resistance by $\sim g_{m2}'r_{o2}$. The result is a much higher-gain, wider-bandwidth inverting amplifier than a single common-source device, at the expense of output swing.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in the figure.

answer.text:
The circuit is an NMOS cascode common-source stage.
$M_{1}$ is the input transconductor, $M_{2}$ is a common-gate
cascode device, $V_{b1}$ is its gate bias and $I_{1}$ is an
active load.  The body of $M_{1}$ is tied to its source, and
the body of $M_{2}$ is tied to its source at $X$, so as drawn

$$V_{BS1}=V_{BS2}=0\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad g_{mb1}=g_{mb2}=0$$

i.e. there is no body effect in $M_{2}$.

### 1.  DC operation

$M_{1}$, $M_{2}$ and $I_{1}$ are in series, hence, neglecting
gate current,

$$I_{D1}=I_{D2}=I_{1}\equiv I_{D}$$

$$ 
V_{GS1}=V_{TH1}+V_{ov1},\qquad 
V_{GS2}=V_{TH2}+V_{ov2}
$$
$$V_{ov i}= \sqrt{\frac{2I_{D}}{\mu_nC_{ox}(W/L)_i}}\;,\qquad 
g_{mi}=\frac{2I_D}{V_{ovi}},\qquad r_{oi}=\frac1{\lambda_i I_D} $$
with $V_{TH2}=V_{TH0}$, since $V_{BS2}=0$.

Node $X$ is fixed by $M_{2}$ acting as a source follower for
dc:
$$
V_X = V_{b1}-V_{GS2}=V_{b1}-V_{TH2}-V_{ov2}=V_{DS1}.
$$
$M_{1}$ in saturation requires $V_{DS1}\ge V_{ov1}$, i.e.

$$
V_{b1}\ge V_{ov1}+V_{ov2}+V_{TH2}.
$$

$M_{2}$ in saturation requires $V_{DS2}\ge V_{ov2}$, i.e.

$$
V_{out}\ge V_X+V_{ov2}=V_{b1}-V_{TH2}.
$$

In addition $V_{out}$ must leave compliance for the real
device implementing $I_{1}$, $V_{out}\le V_{DD}-V_{I1}$.
Choosing $V_{b1}$ at its minimum value maximises swing:
the lowest permissible output is approximately
$V_{ov1}+V_{ov2}$, which is the headroom penalty of the
cascode over a simple common-source stage.

### 2.  Small-signal gain and resistances

Let $R_{L}$ be the (finite) small-signal resistance of the
realisation of $I_{1}$, in parallel with any external load.
The small-signal drain current of $M_{2}$ is
$i_{d2}=-g_{m2}v_x+(v_{out}-v_x)/r_{o2}$, since its gate is at
ac ground and $v_{bs2}=0$, and $i_{d1}=g_{m1}v_{in}+v_x/r_{o1}$,
with $i_{d1}=i_{d2}$.

The resistance looking into the drain of the cascode,
$v_{in}=0$, is the common-gate resistance boosted by
source degeneration $r_{o1}$:

$$
\,R_{\rm down}=r_{o1}+r_{o2}+g_{m2}r_{o1}r_{o2}
      \approx g_{m2}r_{o1}r_{o2}\,\qquad g_mr_o\gg1
$$

i.e. about $g_{m2}r_{o2}$ times the $r_{o1}$ of a simple CS
stage.  Hence

$$
R_{out}=R_{\rm down}\,\|\,R_{L}.
$$

The short-circuit transconductance is essentially $g_{m1}$,
so, to the usual $1/g_mr_o$ accuracy,

$$
\,A_v=\frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}}\approx -\,g_{m1}\bigl(R_{\rm down}\|R_L\bigr)\,
$$

$$
R_{in}\approx\infty\quad\text{(gate input).}
$$

For the idealised load drawn, $R_L\to\infty$, 
$$
A_v=-g_{m1}r_{o1}\bigl(1+g_{m2}r_{o2}\bigr)\approx
-\,(g_{m1}r_{o1})(g_{m2}r_{o2}), 
\qquad R_{out}\approx g_{m2}r_{o1}r_{o2},
$$
of the order of the square of the intrinsic gain $g_mr_o$.
Physically $M_{1}$ gives gain to $X$ and the CG device
gives further gain to the output.

In practice $R_L$ is, e.g., the $r_o$ of a PMOS current
source.  Then $R_{out}\approx R_L$ and $A_v\approx -g_{m1}R_L$:
the full benefit is obtained only if the load is also
cascoded, as in a telescopic-cascode op-amp.

The impedance at the intermediate node is low for a
realistic $R_L$,
$$
R_X = r_{o1}\left\|\frac{R_L+r_{o2}}{1+g_{m2}r_{o2}}
      \approx r_{o1}\right\|\frac1{g_{m2}},
$$
so $v_x/v_{in}=-g_{m1}R_X$ is small, of order $-g_{m1}/g_{m2}$.
This is the well known shielding action of the cascode:
$V_X$ is almost fixed, the Miller multiplication of
$C_{gd1}$ is greatly reduced, reverse isolation is good,
and bandwidth is much better than a simple CS stage with
the same gain.

### 3.  Frequency response, swing and practical remarks

Dominant pole, at the high-impedance output node:
$$
\omega_{p,out}\approx
\frac{1}{R_{out}\,(C_{db2}+C_{gd2}+C_{I1}+C_L)} ,
\qquad\text{GBW}\approx \frac{g_{m1}}{C_L}\; .
$$
Non-dominant pole at $X$:
$$
\omega_{pX}\approx
\frac{1}{R_X\,(C_{db1}+C_{gs2}+C_{sb2}+C_{gd1})},
$$
normally at high frequency because $R_X\sim1/g_{m2}$.
The input pole is set by the source resistance and
$C_{gs1}+C_{gd1}(1-v_x/v_{in})$.

Input-referred noise is dominated by $M_{1}$ and by the
load $I_{1}$; the noise of the cascode device $M_{2}$ is
degenerated by $r_{o1}$ and is largely suppressed at low
frequencies.  $V_{b1}$ must be a clean ac ground, as noise
on it is transmitted to the output through $g_{m2}$.

Remarks:

* High gain and high $R_{out}$, good isolation and
bandwidth, at the cost of at least $V_{ov1}+V_{ov2}$
(plus load) of output headroom and a bias $V_{b1}$.
Open-loop dc $V_{out}$ is ill-defined with two high
impedance devices in series: $I_{1}$ must accurately match
the current set by $V_{in}$, otherwise the stage saturates.
* Tying the body of $M_{2}$ to $X$ removes the body effect,
keeps $V_{TH2}$ low and saves headroom, at the price of
$R_{\rm down}\propto g_{m2}$ rather than $g_{m2}+g_{mb2}$.
In a standard $p$-substrate CMOS process NMOS bodies are
the common substrate and cannot be tied separately to $X$;
this connection requires discrete devices, triple-well or
SOI. With body to ground, replace $g_{m2}$ by $g_{m2}+g_{mb2}$
in $R_{\rm down}$ and use the body-effected $V_{TH2}(V_X)$.

Omitting body effect is explicitly acceptable; the extra body-connection and practical remarks do not change the essential answer.

answers.question: Is the circuit shown in the figure a cascode structure?

answer.text:
No. At first glance it looks stacked like a telescopic cascode, but the transistor symbols show otherwise.

A cascode is a **common-source device driving a common-gate device**: the input transistor's *drain* feeds the CG transistor's source.

Look at the arrow, which marks the source terminal:

* **$M_2$:** the arrow is on the lower terminal and points away from the channel $\;\Rightarrow\;$ NMOS. Its source is the lower terminal, its drain goes to $R_D$, and its gate is at a fixed bias $V_{b1}$. So $M_2$ is indeed a common-gate device.

* **$M_1$:** the arrow is on the *upper* terminal and points toward the channel $\;\Rightarrow\;$ PMOS. Its source is the upper terminal, and its drain is the lower terminal — connected to ground.

So the two sources meet at the intermediate node. $M_1$ has its drain at ac ground, its gate driven by $V_{in}$, and its source delivering the signal: $M_1$ is a **common-drain (source-follower)** device, not a common-source device.

The circuit is therefore a **CD–CG pair** — a source follower driving a common-gate transistor — not a CS–CG cascode. Consistently, it is non-inverting, with (neglecting $r_o$)

$$A_v \approx +\frac{g_{m1}}{g_{m1}+g_{m2}}\,g_{m2}R_D,$$

rather than the inverting $\approx -g_{m1}R_D$ behavior of a true cascode.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly identifies M1 as a PMOS source follower with its drain grounded and M2 as common-gate, so this is a CD–CG pair rather than a CS–CG cascode. The added non-inverting gain description is consistent with that topology.

answers.question: Explain why the Miller effect is less pronounced in a cascode.

answer.text:
In a single common-source (or common-emitter) stage, the
capacitance between input and output, $C_{gd}$ ($C_{bc}$), is
Miller-multiplied:

$$C_{in} = C_{gs} + C_{gd}\bigl(1-A_v\bigr),\qquad 
A_v=\frac{v_d}{v_g}\approx -g_m R_D$$

If $|A_v|=50$, $C_{gd}$ appears $51\times$ larger at the input.
Physically, the drain swings large and opposite to the gate, so
$C_{gd}$ must be charged through a voltage $v_g-v_d\approx 51v_g$.

A cascode splits this gain into two parts:

```
        VDD
         |
         RL
         +---- vout       <- large swing, high impedance
         D
  vbias -M2  common-gate
         S
         +---- vx         <- small swing, low impedance
         D
   vin  -M1  common-source
         S
         |
        GND
```

### 1. The input transistor sees a low load

The impedance looking into the source of the CG device $M_2$ is
approximately

$$R_x \approx \frac{1}{g_{m2}+g_{mb2}}$$

i.e. $\sim 1/g_m$, not $R_L$. So the voltage gain across $C_{gd1}$,
from gate of $M_1$ to its own drain, is only

$$A_x=\frac{v_x}{v_{in}}\approx
-g_{m1}\left(r_{o1}\,\Big\|\,\frac{1}{g_{m2}+g_{mb2}}\right)
\approx -\frac{g_{m1}}{g_{m2}+g_{mb2}}\approx -1$$

for matched devices carrying the same current. The drain of $M_1$
barely moves — $M_2$ essentially clamps it.

### 2. Miller multiplication of $C_{gd1}$ collapses

$$C_{in}\approx C_{gs1}+C_{gd1}\bigl(1-A_x\bigr)
\approx C_{gs1}+2\,C_{gd1}$$

instead of $C_{gs}+C_{gd}(1+g_mR_D)$. The intermediate node also
has a low resistance $\sim 1/g_{m2}$, so its pole is at high frequency.

### 3. The large gain happens where it does no Miller harm

$M_2$ passes $M_1$'s drain current (unity current gain) to the
high-impedance output node, giving the overall gain

$$A_v \approx -g_{m1}\,(R_{out,cascode}\parallel R_L),$$

still large. But this swing is at the drain of $M_2$. Its $C_{gd2}$
connects output to its gate, which is at AC ground — it is simply
part of the output load capacitance, not fed back to the input.
The grounded gate of $M_2$ *shields* $M_1$ from the output swing.

**In short:** Miller effect depends on the gain *across the
feedback capacitor*, not the overall gain. In a cascode that local
gain is $\approx -1$ because the input device drives the low
$1/g_m$ impedance of a common-gate device, so $C_{gd}$ is multiplied
by $\approx 2$ instead of by $1+|A_v|$, and the input pole moves to
much higher frequency.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly identifies M2’s low-impedance source node, derives a local gain near −1, and shows that Cgd1 is multiplied by about 2 rather than by the full-stage gain. It also distinguishes this from the large overall output gain. The phrase that the drain “barely moves” is loose, but the answer’s equations make clear that the Miller effect is reduced, not eliminated.

answers.question: Explain why the Miller effect is less pronounced in a cascode.

answer.text:
In a single common-emitter/common-source stage, the
collector-base (drain-gate) capacitance $C_{\mu}$ resp. $C_{gd}$
connects a node with large inverting swing back to the input.

By Miller's theorem it appears at the input as

$$C_{in}=C_{\pi}+C_{\mu}\bigl(1-A_v\bigr),\qquad 
A_v=\frac{v_c}{v_b}=-g_m R_C$$

so for $|A_v|\gg 1$

$$C_{in}\approx C_{\pi}+C_{\mu}\,(1+|A_v|) .$$

Example: $|A_v|=100$, $C_{\mu}=10\,$fF gives $ \approx 1\,$pF of
Miller capacitance. The physical reason: $v_{bc}=v_b-v_c=
v_b(1+|A_v|)$, so the input source must supply $\sim 101\times$
the charge $C_\mu v_b$.

### What the cascode does

Stack a common-base/common-gate device $Q_2$ on top of the
input device $Q_1$. $Q_1$ no longer drives $R_C$; it drives the
emitter/source of $Q_2$, whose input resistance is very low:

$$R_{in,2}\approx \frac{1}{g_{m2}+g_{mb2}+g_{o1}+g_{o2}}\approx\frac1{g_m}.$$

Hence the voltage gain *of the first device alone*, i.e. the
gain across its own feedback capacitance, is only

$$A_{v1}=\frac{v_{x}}{v_{in}}=-g_{m1}R_{in,2}
= -\,\frac{g_{m1}}{g_{m2}+g_{mb2}+\cdots}\approx -1$$

for matched devices, where $x$ is the intermediate
collector-drain node of $Q_1$.

Therefore the Miller multiplication for $C_{\mu1}/C_{gd1}$ is

$$C_{in}=C_{\pi1/gs1}+C_{\mu1/gd1}\,(1-A_{v1})
\;\approx\; C_{\pi1/gs1}+2\,C_{\mu1/gd1},$$

instead of $C_{\pi}+(1+g_mR_C)C_{\mu}$. The intermediate node $x$
barely moves, so $Q_1$'s collector-base voltage barely changes
and little extra charge is drawn from the input.

### You still get the overall gain

Almost all of $Q_1$'s signal current is passed by $Q_2$
($\alpha\approx 1$ current gain) to the load at the output.
The total gain is still large,

$$A_v \approx -g_{m1}\,(R_{out}\,\|\,R_C),\qquad 
R_{out}\sim g_{m2}r_{o2}r_{o1},$$

but this large output swing does *not* feed back to the input:

* For $Q_2$, the base/gate is at AC ground, so $C_{\mu2}/C_{gd2}$
  connects output to ground, not output to input. It simply adds
  (unmultiplied) to the output capacitance.
* $Q_2$ thus *shields* $Q_1$ from the output swing.

The pole at the intermediate node is also high in frequency,
since its resistance is $\approx 1/g_{m2}$ while its capacitance
is only $C_{\mu1}+C_{\pi2}$ etc.:

$$\omega_{p,x}\approx \frac{g_{m2}}{C_x}\;\text{(large)}.$$

In short: a cascode separates the job of *transconductance*
($Q_1$) from the job of *voltage gain* (done at the high-impedance
output node through $Q_2$). $Q_1$ sees only a $\sim 1/g_m$ load,
so its local gain is $\sim -1$ and its Miller factor is $\sim 2$,
not $\sim 1+|g_m R_C|$.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly identifies the low-impedance cascode node and derives a local gain near −1, giving a Miller factor of about 2 rather than the full-stage gain. Saying the node and capacitor voltage barely move overstates the reduction, but the golden solution treats that as a minor flaw.

answers.question: Explain why the Miller effect is less pronounced in a cascode.

answer.text:
In a single common-source stage, the gate-drain capacitance $C_{gd}$ connects the input node to a node that swings a lot — the drain. By the Miller theorem, a capacitance $C$ bridging an amplifier of voltage gain $A_v$ looks, at the input, like

$$C_{in,Miller} = C_{gd}\,(1 - A_v)$$

For a common-source device, $A_v = -g_m R_D$, so

$$C_{in} \approx C_{gs} + C_{gd}\bigl(1 + g_m R_D\bigr)$$

If $g_m R_D = 50$, $C_{gd}$ is multiplied by $\sim 51$. That huge input capacitance, interacting with the source resistance, is what kills the bandwidth.

### What changes in a cascode

A cascode stacks a common-gate device $M_2$ on top of the common-source input device $M_1$. The key point is this:

> $C_{gd1}$ is **not** connected between the input and the overall output. It is connected between the input (gate of $M_1$) and the *intermediate* node $X$ (drain of $M_1$ / source of $M_2$). So the Miller multiplier depends on the gain from gate to node $X$, not on the total gain of the cascode.

That gain to node $X$ is small, because node $X$ is a low-impedance node. Looking into the source of a common-gate device,

$$R_{in,CG} \approx \frac{1}{g_{m2}+g_{mb2}}$$

so the resistance at the drain of $M_1$ is

$$R_X = r_{o1} \,\Big\|\, R_{in,CG} \approx \frac{1}{g_{m2}+g_{mb2}}$$

Hence the voltage gain from the input to $M_1$'s own drain is only

$$A_{v1} = \frac{V_X}{V_{in}} = -g_{m1} R_X \approx -\frac{g_{m1}}{g_{m2}+g_{mb2}} \approx -1$$

for similarly sized and biased devices (ignoring body effect, exactly $-g_{m1}/g_{m2}$). The Miller factor for $C_{gd1}$ therefore drops from $(1+g_m R_D)$ to roughly

$$1 - A_{v1} \approx 1 + \frac{g_{m1}}{g_{m2}} \approx 2$$

and the input capacitance becomes just

$$C_{in} \approx C_{gs1} + 2C_{gd1}$$

### Where did the overall gain go?

It hasn't been lost — it's been *relocated*. $M_1$ acts mainly as a transconductor, converting $V_{in}$ into a drain current. $M_2$ acts as a current buffer: it passes that current (almost unchanged) up to the high-impedance output node, where the large voltage swing develops across $R_{out} \approx g_{m2}r_{o2}r_{o1} \parallel R_D$.

Intuitively, $M_2$ **shields** $M_1$: it holds the drain voltage of $M_1$ nearly constant (any change in $M_1$'s current is absorbed by $M_2$ rather than moving $V_X$ much), even while the output node swings widely. Since $M_1$'s drain barely moves, $C_{gd1}$ carries little feedback current, and the Miller multiplication collapses.

Two secondary benefits follow:

- **$C_{gd2}$ gets no Miller multiplication at all**, because the gate of $M_2$ is at AC ground — it merely loads the output node.
- **The pole at node $X$ is at high frequency**, since $R_X \approx 1/g_{m2}$ is small, so that node doesn't limit bandwidth either.

So the cascode trades nothing in transconductance: you keep the full overall gain $\approx -g_{m1}R_{out}$, but the capacitance that suffers Miller multiplication only "sees" a gain of about $-1$.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly identifies the low-impedance intermediate node and derives a gate-to-drain gain near −1, so Cgd1 is multiplied by about 2 rather than by the cascode’s full gain. The description of the drain as barely moving is somewhat emphatic, but the quantitative explanation makes clear the effect is reduced, not eliminated.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in the figure.

answer.text:
The circuit is a single ended common-gate stage.
$M_{2}$ is the amplifying device and $M_{1}$ is its
active load.

For $M_{2}$

* gate: $V_{b1}$, a.c. ground
* drain: $V_{out}$
* source: $V_{in}$
* body: tied to the source

For $M_{1}$, a PMOS,

* gate: $V_{b2}$, a.c. ground
* source and body: $V_{DD}$, a.c. ground
* drain: $V_{out}$

Hence the signal enters the source of $M_{2}$, the gate
is at fixed bias, and the signal is taken from the drain.
$M_{1}$ carries the same d.c. current as $M_{2}$ and
presents only its output resistance to the signal at
the output node.

### Bias

Neglecting $\lambda$ for the bias point,

$$
I_D=\frac12\mu_nC_{ox}\Bigl(\frac WL\Bigr)_2
      \bigl(V_{b1}-V_{in}-V_{THN}\bigr)^2
    =\frac12\mu_pC_{ox}\Bigl(\frac WL\Bigr)_1
      \bigl(V_{DD}-V_{b2}-|V_{THP}|\bigr)^2
$$

$V_{b2}$ must be chosen so that the PMOS current source
supplies exactly the current demanded by $M_{2}$ at the
d.c. value of $V_{in}$. $V_{out}$ takes the value that
allows the two currents to be equal.

For both devices to remain in saturation

$$\begin{aligned}
M_{2}:&\quad V_{out}-V_{in}\ge 
      \bigl(V_{b1}-V_{in}\bigr)-V_{THN}
      &&\Longleftrightarrow\quad V_{out}\ge V_{b1}-V_{THN}\\
M_{1}:&\quad V_{DD}-V_{out}\ge 
      \bigl(V_{DD}-V_{b2}\bigr)-|V_{THP}|
      &&\Longleftrightarrow\quad V_{out}\le V_{b2}+|V_{THP}|
\end{aligned}$$

so the useful output swing is
$V_{b1}-V_{THN}\lesssim V_{out}\lesssim V_{b2}+|V_{THP}|$.

Because the body of $M_{2}$ is tied to its source,
$V_{BS2}=0$ at all signal levels. There is therefore
no body effect in $M_{2}$,

$$
g_{mb2}=0,\qquad V_{THN}={\rm const}
$$

at the expense of requiring an isolated $p$-well for
$M_{2}$. $M_{1}$ is in its own $n$-well in the usual way.

### Small-signal gain

With $V_{b1}$ and $V_{b2}$ a.c. ground, the small-signal
model consists of $M_{2}$ with $v_{gs2}=-v_{in}$,
$v_{bs2}=0$, $r_{o2}$ between output and input, and
$M_{1}$ reduced to $r_{o1}$ from $V_{DD}$ (a.c. ground)
to the output.

KCL at the output node,

$$
g_{m2}(-v_{in})+\frac{v_{out}-v_{in}}{r_{o2}}
      +\frac{v_{out}}{r_{o1}}=0
$$

gives

$$
 \frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}}
      =\bigl(g_{m2}+g_{ds2}\bigr)\,
        \bigl(r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2}\bigr)  >0
$$

i.e. approximately, for $g_{m2}r_{o2}\gg1$,

$$
A_v \approx g_{m2}\,\bigl(r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2}\bigr)
$$

The gain is non-inverting. $g_{m1}$ does not appear:
$M_{1}$ is not signal driven, it is only a current-source
load of resistance $r_{o1}$. An external load $R_L$
simply appears in parallel with $r_{o1}$ and $r_{o2}$.

### Input resistance

Applying a test voltage at the source, with the drain
loaded by $r_{o1}$,

$$
 R_{in}= \frac{v_{in}}{i_{in}}
       =\frac{r_{o1}+r_{o2}}{1+g_{m2}r_{o2}}
       \approx \frac{1}{g_{m2}}
         \left(1+\frac{r_{o1}}{r_{o2}}\right) 
$$

For a low resistance drain load this reduces to the
familiar $\approx 1/g_{m2}$ of a common-gate device.
With the high resistance active load here $R_{in}$ is
somewhat larger; e.g. for $r_{o1}=r_{o2}$, $R_{in}\approx
2/g_{m2}$ and $A_v\approx g_{m2}r_{o2}/2$. This is the
characteristic low input resistance of the CG stage,
useful for current-mode inputs and for $50\,\Omega$
termination. If the input is driven through $R_{sig}$,
the gain from the source is $A_v R_{in}/(R_{in}+R_{sig})$.

### Output resistance

With the input source shorted for resistance
calculation, looking into the drain of $M_{2}$ gives
$r_{o2}$, in parallel with $r_{o1}$ from $M_{1}$:

$$
R_{out}\approx r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2}
$$

In general, with a source resistance $R_{sig}$ at the
input, the resistance looking into the drain of $M_{2}$
is boosted to $r_{o2}+R_{sig}+g_{m2}r_{o2}R_{sig}$, and
this is in parallel with $r_{o1}$.

### Remarks

The grounded gate shields input from output, so
$C_{gd2}$ is not Miller multiplied. The low $R_{in}$
makes the input pole high in frequency, and the
dominant pole is normally at the output,
$\omega_{p,out}\approx 1/[(r_{o1}\!\parallel\! r_{o2})C_L]$.
The stage therefore has wide bandwidth and good reverse
isolation, at the cost of low input resistance, limited
headroom set by the two saturation conditions above,
and noise contributions from both $M_{2}$ and the PMOS
load $M_{1}$.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly identifies the common-gate NMOS stage, source input, bias voltages, non-inverting gain, low input resistance, and the required gain expression. The additional body-tie assumption does not contradict the essential topology or gain mechanism.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in the figure.

answer.text:
$M_{1}$ is $p$--channel, $M_{2}$ is $n$--channel.
For $M_{1}$ the source and the bulk go to $V_{DD}$, for
$M_{2}$ the bulk is tied to the source.  Hence, as drawn,
there is no bulk effect in either device, $v_{bs}\equiv 0$.
$V_{b1}$ and $V_{b2}$ are d-c biases, i.e. a-c ground.

The signal is applied to the source of $M_{2}$, its gate
being fixed, its drain driving the output node.  $M_{1}$,
with fixed $v_{sg}$, is simply the active load in the drain
of $M_{2}$.  It is a common gate stage with a $p$MOS current
source load.  The signal source must sink the d-c drain
current of $M_{2}$.

### Bias

In the quiescent state $I_{D1}=I_{D2}=I_{D}$, with, $\lambda\ne 0$
in general,

$$ 
I_D\approx \tfrac12\mu_nC_{ox}\Bigl(\frac WL\Bigr)_2
      \bigl(V_{b1}-V_{in,Q}-V_{thn}\bigr)^{2}(1+\lambda_nV_{DS2})
     =\tfrac12\mu_pC_{ox}\Bigl(\frac WL\Bigr)_1
      \bigl(V_{DD}-V_{b2}-|V_{thp}|\bigr)^{2}(1+\lambda_pV_{SD1})
$$

$V_{out,Q}$ settles where the two currents are equal.
Saturation of $M_{2}$ and of $M_{1}$ requires

$$V_{DS2}\ge V_{GS2}-V_{thn},\qquad 
  V_{SD1}\ge V_{SG1}-|V_{thp}|$$

i.e. for the (small signal) output voltage

$$ V_{b1}-V_{thn}\;\lesssim\;V_{out}\;\lesssim\;V_{b2}+|V_{thp}| $$

which is the useful output swing.  Also
$V_{in,Q}<V_{b1}-V_{thn}$ for $M_{2}$ to be on.

### Small signal voltage gain

For $M_{1}$, $v_{sg1}=0$ (gate and source both a-c ground);
in small signal it is just $r_{o1}$ from $V_{DD}$ to the
output.  For $M_{2}$

$$v_{gs2}=v_g-v_s=-v_{in},\qquad v_{ds2}=v_{out}-v_{in},\qquad
  i_{d2}=g_{m2}v_{gs2}+ \frac{v_{ds2}}{r_{o2}},\qquad 
  r_{oi}=\frac1{\lambda_i I_D} .$$

KCL at the output node, $i_{d1}=i_{d2}$ with
$i_{d1}=-v_{out}/r_{o1}$, gives

$$ -\frac{v_{out}}{r_{o1}}
      =-g_{m2}v_{in}+\frac{v_{out}-v_{in}}{r_{o2}} $$

$$\,A_v=\frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}}
      =\frac{g_{m2}+1/r_{o2}}{1/r_{o1}+1/r_{o2}}
      =\frac{\,1+g_{m2}r_{o2}\,}{r_{o1}+r_{o2}}\,r_{o1}
      \;\approx\;g_{m2}\,(r_{o1}\!\parallel\! r_{o2})\,>0 $$

for $g_{m2}r_{o2}\gg1$.  The stage is non-inverting:
$v_{in}\uparrow\;\Rightarrow\;v_{gs2}\downarrow\;\Rightarrow\;i_{d2}\downarrow\;
\Rightarrow$ less drop in $M_{1}$ $\Rightarrow v_{out}\uparrow$.
$g_{m1}$ does not enter to first order; $M_{1}$ contributes
only $r_{o1}$.  With $r_{o1}\to\infty$, $A_v\to1+g_{m2}r_{o2}$,
the intrinsic gain of $M_{2}$.

Remark: if $M_{2}$'s bulk were a-c ground instead of tied
to its source, replace $g_{m2}$ by $g_{m2}+g_{mb2}$ in the
approximate formulae.

### Input and output resistance

The current drawn, with sign reversed, from the $v_{in}$
source is $i_{d2}$.  From above,

$$ 
R_{in}=\frac{v_{in}}{-i_{d2}}
     =\frac{r_{o1}+r_{o2}}{1+g_{m2}r_{o2}}
     \approx\frac1{g_{m2}}\Bigl(1+\frac{r_{o1}}{r_{o2}}\Bigr)
$$

in particular $R_{in}\approx1/g_{m2}$ to zeroth order in
$\lambda$ -- the familiar low input resistance of a CG
device, increased somewhat by the large drain load $r_{o1}$.

With $v_{in}$ shorted,

$$ R_{out}=r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2} .$$

With a finite resistance $R_S$ in series with $v_{in}$ the
resistance looking into the drain of $M_{2}$ is boosted to
$\approx r_{o2}+(1+g_{m2}r_{o2})R_S$, in parallel with $r_{o1}$.

Hence the circuit is a wide-band, non-inverting voltage
amplifier/current buffer: low $R_{in}\approx1/g_{m2}$, high
$R_{out}$, gain $\approx g_{m2}(r_{o1}\!\parallel\!r_{o2})$, no
Miller multiplication of $C_{gd2}$.  The dominant pole is
normally at the output, $\approx[(r_{o1}\!\parallel\!r_{o2})C_L]^{-1}$.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly identifies the source-driven common-gate NMOS with a PMOS current-source load, its biasing, non-inverting gain, and low input resistance. The gain expression matches the required approximation; minor modeling details do not contradict the essential analysis.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in the figure.

answer.text:
The circuit is a source-driven common-gate stage
with an active load.

$M_{2}$ is NMOS. Its gate is at the fixed bias $V_{b1}$,
its drain is the output and the signal is applied to its
source. Its bulk is tied to its source.

$M_{1}$ is PMOS. Its source and bulk are at $V_{DD}$, its
gate is at the fixed bias $V_{b2}$ and its drain is the
output. For signals $M_{1}$ is therefore not an amplifying
device: $v_{sg1}=0$. It is a current-source load presenting
only $r_{o1}$ from $V_{DD}$, ac ground, to the output.

Since the bulk of each device is tied to its source,
$v_{bs1}=v_{bs2}=0$ and there is no body effect,
$g_{mb1}=g_{mb2}=0$, for the two devices.

### DC operation

Neglecting second order terms the same current flows in
$M_{1}$ and $M_{2}$,

$$
\begin{aligned}
I_D&=\frac{\beta_n}{2}\,(V_{b1}-V_{in}-V_{thn})^{2}
      \bigl[1+\lambda_n(V_{out}-V_{in})\bigr] \\
    &=\frac{\beta_p}{2}\,(V_{DD}-V_{b2}-|V_{thp}|)^{2}
      \bigl[1+\lambda_p(V_{DD}-V_{out})\bigr] ,
\end{aligned}
$$
$\beta=\mu C_{ox}W/L$.  In practice $V_{b2}$ essentially sets
the bias current and $V_{b1}-V_{in}$ sets $V_{GS2}$ to pass
that current.  With $\lambda=0$ the input dc level is pinned to

$$
V_{in}\approx V_{b1}-V_{thn}-V_{ov2},\qquad
V_{ov2}=\sqrt{\frac{2I_D}{\beta_n}}\; .
$$

For both devices to be saturated

$$
V_{DS2}\ge V_{GS2}-V_{thn},\qquad 
V_{SD1}\ge V_{SG1}-|V_{thp}|
$$

i.e.

$$
\,V_{b1}-V_{thn}\;\le\;V_{out}\;\le\;V_{b2}+|V_{thp}|\,
$$

or, in terms of overdrives,

$$
V_{in}+V_{ov2}\le V_{out}\le V_{DD}-V_{ov1}.
$$

Hence the usable swing is about $V_{DD}-V_{ov1}-V_{ov2}$,
larger than in a cascode, at the expense of only one
device's intrinsic gain.

An increase in $V_{in}$ decreases $V_{GS2}$, decreases
$I_{D2}$, and the nearly constant current of $M_{1}$ pulls
$V_{out}$ up: the stage is non-inverting.

### Small-signal gain

For $M_{2}$, $v_{gs2}=-v_{in}$.  KCL at the output node,
with no external load, is

$$
\frac{v_{out}}{r_{o1}}-g_{m2}v_{in}
      +\frac{v_{out}-v_{in}}{r_{o2}}=0,
$$

so that

$$
\, 
\frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}}=
\frac{g_{m2}+1/r_{o2}}{1/r_{o1}+1/r_{o2}}
     =\frac{(g_{m2}r_{o2}+1)\,r_{o1}}{r_{o1}+r_{o2}}
     \;\approx\; g_{m2}\,(r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2})\,
$$

for $g_mr_o\gg1$.  The gain is the intrinsic gain of the
CG device loaded by the output resistance of the PMOS
current source.  With an external load $R_L$ replace
$r_{o1}$ by $r_{o1}\parallel R_L$ and

$$
A_v\approx g_{m2}\,(r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2}\parallel R_L).
$$

$g_{m1}$ does not appear in the signal gain; $M_{1}$
contributes only $r_{o1}$, its noise, and supply coupling.

### Input resistance

Looking into the source of a CG device terminated at the
drain by $R_L'=r_{o1}$ ($\,\parallel R_L$ if present),

$$
\,R_{in}= \frac{R_L'+r_{o2}}{1+g_{m2}r_{o2}}\,
\qquad\approx\;
\frac{1+R_L'/r_{o2}}{g_{m2}} .
$$

For a small drain load this reduces to the familiar
$R_{in}\approx1/g_{m2}$.  Here $R_L'=r_{o1}\sim r_{o2}$,
so $R_{in}\approx 2/g_{m2}$ if $r_{o1}\approx r_{o2}$.
This low $R_{in}$ makes the stage useful as a current
buffer and for terminating e.g. a $50\,\Omega$ source,
$1/g_{m2}$ being set to the termination value, but it
loads a preceding voltage source.  Essentially all of the
signal current injected into the source appears at the drain.

### Output resistance

With the input source shorted for signals,

$$
\,R_{out}=r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2}\,.
$$

If the signal source has resistance $R_S$ in series with
the source of $M_{2}$, the resistance looking into the
drain of $M_{2}$ is boosted to 
$r_{o2}+(1+g_{m2}r_{o2})R_S$, in parallel with $r_{o1}$.

### Frequency response and use

The gate of $M_{2}$ is at ac ground, so there is no Miller
multiplication of $C_{gd2}$. $C_{gd1},C_{gd2},C_{db1},C_{db2}$
and $C_L$ appear at the output, giving the usual dominant
output pole

$$
\omega_{p,out}\approx
\frac{1}{(r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2})C_{out}} .
$$

The input pole is at a high frequency because it sees
$R_S\parallel R_{in}$, with $R_{in}$ small, times $C_{gs2}$.

In summary: a wideband, non-inverting, low-input-impedance,
high-output-impedance voltage/current buffer with
$A_v\approx g_{m2}(r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2})$, widely used as
the input device of cascodes and low-noise amplifiers.
Its limitations are the loading of the source, bias
sensitivity of the source-driven device, output swing
limited by the two saturation conditions above, and noise
and $V_{DD}$ coupling contributed by the PMOS load $M_{1}$.

The (small signal) nodes that are not a-c ground are
only

* $X$ : the gate of $M_{1}$
* $Y$ : the drain of $M_{1}$ - drain of $M_{2}$, i.e. $V_{out}$

At $Y$,

$$C_{DB},\qquad C_{GD2},\qquad C_{DB2}$$

are all connected between the same pair of a-c nodes, $Y$ and
ground.  They are in parallel,

$$ C_{Y}=C_{DB}+C_{GD2}+C_{DB2}\qquad Y\to {\rm gnd}. $$

There remains

* $C_{GS}$ : $X\to {\rm gnd}$
* $C_{GD}$ : $X\to Y$
* $C_{Y}$  : $Y\to {\rm gnd}$

i.e. two independent node voltages $V_X$, $V_Y$.
The nodal equations are of the form

$$
\begin{bmatrix}
C_{GS}+C_{GD} & -C_{GD}\\[2pt]
-C_{GD} & C_{Y}+C_{GD}
\end{bmatrix}
\frac{d}{dt}
\begin{bmatrix}V_X\\ V_Y\end{bmatrix}
+
\begin{bmatrix} \cdot & \cdot \\ \cdot & \cdot \end{bmatrix}
\begin{bmatrix}V_X\\ V_Y\end{bmatrix}
=
\begin{bmatrix}V_{in}/R_S\\0\end{bmatrix}
$$

with non-singular capacitance matrix. The system is second
order. In particular $V_{out}/V_{in}$ has a quadratic denominator.

$$2\ \text{poles}$$

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in the figure.

answer.text:
The two devices are NMOS devices in series between the
resistive load and ground

$$
V_{DD}-R_{D}-V_{out}-M_{2}-V_{X}-M_{1}-GND\qquad 
V_{G1}=V_{G2}=V_{in}
$$

as drawn the bulks are tied to the respective sources, so
there is no body effect. It looks like a cascode, but it is
not: the upper gate is not at a fixed a.c. potential, it
moves with the input. In fact it behaves, to first order,
as one composite common-source transistor.

Let 
$$\beta_i=\mu_nC_{ox}(W/L)_i\qquad 
V_{OV}=V_{in}-V_{T}\;(>0\;{\rm for\;conduction})$$
and neglect $\lambda$ for the bias calculation.

### DC behaviour

The same $I_D$ flows in $M_1$ and $M_2$.

$M_1$ and $M_2$ cannot both be in strong-inversion saturation.
Indeed $M_1$ in saturation would require

$$V_{DS1}=V_X\ge V_{GS1}-V_T=V_{OV}\;\;\Longrightarrow\;\;
V_{GS2}=V_{in}-V_X\le V_T ,$$

i.e. $M_2$ would be off. The self-consistent regime for
$V_{out}$ sufficiently large is

* $M_1$ in triode,
* $M_2$ in saturation.

Then

$$\begin{aligned}
I_D &=\beta_1\!\left[V_{OV}V_X-\frac{V_X^{2}}{2}\right] && M_1\;{\rm triode}\\
I_D &=\frac{\beta_2}{2}\bigl(V_{in}-V_X-V_T\bigr)^{2}
      =\frac{\beta_2}{2}\bigl(V_{OV}-V_X\bigr)^{2} && M_2\;{\rm sat.}
\end{aligned}$$

Put $v=V_{OV}-V_X=V_{GS2}-V_T$. The first equation is
$I_D=\tfrac{\beta_1}{2}(V_{OV}^{2}-v^{2})$. Equating,

$$ \beta_1V_{OV}^{2}=(\beta_1+\beta_2)v^{2},\qquad 
v=V_{OV}\sqrt{\frac{\beta_1}{\beta_1+\beta_2}} $$

$$V_{X}=V_{OV}\left[1-\sqrt{\frac{\beta_1}{\beta_1+\beta_2}}\right],
\qquad 
I_D=\frac12\beta_{\rm eff}V_{OV}^{2}$$

with

$$\;\beta_{\rm eff}= \frac{\beta_1\beta_2}{\beta_1+\beta_2}
      =\frac{1}{1/\beta_1+1/\beta_2}\; $$

i.e. exactly a single NMOS of transconductance parameter
$\beta_{\rm eff}$. For equal widths $1/\beta\propto L$, so
$L_{\rm eff}=L_1+L_2$.  For $\beta_1=\beta_2=\beta$,

$$V_X=\left(1-\frac1{\sqrt2}\right)V_{OV}\approx0.29V_{OV},\qquad 
I_D=\frac{\beta}{4}V_{OV}^{2},\qquad \beta_{\rm eff}=\beta/2 .$$

With the load $$V_{out}=V_{DD}-I_DR_D,$$
in the composite-saturation region, $V_{out}\ge V_{in}-V_T$,

$$V_{out}=V_{DD}-\frac{R_D\beta_{\rm eff}}{2}
      (V_{in}-V_T)^2\qquad V_{in}>V_T ,$$

a normal resistive-load CS transfer characteristic.
For $V_{in}<V_T$, $I_D\approx0$ and $V_{out}\approx V_{DD}$.
For $V_{out}<V_{in}-V_T$, $M_2$ also enters triode and the
composite device is in triode,
$I_D=\beta_{\rm eff}[(V_{in}-V_T)V_{out}-V_{out}^{2}/2]$,
and the gain collapses. Saturation at the $Q$ point needs
$V_{outQ}\ge V_{OVQ}$.

### Small-signal gain and output resistance

At the $Q$ point above, with $\lambda$ restored,

$$\begin{aligned}
g_{m1}&=\beta_1V_{XQ}, &
g_{ds1}&=\beta_1(V_{OV}-V_{XQ})\;\; \text{(triode, large)},\\
g_{m2}&=\beta_2(V_{OV}-V_{XQ}), &
g_{ds2}&=\lambda_2I_D=1/r_{o2}.
\end{aligned}$$

KCL at $X$ and at the output, $i_{d1}=i_{d2}=i_d$,

$$\begin{aligned}
i_d &= g_{m1}v_{in}+g_{ds1}v_x\\
i_d &= g_{m2}(v_{in}-v_x)+g_{ds2}(v_{out}-v_x)
\end{aligned}$$

Eliminating $v_x$,

$$i_d = g_{m,\rm eff}\,v_{in}+g_{out,\rm eff}\,v_{out}$$

$$\begin{aligned}
g_{m,\rm eff}&=
\frac{g_{m1}(g_{m2}+g_{ds2})+g_{m2}g_{ds1}}
     {\,g_{m2}+g_{ds1}+g_{ds2}\,},\\[2mm]
g_{out,\rm eff}&=
\frac{g_{ds1}g_{ds2}}{\,g_{m2}+g_{ds1}+g_{ds2}\,} .
\end{aligned}$$

Neglecting $\lambda$ in $g_{m,\rm eff}$ this is simply
$g_{m,\rm eff}=\beta_{\rm eff}V_{OV}=\sqrt{2\beta_{\rm eff}I_D}$.
The resistance looking into the drain of the stack is

$$\;R_{\rm dev}=\frac1{g_{out,\rm eff}}
      =r_{o2}+r_{ds1}+g_{m2}r_{ds1}r_{o2}\;$$
$r_{ds1}=1/g_{ds1}$ being the small triode resistance of $M_1$.
Hence, with no extra load,

$$\;A_v=\frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}}
      =-g_{m,\rm eff}\,\bigl(R_D\parallel R_{\rm dev}\bigr)\;$$

For identical devices $g_{m1}=0.29\beta V_{OV}$,
$g_{m2}=g_{ds1}=0.71\beta V_{OV}$, so
$g_{m,\rm eff}=0.50\beta V_{OV}$ and
$g_{m2}r_{ds1}\approx1$, i.e.

$$R_{\rm dev}\approx 2r_{o2},\qquad 
A_v\approx-0.5\beta V_{OV}\,(R_D\parallel2r_{o2}).$$

In a common $p$-substrate $M_2$ has body effect; then
$g_{m2}$ in the $v_x$ terms is replaced by $g_{m2}+g_{mb2}$
and $V_{T2}$ is increased by $V_X$.

### Interpretation

* It is not a true cascode. A true cascode has $M_1$ in
saturation, $R_{out}\approx g_{m2}r_{o2}r_{o1}$, and the
CG gate shields the input from Miller effect. Here
$M_1$ is in triode, $r_{ds1}$ is small, so the output
resistance is only modestly enhanced, $\sim2r_{o2}$ for
equal devices, consistent with doubling the effective
channel length.
* The price is halved $g_m$ and $I_D$ for the same $V_{OV}$
(equal devices), roughly doubled input capacitance,
$C_{gs1}+C_{gs2}$ plus Miller-multiplied $C_{gd2}$, and an
extra pole at $X$, $\;\omega_{pX}\approx(g_{m2}+g_{ds1})/C_X$.
* Benefits are those of a long-channel composite device:
higher intrinsic gain $g_{m,\rm eff}R_{\rm dev}$, less
short-channel/DIBL effect, and, in the off state, the
usual stack-effect reduction of subthreshold leakage.

In short, for amplifier design the circuit may be treated
as one common-source NMOS with $\beta\to\beta_1\beta_2/
(\beta_1+\beta_2)$, $g_m=\beta_{\rm eff}(V_{in}-V_T)$,
output resistance as above, and gain
$-g_{m,\rm eff}(R_D\parallel R_{\rm dev})$.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in the figure.

answer.text:
The two devices have the same gate voltage, but they do
not form a cascode.  Let $M_{1}=M_{2}$, $(W/L)$, $\beta =\mu_{n}C_{ox}W/L$,
threshold $V_{t}$, the (body to source) symbols implying no body
effect, and let

$$V_{X}= {\rm drain\;of\;}M_{1}={\rm source\;of\;}M_{2}\qquad 
A\equiv V_{in}-V_{t}\;.$$

$\lambda =0$ is used first.

### The intermediate node

$$V_{GS1}=V_{in},\qquad V_{GS2}=V_{in}-V_{X},\qquad 
V_{DS1}=V_{X},\qquad V_{DS2}=V_{out}-V_{X}$$

and the same $I_{D}$ flows in $M_{1},M_{2},R_{D}$.

Both devices cannot be in saturation.  In saturation, with
$\lambda =0$, $I_{D}$ equality would give $V_{GS1}-V_{t}=V_{GS2}-V_{t}$,
i.e. $V_{X}=0$, contradicting $V_{DS1}\ge V_{GS1}-V_{t}$.
$M_{1}$ saturated with $M_{2}$ on is likewise impossible.
Hence, when on,

* $M_{2}$ is in saturation,
* $M_{1}$ is in the triode region,

i.e. the pinch-off occurs in the upper device, the lower
device is a part of the channel still in the linear regime.
Indeed

$$\begin{aligned}
I_{D}&=\frac{\beta}{2}\bigl(V_{in}-V_{X}-V_{t}\bigr)^{2} &&M_{2}\ {\rm sat}\\
I_{D}&=\beta\Bigl[(V_{in}-V_{t})V_{X}-\frac{V_{X}^{2}}2\Bigr] &&M_{1}\ {\rm triode}
\end{aligned}$$

Equating, with $a=A-V_{X}$,

$$\tfrac12a^{2}= \tfrac12\bigl(A^{2}-a^{2}\bigr)\;\;\Longrightarrow\;\;
a=\frac{A}{\sqrt2}$$

$$\;V_{X}=A\Bigl(1-\frac1{\sqrt2}\Bigr)\approx0.29\,(V_{in}-V_{t})\;$$
$$\;I_{D}= \frac{\beta}{4}\,(V_{in}-V_{t})^{2}\qquad V_{in}>V_{t}\;$$

For unequal devices $\beta_{eq}^{-1}=\beta_{1}^{-1}+\beta_{2}^{-1}$ in
what follows.  In words: the stack is exactly, to first order,
one NMOS of

$$\beta_{eq}=\frac{\beta}{2}\qquad{\rm i.e.}\qquad 
\left(\frac WL\right)_{eq}=\frac{W}{2L}$$

a single device of twice the channel length. $V_{X}$ is
simply the potential part way along that long channel.  In
particular there is no extra cascode headroom: $M_{2}$,
and the equivalent device, saturate for

$$V_{DS2}\ge V_{GS2}-V_{t}\iff V_{out}\ge V_{in}-V_{t} .$$

### Large signal transfer

For $V_{in}\le V_{t}$: $I_{D}\approx0$, $V_{out}=V_{DD}$, $V_{OH}=V_{DD}$.

For $V_{in}>V_{t}$ and $V_{out}\ge V_{in}-V_{t}$, saturation,

$$\;V_{out}=V_{DD}-I_{D}R_{D}
      =V_{DD}-\frac{\beta_{eq}R_{D}}{2}\,(V_{in}-V_{t})^{2}\;,
\qquad \beta_{eq}=\beta/2 $$

a resistor loaded common source inverter characteristic,
quadratic in $V_{in}$.  For $V_{out}<V_{in}-V_{t}$ the equivalent
device is in triode,
$I_{D}= \beta_{eq}\!\left[A V_{out}-V_{out}^{2}/2\right]$ with
$V_{out}=V_{DD}-I_{D}R_{D}$, e.g. for $V_{in}=V_{DD}$,
$V_{OL}\approx V_{DD}/\bigl[1+\beta_{eq}R_{D}(V_{DD}-V_{t})\bigr]$.
The switching threshold $V_{in}=V_{out}=V_{M}$ in saturation is
$V_{M}=V_{DD}-\tfrac{\beta_{eq}R_{D}}2(V_{M}-V_{t})^{2}$.

### Small signal, saturation

At the bias point

$$\begin{aligned}
g_{m2}&=\beta\,(V_{GS2}-V_{t})=\beta A/\sqrt2\\
g_{m1}^{tri}&=\left.\frac{\partial I_{D1}}{\partial V_{GS1}}\right|_{V_{DS1}}
            =\beta V_{X},\qquad
g_{ds1}= \frac{\partial I_{D1}}{\partial V_{DS1}}=\beta A/\sqrt2=g_{m2}\\
r_{ds1}&=1/g_{m2}\;\;{\rm (triode\;resistance\;of\;}M_{1}{\rm )}.
\end{aligned}$$

At node $X$, $i_{d}=g_{m2}(v_{in}-v_{x})=g_{m1}^{tri}v_{in}+g_{ds1}v_{x}$,
giving $v_{x}\approx0.29\,v_{in}$ and

$$\frac{i_{d}}{v_{in}}\equiv g_{m,eq}
      =\frac{\beta A}{2}= \beta_{eq}(V_{in}-V_{t})
      =\frac{2I_{D}}{V_{in}-V_{t}} .$$

Hence, restoring $\lambda$ for $M_{2}$,

$$\;A_{v}=\frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}}
      =-g_{m,eq}\,\bigl(R_{D}\parallel R_{out}\parallel R_{L}\bigr)\;  $$

The resistance looking into the drain of $M_{2}$ is that of a
CG device source-degenerated by the *triode* resistance
$r_{ds1}\approx1/g_{m2}$, not by an $r_{o1}$:

$$R_{out}\approx r_{o2}+r_{ds1}+g_{m2}r_{o2}r_{ds1}
        \approx 2r_{o2}+\frac1{g_{m2}}\approx2r_{o2},$$

$r_{o2}=1/\lambda I_{D}$, i.e. the $r_{o}$ of a $2L$ device,
$\lambda_{eq}\approx\lambda/2$.  The intrinsic gain
$g_{m,eq}R_{out}\approx4/\lambda A$ is that of the long device.

### Conclusions

* It is a common-source (resistor-load inverter) stage whose
transistor is split into two series $L$ devices $\equiv$ one
$2L$ device: same $I$--$V$, half the $g_{m}$ and half the current
of one constituent device at the same $V_{in}-V_{t}$, twice its $r_{o}$.
* It is *not* a cascode: in a cascode the upper gate is at ac
ground, both devices saturate, $R_{out}\sim g_{m2}r_{o2}r_{o1}$ and
$g_{m}\approx g_{m1}$.  Here $M_{1}$ is in triode, $R_{out}$ is only
$\sim2r_{o}$, and driving $M_{2}$'s gate with $v_{in}$ makes
$v_{x}$ follow $v_{in}$, reducing $v_{gs2}$ to $\approx0.71v_{in}$.
* Advantages are those of a long channel device - lower
$\lambda$, higher intrinsic gain, stack leakage reduction -
at the cost of area, $\approx$ twice the gate capacitance, and
lower $g_{m}$ for a given current.  In a common $p$-substrate
process $M_{2}$ in addition suffers body effect, $V_{t2}(V_{X})$
and $g_{mb2}$, somewhat reducing $g_{m,eq}$ further.
