The added small-signal and output-resistance analysis is consistent with the golden solution.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in the figure.

answer.text:
The circuit is a resistively loaded common-source
amplifier whose driver is not a single MOS transistor but
two NMOS in series, with their gates tied together.
It is the *self-cascode*, or composite transistor, connection.

$M_{1}$ and $M_{2}$ carry the same current, the current
in $R_{D}$. Let

$$
V_{X}=\text{voltage at }M_{1}\text{ drain-}M_{2}\text{ source},\qquad 
\beta_i=\mu_nC_{ox}\left(\frac WL\right)_i ,\qquad A=V_{in}-V_{th}
$$

The bodies are tied to the respective sources in the
diagram, so that, as drawn, $V_{BS1}=V_{BS2}=0$ and there
is no body effect. In a common p-substrate this tie for
$M_{2}$ would require a triple well, SOI or discrete devices.

### 1.  Large signal operation

For $V_{in}<V_{th}$ both devices are off,

$$
I_D=0,\qquad V_{out}=V_{DD}\; .
$$

For appreciable conduction $M_{1}$ and $M_{2}$ cannot both
be in saturation. Indeed $M_{1}$ saturated would require

$$
V_X\ge V_{GS1}-V_{th}=V_{in}-V_{th},
$$

whereas $M_{2}$ on requires

$$V_{GS2}=V_{in}-V_X>V_{th}\;\;\Longleftrightarrow\;\;
V_X<V_{in}-V_{th} .$$

Hence in the useful conducting region, apart from the
zero current boundary,

$$ M_{1}:\ \text{triode},\qquad M_{2}:\ \text{saturation} $$

provided $M_{2}$ is saturated, i.e.

$$
V_{DS2}\ge V_{GS2}-V_{th}\iff
V_{out}-V_X\ge V_{in}-V_X-V_{th}\iff V_{out}\ge V_{in}-V_{th}.
$$

Neglecting $\lambda$ for the d.c. calculation,

$$\begin{aligned}
I_D&=\frac{\beta_2}{2}\bigl(V_{in}-V_X-V_{th}\bigr)^{2}
      &&M_{2}\ {\rm sat.}\\
I_D&=\beta_1\Bigl[(V_{in}-V_{th})V_X-\frac{V_X^{2}}2\Bigr]
      &&M_{1}\ {\rm triode}
\end{aligned}$$

Put $\delta=V_{in}-V_{th}-V_X=V_{GS2}-V_{th}$. Then
$I_D=\tfrac{\beta_1}{2}(A^{2}-\delta^{2})
      =\tfrac{\beta_2}{2}\delta^{2}$, whence

$$
\;\delta = A\sqrt{\frac{\beta_{1}}{\beta_{1}+\beta_{2}}}\;,\qquad
\;V_X = A\left[1-\sqrt{\frac{\beta_{1}}{\beta_{1}+\beta_{2}}}\right]\;
$$

and

$$
\,I_D=\frac12\,\beta_{\rm eff}\,(V_{in}-V_{th})^{2}\,,\qquad 
\frac1{\beta_{\rm eff}}=\frac1{\beta_{1}}+\frac1{\beta_{2}}\,,\qquad
V_{out}=V_{DD}-I_DR_D .
$$

For equal $W$ this is $\beta_{\rm eff}=
\mu_nC_{ox}W/(L_1+L_2)$: d.c. the pair behaves exactly
like one transistor of length $L_1+L_2$.  For
$\beta_1=\beta_2=\beta$, $V_X=0.29\,(V_{in}-V_{th})$,
$V_{GS2}-V_{th}=0.71\,(V_{in}-V_{th})$,
$I_D=\beta (V_{in}-V_{th})^{2}/4$.

The amplifying region ends when $V_{out}$ falls to
$V_{in}-V_{th}$. For larger $V_{in}$, $M_{2}$ also enters
the triode region, the gain collapses, and the circuit
tends to the ordinary resistive-load inverter state,
$V_{out}$ low.

### 2.  Small signal behaviour

In the region above, with $\lambda$ restored,

$$\begin{array}{ll}
M_{1}\ {\rm triode:}& g_{m1}= \beta_{1}V_X,\qquad 
g_{ds1}= \beta_{1}(A-V_X)=\beta_{1}\delta ,\\[2pt]
M_{2}\ {\rm sat.:}& g_{m2}= \beta_{2}\delta
      =\dfrac{2I_D}{\delta},\qquad 
g_{ds2}= \lambda_{2}I_D=1/r_{o2}.
\end{array}$$

$M_1$ is represented by $g_{m1}v_{in}$ in parallel with
$g_{ds1}$ from $X$ to ground; $M_2$ by
$g_{m2}(v_{in}-v_x)$ in parallel with $g_{ds2}$ from
$V_{out}$ to $X$. Eliminating $v_x$, the short-circuit
transconductance of the composite device is

$$
G_m=\frac{i_d}{v_{in}}\Big|_{v_{out}=0}
 =\frac{g_{m1}(g_{m2}+g_{ds2})+g_{m2}g_{ds1}}
        {g_{m2}+g_{ds1}+g_{ds2}}
 \;\approx\; \beta_{\rm eff}(V_{in}-V_{th})
      =\sqrt{2\beta_{\rm eff}I_D}\;,
$$

exactly the $g_m$ of the equivalent long transistor
obtained above.

The resistance looking into the drain of the composite
device, $v_{in}=0$, is that of a common-gate $M_{2}$
source-degenerated by the triode resistance
$r_{ds1}=1/g_{ds1}$ of $M_{1}$:

$$
\,R_{\rm dev}=r_{ds1}+r_{o2}+g_{m2}r_{ds1}r_{o2}
      \approx r_{o2}\bigl(1+g_{m2}r_{ds1}\bigr)
      =r_{o2}\left(1+\frac{\beta_{2}}{\beta_{1}}\right)\,  .
$$

For $\beta_1=\beta_2$, $R_{\rm dev}\approx2r_{o2}$, i.e.
in essence the $r_o$ of a device of length $L_1+L_2$.
It is larger than that of $M_2$ alone, but the boost is
not the $g_mr_o$ of a true cascode, because the lower
device is in triode and $r_{ds1}$ is small,
$r_{ds1}=1/g_{m2}$ for identical devices. Making
$\beta_{1}$ small compared with $\beta_{2}$ raises
$1+\beta_2/\beta_1$, at the expense of $G_m$ and of
voltage dropped at $X$.

Hence, with $R_D$ to $V_{DD}$,

$$
\,A_v=\frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}}
      =-G_m\,\bigl(R_D\parallel R_{\rm dev}\bigr)\,
\qquad\text{inverting,}
$$

$R_{in}\approx\infty$ at low frequencies, and the
resistance at the output terminal is $R_D\parallel
R_{\rm dev}$. If $R_D\ll R_{\rm dev}$, $A_v\approx-G_mR_D$.

### 3.  Remarks

* No separate cascode bias is needed, and $M_{2}$
saturates for $V_{out}\ge V_{in}-V_{th}$, i.e. about one
overdrive of output headroom, like a single device and
much better than a conventional two-overdrive cascode.
This is the attraction of the self-cascode at low
$V_{DD}$.
* The price is the $G_m$ of the equivalent long device,
$\beta_{\rm eff}<\beta_{1},\beta_{2}$, extra area, and
the capacitance at the internal node $X$. The resistance
at $X$ is $\sim (g_{ds1}+g_{m2})^{-1}$, so the $X$ pole
is normally high.
* Bias must satisfy $V_{DD}-I_DR_D\ge V_{in}-V_{th}$ with
$I_D=\tfrac12\beta_{\rm eff}(V_{in}-V_{th})^{2}$. For
$V_{in}$ too large both devices go triode and the circuit
is a switch, for $V_{in}<V_{th}$ it is off with
$V_{out}=V_{DD}$. ∎

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly identifies the common-gate series NMOS pair, with M1 in triode and M2 saturated, and derives the key result that it behaves approximately like one longer-channel device (L_eff ≈ L1 + L2 for equal widths). Its output-resistance discussion also matches the modest self-cascode increase, not a true cascode boost.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in the figure.

answer.text:
The transistors are NMOS. $M_{1}-M_{2}$ is a source
coupled pair with a tail current $I_{1}$, a resistive load
in the drain of $M_{2}$ only, a signal input to $M_{1}$ and a
d-c bias, a-c ground, to $M_{2}$.  It is the usual
differential to single ended stage. Let the common source
node be $X$, $M_{1}=M_{2}$ in the first instance,
$\beta =\mu_{n}C_{ox}W/L$, $\lambda\ne 0$ in general.

### D-C bias

$$ I_{D1}+I_{D2}=I_{1}\qquad 
V_{X}=V_{in,DC}-V_{GS1}=V_{b}-V_{GS2} $$
$$ V_{out,Q}=V_{DD}-I_{D2}R_{D} $$

For balanced operation the d-c component of $V_{in}$ is made
equal to $V_{b}$. Then, for matched devices,

$$ I_{D1}=I_{D2}=\frac{I_{1}}2,\qquad 
V_{GS}=V_{th}+V_{ov},\;\;
V_{ov}= \sqrt{\frac{I_{1}}{\beta}} $$
$$ V_{X}=V_{b}-V_{th}-V_{ov},\qquad 
V_{out,Q}=V_{DD}-\frac{I_{1}}2R_{D},\qquad 
g_{m}= \sqrt{\beta I_{1}}=\frac{I_{1}}{V_{ov}}  $$

in saturation.  In particular $M_{2}$ in saturation requires

$$V_{out,Q}-V_{X}\ge V_{ov}\iff V_{out,Q}\ge V_{b}-V_{th}
\iff V_{DD}-\frac{I_{1}}2R_{D}\ge V_{b}-V_{th}$$

and $V_{X}$ must remain large enough to keep the $I_{1}$
source in saturation.  The permissible common mode level is
roughly

$$V_{th}+V_{ov}+V_{min,I_{1}}\;\lesssim\;V_{CM}\;\lesssim\;
V_{DD}-\frac{I_{1}}2R_{D}+V_{th} .$$

$V_{out}$ can swing up to $\approx V_{DD}$, $I_{D2}\to0$, and
down to $\approx V_{b}-V_{th}$, $M_{2}$ at the edge of saturation.

Large signal, $\lambda =0$, with $V_{id}=V_{in}-V_{b}$,

$$\begin{aligned}
I_{D1}-I_{D2}&=\frac{\beta}{2}V_{id}
\sqrt{\frac{4I_{1}}{\beta}-V_{id}^{2}},\qquad 
|V_{id}|\le \sqrt{\frac{2I_{1}}{\beta}}=\sqrt2\,V_{ov}\\
V_{out}&=V_{DD}-R_{D}I_{D2}
      =V_{DD}-\frac{I_{1}R_{D}}2+\frac{R_{D}}2\,(I_{D1}-I_{D2}) .
\end{aligned}$$

For $|V_{id}|\gtrsim \sqrt2V_{ov}$ the current is completely
steered to one side: $V_{in}\gg V_{b}$, $I_{D2}\to0$, $V_{out}\to V_{DD}$;
$V_{in}\ll V_{b}$, $I_{D2}\to I_{1}$, $V_{out}\to V_{DD}-I_{1}R_{D}$.

### Small signal gain

$V_{DD}$ and $V_{b}$ are a-c ground, $I_{1}$ is a-c open.
Neglecting $r_{o}$ for the moment,
at $X$

$$ i_{d1}=g_{m1}(v_{in}-v_{x}),\qquad i_{d2}=g_{m2}(0-v_{x}),\qquad 
i_{d1}+i_{d2}=0 $$

i.e. an increase in $i_{d1}$ must be met by an equal decrease
in $i_{d2}$.  Hence

$$ v_{x}= \frac{g_{m1}}{g_{m1}+g_{m2}}v_{in},\qquad
i_{d2}= -\,\frac{g_{m1}g_{m2}}{g_{m1}+g_{m2}}v_{in}  $$

and $v_{out}=-i_{d2}R_{D}$,

$$\,A_{v}\equiv\frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}}
      =\frac{g_{m1}g_{m2}}{g_{m1}+g_{m2}}R_{D}\,  $$

in particular for matched devices $v_{x}\approx v_{in}/2$,

$$ A_{v}\approx +\frac{g_{m}R_{D}}{2} $$

The $+$ sign: $v_{in}\uparrow\;\Rightarrow\;i_{d1}\uparrow\;
\Rightarrow\;i_{d2}\downarrow\;\Rightarrow\;v_{out}\uparrow$.
From the $M_{2}$ gate the gain is $-g_{m}R_{D}/2$, i.e. in
general $v_{out}\approx \tfrac{g_{m}R_{D}}2\,(v_{in}-v_{b})$.
The gain is one half that of a common source stage
$g_{m}R_{D}$, the price of single ended output.  The
body effect, if the bodies are to ground, changes $v_{x}$
but not, for matched devices, the $g_{m}R_{D}/2$ result to
first order.

With $r_{o1}=r_{o2}=r_{o}$ matched,

$$ A_{v}= \frac{g_{m}}{\,2/R_{D}+1/r_{o}\,}
       =\frac{g_{m}}2\,\bigl(R_{D}\,\|\,2r_{o}\bigr)
       \;\xrightarrow[r_{o}\gg R_{D}]{}\;\frac{g_{m}R_{D}}2 .$$

### Resistances, common mode

Input resistance at the gate is essentially infinite at
low frequency, $C_{in}\approx C_{gd1}+C_{gs1}/2$, there being
no Miller effect on $M_{1}$ whose drain is at a-c ground.

Looking into the drain of the common gate device $M_{2}$ the
resistance is boosted by the resistance at $X$,
$\approx 1/g_{m1}\parallel R_{tail}$.  For matched devices and
ideal $I_{1}$ it is $\approx 2r_{o}$, so

$$ R_{out}\approx R_{D}\,\|\,2r_{o}\;\approx\;R_{D}\quad (R_{D}\ll r_{o}). $$

For a pure common mode signal, with $r_{o}\to\infty$ and ideal
$I_{1}$, $i_{d1}$ and $i_{d2}$ cannot change: $A_{cm}\approx0$,
infinite CMRR.  With a real tail resistance $R_{1}$,

$$ A_{cm}\approx -\frac{g_{m}R_{D}}{1+2g_{m}R_{1}},\qquad
\left|\frac{A_{d}}{A_{cm}}\right|\approx\frac{1+2g_{m}R_{1}}2,
\qquad A_{d}=\frac{g_{m}R_{D}}2, $$

for single ended output.  The dominant high frequency pole
is normally at the output,

$$ f_{p,out}\approx\frac1{2\pi R_{out}C_{L,tot}},\qquad
C_{L,tot}=C_{L}+C_{db2}+C_{gd2}+\cdots $$

the pole at $X$ being at $\approx (g_{m1}+g_{m2})/2\pi C_{X}$,
usually much higher.

In short: a non-inverting differential pair stage,
biased at $I_{1}/2$ per side, $V_{out,Q}=V_{DD}-I_{1}R_{D}/2$,
with voltage gain $\approx g_{m}R_{D}/2$, output resistance
$\approx R_{D}$, infinite input resistance, and good common
mode rejection set by the tail current source. It is the
standard first stage / differential-to-single-ended converter
in CMOS op amps.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly identifies the circuit as a source-coupled differential pair with M2 biased at Vb and the output at M2’s drain. It also gives the correct non-inverting gain, approximately gmRD/2 for matched devices.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in the figure.

answer.text:
The circuit is an NMOS differential pair $M_1-M_2$ with a
tail current $I_1$, a resistive load in only one branch, single-ended
input and single-ended output. $V_{in}$ is the non-inverting input and
$V_b$ is the inverting input, normally a d.c. reference.
Equivalently, in signal terms, it is a common-drain device $M_1$
driving the common-gate device $M_2$. As drawn the bulk is tied to
the source, so there is no body effect. Assume matched devices in
saturation and, at first, $\lambda =0$.

### 1. D.C. bias

For balanced operation $V_{in,DC}=V_b\equiv V_{CM}$. Then the tail
current splits equally,

$$
I_{D1}=I_{D2}=\frac{I_1}{2},\qquad 
V_{GS}=V_{TH}+V_{ov},\qquad 
V_{ov}=\sqrt{\frac{I_1}{\mu_nC_{ox}(W/L)}}
$$

$$
V_X = V_{CM}-V_{GS},\qquad 
V_{out,Q}=V_{DD}-\frac{I_1}{2}R_D ,
\qquad 
g_m=\frac{I_1}{V_{ov}},\;\; r_o=\frac{2}{\lambda I_1}.
$$

$M_2$ in saturation requires $V_{out}\ge V_X+V_{ov}$, i.e.

$$
V_{out,Q}\ge V_b-V_{TH}.
$$

The input common-mode range is bounded below by the compliance
$V_{X,\min}$ of the tail source,
$V_{CM,\min}=V_{X,\min}+V_{GS}$, and above by $M_2$ leaving
saturation,

$$
V_{CM,\max}=V_{DD}-\frac{I_1}{2}R_D+V_{TH}.
$$

### 2. Large-signal transfer

Let $V_{id}=V_{in}-V_b$, $K_n=\tfrac12\mu_nC_{ox}(W/L)$. For
$|V_{id}|\le \sqrt{I_1/K_n}=\sqrt2\,V_{ov}$,

$$
I_{D1}-I_{D2}=V_{id}\sqrt{2K_nI_1-K_n^{2}V_{id}^{2}},\qquad
I_{D2}=\frac{I_1-(I_{D1}-I_{D2})}{2},
$$

$$
V_{out}=V_{DD}-R_DI_{D2}
      =V_{DD}-\frac{I_1R_D}{2}+\frac{R_D}{2}(I_{D1}-I_{D2}).
$$

For large positive $V_{id}$, $M_1$ takes all of $I_1$, $M_2$ turns
off and $V_{out}\to V_{DD}$. For large negative $V_{id}$, $M_2$ takes
all of $I_1$ and $V_{out}\to V_{DD}-I_1R_D$. The useful output swing
is further limited by $M_2$ remaining in saturation.

### 3. Small-signal gain

Let $v_x$ be the common-source node. With an ideal tail,
$i_{d1}+i_{d2}=0$. Neglecting $r_o$,

$$
g_{m1}(v_{in}-v_x)=g_{m2}v_x
\;\;\Longrightarrow\;\;
v_x=\frac{g_{m1}}{g_{m1}+g_{m2}}v_{in}.
$$

This is the source-follower action of $M_1$ loaded by the
$1/g_{m2}$ impedance looking into the source of $M_2$. Then
$i_{d2}=-g_{m2}v_x$ and $v_{out}=-i_{d2}R_D$, so

$$
\boxed{\;
\frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}}
= \frac{g_{m1}g_{m2}}{g_{m1}+g_{m2}}\,R_D
\;}
$$

positive: the stage is non-inverting. For matched devices
$g_{m1}=g_{m2}=g_m$,

$$
A_v=+\frac{g_mR_D}{2}
     =\frac{I_1R_D}{2V_{ov}}
     =\frac{V_{DD}-V_{out,Q}}{V_{ov}} .
$$

It is half the gain of a common-source $M_2$ alone: a 6 dB penalty
paid for differential operation. In terms of the differential input,
$v_{out}/(v_{in}-v_b)\approx g_mR_D/2$; a signal on $V_b$ alone gives
$-g_mR_D/2$.

Including channel-length modulation, for matched devices,

$$
\boxed{\;
A_v=\frac{g_m}{\,2/R_D+1/r_o\,}
    =\frac{g_m}{2}\bigl(R_D\parallel 2r_o\bigr)
\;}
$$

so for $R_D\gg r_o$ the gain tends to the intrinsic limit $g_mr_o/2$.

### 4. Resistances

Input resistance is that of a MOS gate: essentially infinite at d.c.

At the output, $M_2$ is a common-gate device whose source is
degenerated by the impedance looking into the source of $M_1$,
$\approx 1/g_{m1}$. Hence the resistance looking into the drain of
$M_2$ is $r_{o2}\bigl(1+g_{m2}/g_{m1}\bigr)+1/g_{m1}\approx 2r_o$ for
matched devices, and

$$
R_{out}\approx R_D\parallel 2r_o .
$$

### 5. Common-mode behaviour, frequency response

With a perfectly matched pair and ideal $I_1$, a common-mode signal
applied to both gates produces no output: the ideal CMRR is infinite.
With a real tail impedance $R_{SS}$,
$A_{CM}\approx -R_D/(2R_{SS})$ (single-ended), giving
$|CMRR|\approx g_mR_{SS}$; device/load mismatch degrades this further.

There are two principal poles. The output pole is normally dominant,

$$
\omega_{p,out}\approx\frac{1}{R_{out}C_{out}},\qquad 
R_{out}\approx R_D\parallel 2r_o .
$$

At node $X$ the resistance is low,
$R_X\approx 1/(g_{m1}+g_{m2})$, so

$$
\omega_{p,X}\approx\frac{g_{m1}+g_{m2}}{C_X},
$$

with $C_X$ containing $C_{gs1}+C_{gs2}$ and tail capacitance. Because
$M_2$ is common-gate there is no Miller multiplication of $C_{gd2}$,
and $M_1$ has its drain at a.c. ground; the CD-CG signal path is
therefore considerably wider-band than a simple common-source stage.

In summary: a non-inverting differential-input, single-ended-output
amplifier with $A_v\approx +g_m(R_D\parallel2r_o)/2$, high input
impedance, output impedance $R_D\parallel2r_o$, output quiescent level
$V_{DD}-I_1R_D/2$, and full current steering over
$|V_{in}-V_b|\approx\sqrt2\,V_{ov}$.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly identifies the source-coupled differential pair and its equivalent source-follower driving a common-gate stage, with M2 gated at Vb and output at its drain. The gain is correctly non-inverting; the golden solution’s full-credit rule applies.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in the figure.

answer.text:
The $M_{1}-M_{2}$ pair is a source coupled pair.
The sources are tied together to the (ideal) tail source
$I_{1}$, $M_{1}$ has its drain at a-c ground, $M_{2}$ has the
resistive load $R_{D}$ in its drain.  $V_{b}$ is a d-c bias,
i.e. a-c ground.  The body is tied to the source in the
symbol, so there is no body effect to first order.
In the sequel $M_{1},M_{2}$ are taken matched, in saturation,
$\beta =\mu_{n}C_{ox}W/L$.

### D-C and large signal behaviour

With $V_{GS1}=V_{in}-V_{X}$, $V_{GS2}=V_{b}-V_{X}$,
$V_{X}$ the common source node,

$$ I_{D1}+I_{D2}=I_{1},\qquad 
I_{Di}=\frac{\beta}{2}\bigl(V_{GSi}-V_{TH}\bigr)^{2}(1+\lambda V_{DSi}) $$

For the usual bias $V_{inQ}=V_{b}$

$$ I_{D1Q}=I_{D2Q}\approx \frac{I_{1}}2 ,\qquad 
V_{outQ}=V_{DD}-\frac{I_{1}}2R_{D},\qquad
V_{XQ}=V_{b}-V_{GS},\;\; V_{GS}=V_{TH}+V_{OV} $$

$$ V_{OV}= \sqrt{\frac{I_{1}}{\beta}},\qquad 
g_{m}= \beta V_{OV}= \frac{I_{1}}{V_{OV}}\;\;{\rm at\;the\;Q\;point}. $$

Saturation of $M_{2}$ requires
$V_{out}\ge V_{X}+V_{OV}$, i.e. $V_{outQ}\gtrsim V_{b}-V_{TH}$,
and $V_{X}$ must leave headroom for $I_{1}$.  $\lambda$ makes
$I_{D1}$ slightly larger than $I_{D2}$ at $V_{in}=V_{b}$ because
$V_{DS1}\gg V_{DS2}$.

For a differential voltage $v_{id}=V_{in}-V_{b}$ the current
is steered between the two sides,
$$ I_{D1}-I_{D2}= \frac{\beta v_{id}}2
\sqrt{\frac{4I_{1}}{\beta}-v_{id}^{2}},\qquad 
V_{out}=V_{DD}-I_{D2}R_{D}, $$
for $|v_{id}|<\sqrt2\,V_{OV}$.  For $v_{id}>+\sqrt2V_{OV}$,
$M_{2}$ is off, $V_{out}\to V_{DD}$; for $v_{id}<-\sqrt2V_{OV}$,
$M_{1}$ is off, $I_{D2}=I_{1}$, $V_{out}=V_{DD}-I_{1}R_{D}$.
It is a differential, current steering, stage.

### Small signal gain

Let $v_b=0$ a-c, $R_{D}'=R_{D}\parallel R_{L}$, $I_{1}$ ideal
for the moment, $\lambda=0$ first.  At node $X$, $i_{d1}+i_{d2}=0$:

$$ g_{m1}(v_{in}-v_{x})-g_{m2}v_{x}=0
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad 
v_{x}= \frac{g_{m1}}{g_{m1}+g_{m2}}\,v_{in} $$

i.e. $M_{1}$ is a source follower driving the low impedance,
$\approx 1/g_{m2}$, seen into the source of the common gate
device $M_{2}$.  The drain current of $M_{2}$ is
$i_{d2}=-g_{m2}v_{x}$, so

$$ v_{out}=-i_{d2}R_{D}'=
\frac{g_{m1}g_{m2}}{g_{m1}+g_{m2}}\,R_{D}'\,v_{in} $$

In particular for matched devices $g_{m1}=g_{m2}=g_{m}$

$$ A_{v}\equiv\frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}}=+\,\frac{g_{m}}2\,R_{D}' $$

non-inverting: $v_{in}\uparrow\;\Rightarrow\;I_{D1}\uparrow\;
\Rightarrow I_{D2}=I_{1}-I_{D1}\downarrow\;\Rightarrow\;
V_{DD}-I_{D2}R_{D}\uparrow$.
In general $v_{out}= \dfrac{g_{m1}g_{m2}}{g_{m1}+g_{m2}}R_{D}'
\,(v_{in}-v_{b})$; a common mode $v_{in}=v_{b}$ gives,
ideally, no output.  A signal on $V_{b}$ is amplified with
$-g_{m}R_{D}'/2$, so $V_{b}$ must be a clean a-c ground.
The gain is half that of a common source stage of the same
$g_{m}$ and $R_{D}$ - the price of the dummy $M_{1}$ branch.

With $r_{o1}=r_{o2}=r_{o}$ the finite $r_{o}$, and the loading
of $M_{2}$'s source by $M_{1}$, give for the matched case

$$ A_{v}= \frac{g_{m}R_{D}'}{2+R_{D}'/r_{o}}
      =\frac{g_{m}}2\Bigl(R_{D}'\parallel 2r_{o}\Bigr)
      \;\xrightarrow[r_{o}\to\infty]{}\;\frac{g_{m}R_{D}'}2 . $$

A finite tail impedance $R_{1}$ replaces $g_{m1}+g_{m2}$ by
$g_{m1}+g_{m2}+1/R_{1}$ in $v_{x}$, a small correction for
$g_{m}R_{1}\gg1$, and produces finite common mode gain.

### Resistances, swing, bandwidth

* Input: gate input, $R_{in}\approx\infty$ at low frequency.
  The capacitance at the input is roughly
  $C_{gd1}+C_{gs1}g_{m2}/(g_{m1}+g_{m2})$, no Miller effect,
  $M_{1}$'s drain being a-c ground.
* Output: resistance into $M_{2}$'s drain with its source
  terminated in $R_{S}\approx R_{1}\parallel 1/g_{m1}$ is
  $R_{o2}\approx r_{o2}\bigl[1+g_{m2}R_{S}\bigr]+R_{S}
  \approx 2r_{o}$ matched, so

$$ R_{out}=R_{D}\parallel R_{o2}\approx R_{D}\quad (R_{D}\ll r_{o}). $$

* Swing: $V_{out,max}\approx V_{DD}$ ($M_{2}$ off),
  $V_{out,min}\approx V_{DD}-I_{1}R_{D}$, limited in practice
  by $M_{2}$ saturation, $V_{out}\ge V_{b}-V_{TH}$.
* Poles: a low impedance pole at $X$,
  $R_{X}\approx1/(g_{m1}+g_{m2})$, $C_{X}=C_{gs1}+C_{gs2}+\cdots$,
  usually non-dominant, and the dominant output pole
  $ \approx \bigl[\,2\pi R_{out}(C_{L}+C_{db2}+C_{gd2})\bigr]^{-1}$.
  There is essentially no Miller multiplication.

In short, it is the single-ended-input, single-ended-output
NMOS differential pair: a source follower $M_{1}$ current-steering
a common-gate $M_{2}$, gain $+g_{m}R_{D}/2$, high input impedance,
output impedance $\approx R_{D}$, used universally as the input
stage of differential amplifiers and comparators.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly identifies the source-coupled pair as a source follower driving a common-gate stage, with M2 biased at Vb and the output at its drain. The stated small-signal gain is non-inverting, consistent with the signal path.

answers.question: Explain why the output impedance of the circuit shown in the figure can be inductive.

answer.text:
$M_1$ is a source follower and $M_2$ is a current-source load. The inductive behaviour comes from $M_1$, its gate-source capacitance, and the finite resistance $R_S$ driving its gate.

To find $Z_{out}$, set $V_{in}=0$ and apply a test voltage $V_x$ at the output. Neglect $r_{o1}$ and $r_{o2}$ initially; they will simply appear in parallel at the end.

The gate node is loaded by $R_S$ to ground, $C_{gd}$ to $V_{DD}$ (ac ground), and $C_{gs}$ to the output node. KCL at the gate gives

$$
V_g\left[\frac{1}{R_S}+s(C_{gs}+C_{gd})\right]=sC_{gs}V_x ,
$$

so that

$$
V_{gs}=V_g-V_x
      =-\,\frac{1+sR_SC_{gd}}{1+sR_S(C_{gs}+C_{gd})}\,V_x .
$$

The test current (excluding $r_o$ currents) is $I_x=-g_mV_{gs}$, hence

$$
Z_{out}'(s)=\frac{V_x}{I_x}
 =\frac{1}{g_m}\,
   \frac{1+sR_S(C_{gs}+C_{gd})}{1+sR_SC_{gd}} .
$$

This has a zero at $\omega_z=1/[R_S(C_{gs}+C_{gd})]$ and a pole at the higher frequency $\omega_p=1/(R_SC_{gd})$. Between them $|Z_{out}|$ rises with frequency and $\angle Z_{out}>0$ — i.e. the current drawn lags the applied voltage, exactly as for an inductor.

If $C_{gd}$ is small, this reduces to the transparent form

$$
Z_{out}'(s)\;\approx\;\frac{1+sR_SC_{gs}}{g_m}
 \;=\;\frac{1}{g_m}+s\,\frac{R_SC_{gs}}{g_m}
 \;=\;\frac{1}{g_m}+sL_{eq},
\qquad 
L_{eq}=\frac{R_SC_{gs}}{g_m}.
$$

With $C_{gd}$ retained, $Z_{out}'$ is $1/g_m$ in series with $L_{eq}$ shunted by $C_{gs}/(g_mC_{gd})$. The complete result is approximately $Z_{out}\approx Z_{out}'\parallel r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2}$.

Physically: at low frequency $C_{gs}$ is open, the gate is held fixed through $R_S$, $V_{gs}=-V_x$, and the device presents the usual $1/g_m$. At higher frequency the output signal couples through $C_{gs}$ onto the gate; the gate can no longer be treated as fixed, and the voltage developed across $R_S$ by the $C_{gs}$ current reduces and phase-shifts $V_{gs}$. The $g_m$ current therefore lags $V_x$, which is the signature of an inductance. The transistor acts as a gyrator, converting the gate capacitance terminated in $R_S$ into an inductance at the source.

Note that $R_S=0$ kills the effect ($L_{eq}=0$, $Z_{out}=1/g_m$). This synthesized inductance can resonate with a capacitive load at the output, producing peaking and ringing — the familiar capacitive-load instability of source followers.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: It correctly identifies the source follower and the role of the finite gate resistance and Cgs, but omits the Cgs displacement current in the output test current. This gives an incorrect impedance and inductance, misses the high-frequency limit of Rs and the condition Rs > 1/gm, and incorrectly implies the impedance always rises.

answers.question: Explain why the output impedance of the circuit shown in the figure can be inductive.

answer.text:
The circuit is a source follower $M_{1}$ biased by the
current source $M_{2}$.  $M_{2}$, whose gate is at ac ground,
contributes essentially $r_{o2}$ in parallel with the output.
The interesting part is the impedance looking into the source
of $M_{1}$ when its gate is terminated in a resistance.

For the output resistance set $V_{in}=0$.  The gate of $M_{1}$
is then returned to ac ground through $R_{S}$.  Apply a test
voltage $V_{x}$ at the output and find the current $I_{x}$
drawn from the test source.  Neglect $r_{o1},r_{o2}$ and $C_{gd1}$
for the moment; they will be put back in parallel at the end.

The gate node is coupled to the source node by $C_{gs1}$.
Gate KCL gives

$$
\frac{V_{g}}{R_{S}}+(V_{g}-V_{x})sC_{gs1}=0
$$

i.e.

$$
V_{g}=V_{x}\,\frac{sC_{gs1}R_{S}}{1+sC_{gs1}R_{S}},\qquad
V_{gs1}=V_{g}-V_{x}= -\,\frac{V_{x}}{1+sC_{gs1}R_{S}} .
$$

KCL at the output node then gives, for the current entering
the source of $M_{1}$,

$$
I_{x}= -g_{m1}V_{gs1}+ (V_{x}-V_{g})sC_{gs1}
      =V_{x}\,\frac{g_{m1}+sC_{gs1}}{1+sC_{gs1}R_{S}} .
$$

Hence the impedance looking into the source is

$$
Z_{s}(s)=\frac{V_{x}}{I_{x}}=
\frac{1+sC_{gs1}R_{S}}{\,g_{m1}+sC_{gs1}\,},
\qquad 
Z_{out}\approx Z_{s}\;\big\|\;r_{o1}\;\big\|\;r_{o2} .
$$

At dc, $Z_{s}=1/g_{m1}$, the familiar source-follower result.
On $s=j\omega$,

$$
Z_{s}(j\omega)=
\frac{g_{m1}+\omega^{2}C_{gs1}^{2}R_{S}
      +j\omega C_{gs1}\big(g_{m1}R_{S}-1\big)}
     {g_{m1}^{2}+\omega^{2}C_{gs1}^{2}} .
$$

Therefore

$$
\operatorname{Im} Z_{s}(j\omega)=
\frac{\omega C_{gs1}\,(g_{m1}R_{S}-1)}
     {g_{m1}^{2}+\omega^{2}C_{gs1}^{2}} .
$$

If

$$
R_{S}>\frac{1}{g_{m1}}
$$

the imaginary part is positive: the terminal voltage leads
the terminal current, as for an inductor.  Indeed for
$\omega \ll g_{m1}/C_{gs1}$,

$$
Z_{s}\approx \frac1{g_{m1}}+sL_{eq},
\qquad
L_{eq}= \frac{C_{gs1}}{g_{m1}}\!\left(R_{S}-\frac1{g_{m1}}\right)
      =\frac{C_{gs1}\big(g_{m1}R_{S}-1\big)}{g_{m1}^{2}}>0 .
$$

More exactly, $Z_{s}$ is $1/g_{m1}$ in series with the parallel
combination of $L_{eq}$ and $R_{S}-1/g_{m1}$, in parallel with
$r_{o1}\|r_{o2}$.

Physically, $C_{gs1}$ tries to make the gate follow the
source voltage $V_{x}$, but it can do so only by charging
through $R_{S}$.  The gate therefore follows the output with
an $R_{S}C_{gs1}$ lag.  The resulting $V_{gs1}$, and hence the
$g_{m1}V_{gs1}$ current supplied by $M_{1}$, contains a
component in quadrature with, and lagging, $V_{x}$.  A lagging
current is precisely the terminal behaviour of an inductor.
With $R_{S}=0$ the gate is clamped and $Z_{s}=1/(g_{m1}+sC_{gs1})$,
resistive-capacitive; the finite gate resistance is essential.

This is an active, synthesized inductance, useful only over
roughly $1/(R_{S}C_{gs1})\lesssim\omega\lesssim g_{m1}/C_{gs1}$;
parasitic capacitances at the output eventually dominate.
In particular the inductive $Z_{out}$ can resonate with a
capacitive load, producing peaking and ringing in a source
follower.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly identifies the source follower and derives the output-impedance expression. It shows that the impedance is inductive when Rs > 1/gm1 and explains the role of Cgs1 and the gate resistance; the high-frequency limit Rs follows from the expression.

answers.question: Explain why the output impedance of the circuit shown in the figure can be inductive.

answer.text:
$M_1$ is a source follower and $M_2$, with fixed gate bias, is
essentially a current-source load. To find $Z_{out}$ set $V_{in}=0$,
so the gate of $M_1$ is returned to ac ground through $R_S$, and
apply a test voltage $V_x$ at the output.

Neglect $r_{o1},r_{o2}$ and $C_{gd1}$ for the moment; they will only
appear in parallel with the result. The important element is
$C_{gs1}$.

At the gate node,
$$
\frac{V_g}{R_S}+sC_{gs}(V_g-V_x)=0
$$
so that
$$
V_g=V_x\,\frac{sC_{gs}R_S}{1+sC_{gs}R_S},
\qquad
V_{gs}=V_g-V_x=-\,\frac{V_x}{1+sC_{gs}R_S}.
$$

The current drawn into the source of $M_1$ is
$$
I_x=-(g_m+sC_{gs})V_{gs}
     =(g_m+sC_{gs})\frac{V_x}{1+sC_{gs}R_S},
$$
hence the impedance looking into the source is
$$
Z_1(s)=\frac{V_x}{I_x}
      =\frac{1+sC_{gs}R_S}{\,g_m+sC_{gs}\,},
\qquad 
Z_{out}\approx Z_1\parallel r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2}.
$$

At $s=j\omega$,
$$
\operatorname{Im} Z_1(j\omega)
   =\frac{\omega C_{gs}\,(g_mR_S-1)}
          {g_m^{2}+(\omega C_{gs})^{2}} .
$$
Thus, if
$$
g_mR_S>1,
$$
then $\operatorname{Im}Z_1>0$: the output voltage leads the
output current, i.e. the output impedance is inductive.
For frequencies well below $g_m/C_{gs}$,
$$
Z_1(s)\approx \frac{1}{g_m}+s\,
       \frac{C_{gs}(R_S-1/g_m)}{g_m}
     =\frac1{g_m}+sL_{eq},
\qquad
L_{eq}\approx \frac{C_{gs}R_S}{g_m}.
$$

Physically, $V_{gs}$, and therefore the $g_m$ current, does not
respond instantly to $V_x$. A change in $V_x$ must change the
voltage on $C_{gs}$ through the finite resistance $R_S$, so $V_g$
follows $V_x$ imperfectly and with a phase lag. Consequently
$$
-g_mV_{gs}=\frac{g_m}{1+sC_{gs}R_S}V_x
$$
is a current that lags the applied voltage, exactly as the
current in an inductor lags its voltage. The circuit is a
gyrator: $C_{gs}$, acted on by $g_m$ and $R_S$, is reflected to
the source as an inductance $ \sim C_{gs}R_S/g_m$.

At low frequency $Z_{out}\approx 1/g_m\parallel r_{o1}\parallel r_{o2}$,
as usual. At intermediate frequencies the inductive term appears,
and it can resonate with a capacitive load at the output,
producing peaking or ringing. No physical inductor is present;
the energy storage is in $C_{gs}$.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly identifies the source follower and derives the output impedance, including the condition gm·RS > 1 for inductive behavior and the equivalent-inductance term. The phase-lag explanation is consistent with the mechanism; minor comments about neglected parasitics do not affect the main result.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in the figure.

answer.text:
Both devices are NMOS, with source and bulk to ground,
so there is no body effect. The connections are

$$
\begin{array}{c|ccc}
 & G & D & S\\ \hline
M_{1}&X&V_{out}&0\\
M_{2}&V_{out}&X&0
\end{array}
$$

i.e. the gate of each is tied to the drain of the other.
It is a cross-coupled pair with very asymmetric drain loads:
$R_{D1}$ in $M_{1}$ and the (ideal) current source $I_{in}$
in $M_{2}$. It is a regenerative, positive feedback cell --
in essence a MOS latch / negative resistance cell, not a
conventional linear amplifier.

### 1.  Formal d-c solution in saturation

Gate currents are zero, so KCL at $X$ gives, in any
finite d-c equilibrium,

$$
I_{D2}=I_{in}\tag{1}
$$

and at the output

$$
I_{D1}=\frac{V_{DD}-V_{out}}{R_{D1}} .\tag{2}
$$

With $k_{ni}=\mu_nC_{ox}(W/L)_i$, $\lambda\ne0$ in general,

$$\begin{aligned}
I_{in}&=\tfrac{k_{n2}}2\,(V_{out}-V_{th})^{2}(1+\lambda V_X)\\
\frac{V_{DD}-V_{out}}{R_{D1}}&=
 \tfrac{k_{n1}}2\,(V_{X}-V_{th})^{2}(1+\lambda V_{out}) .
\end{aligned}\tag{3}$$

For $\lambda\to0$ this decouples,

$$
\,V_{out}\approx V_{th}+\sqrt{\frac{2I_{in}}{k_{n2}}}\,,\qquad
\,V_{X}\approx V_{th}+\sqrt{\frac{2I_{D1}}{k_{n1}}}\,,\qquad
I_{D1}=\frac{V_{DD}-V_{out}}{R_{D1}}  \tag{4}
$$

with saturation requiring
$V_{out}\ge V_X-V_{th}$, $V_X\ge V_{out}-V_{th}$.
A SPICE operating point will often find (3)-(4).  It is,
however, unstable, as shown next.

### 2.  Small signals, loop gain

Let $C_X$ be the capacitance at $X$
($C_{gs1}+C_{db2}+\dots$) and $C_O$ at the output
($C_{gs2}+C_{db1}+\dots$).  With
$g_{mi},\,r_{oi}$ at the point (4),

$$\begin{aligned}
(sC_X+g_{o2})v_x+g_{m2}v_{out}&=i_{in}\\
g_{m1}v_x+(sC_O+G_D)v_{out}&=0
\end{aligned}\qquad 
G_D\equiv\frac1{R_{D1}}+\frac1{r_{o1}},\;\;g_{o2}=\frac1{r_{o2}} \tag{5}$$

Breaking the loop at the gate of $M_{1}$ (node $X$):
$M_{1}$ is a common-source stage,
$v_{out}/v_x=-g_{m1}(R_{D1}\!\parallel\! r_{o1})$;
$M_{2}$ is a second common-source stage returning a
signal to $X$ with gain $-g_{m2}r_{o2}$.  Hence

$$
L(s)=\frac{g_{m1}g_{m2}}
{(sC_X+g_{o2})(sC_O+G_D)},\qquad 
L(0)=g_{m1}g_{m2}r_{o2}\bigl(R_{D1}\!\parallel\! r_{o1}\bigr)>0 \tag{6}
$$

Two inversions make the feedback positive, and normally
$L(0)\gg1$ since it is the product of two intrinsic
stage gains.

Formally, from (5),

$$
\frac{v_{out}}{i_{in}}=
\frac{1}{\,g_{m2}-\dfrac{1}{g_{m1}r_{o2}(R_{D1}\!\parallel\! r_{o1})}\,}
\;\approx\;\frac{1}{g_{m2}}\frac{1}{1-1/L(0)}
\;\approx\;\frac1{g_{m2}} \tag{7}
$$

but this is the (differential) slope of the unstable
branch (3).  The characteristic equation $1-L(s)=0$ is

$$
(sC_X+g_{o2})(sC_O+G_D)-g_{m1}g_{m2}=0, \tag{8}
$$

whose constant term $g_{o2}G_D-g_{m1}g_{m2}<0$ for $L(0)>1$.
Hence one pole is in the right half plane, approximately

$$
s_{+}\approx
\frac{g_{m1}g_{m2}-g_{o2}G_D}{C_XG_D+C_Og_{o2}}>0,
$$

and the saturated bias point repels transients
regeneratively, with time constant $\approx 1/s_{+}$,
until a device leaves saturation.

### 3.  Negative port resistances

Apply a test voltage at the output with $i_{in}=0$ (a-c).
KCL at the floating node $X$ gives $g_{m2}v_{out}+v_x/r_{o2}=0$,
i.e. $v_x=-g_{m2}r_{o2}v_{out}$.  Thus

$$
R_{out}=\frac{v_{out}}{i_t}
=\left[\frac1{R_{D1}}+\frac1{r_{o1}}-g_{m1}g_{m2}r_{o2}\right]^{-1}
\;\approx\;-\,\frac{1}{g_{m1}g_{m2}r_{o2}}\;<\;0 . \tag{9}
$$

Similarly, looking into node $X$ with the output
terminated in $R_{D1}$,

$$
R_{X}= \left[\frac1{r_{o2}}-g_{m1}g_{m2}
\bigl(R_{D1}\!\parallel\! r_{o1}\bigr)\right]^{-1}
\approx -\frac{1}{g_{m1}g_{m2}(R_{D1}\!\parallel\! r_{o1})}<0 . \tag{10}
$$

$g_{m2}$ is set by the bias $I_{D2}=I_{in}$,
$g_{m2}\approx\sqrt{2k_{n2}I_{in}}$, and $g_{m1}$ by
$I_{D1}$ in (2), so $I_{in}$ controls $|R_{out}|$.
With an $LC$ tank at $V_{out}$ this negative resistance
can cancel the tank loss, $|R_{out}|<R_{p,\text{tank}}$,
giving a (nonlinearly amplitude-limited) oscillator;
without a tank it simply latches.

### 4.  Large-signal behaviour

The physically stable high state is

* $M_{1}$ essentially off, $M_{2}$ on in triode,
* $V_{out}\approx V_{DD}$ (no drop in $R_{D1}$),
* $I_{in}=k_{n2}\!\left[(V_{DD}-V_{th})V_X-V_X^{2}/2\right]$,
  $V_X$ small, $V_X<V_{th1}$.

Here $g_{m1}\approx0$, the loop is open, and the state is
stable.  As $I_{in}$ (or a disturbance at $X$) raises
$V_X$ toward $V_{th1}$, $M_{1}$ turns on, $V_{out}$ falls,
$M_{2}$ must raise $V_X$ further to keep carrying
$I_{in}$, and the loop gain passes through unity:
snap-action.  The trigger current is of the order of
$I_{D2}$ evaluated at $V_X\!\approx\! V_{th1}$, $V_{GS2}=V_{DD}$,

$$
I_{\text{trig}}\;\sim\;
k_{n2}\Bigl[(V_{DD}-V_{th})V_{th}-\tfrac12V_{th}^{2}\Bigr].
$$

After triggering, $M_{2}$ is off, $M_{1}$ is on in triode
carrying $\approx V_{DD}/R_{D1}$, $V_{out}\approx0$;
in the ideal model $V_X$ then runs to the compliance of
the $I_{in}$ source (in practice limited by the source,
leakage or breakdown, and a reset device is normally
added to discharge $X$).  The saturated point (4) is
the separatrix between the two basins.

In short: $M_{1}$-$M_{2}$ is a positive-feedback
cross-coupled latch presenting
$R_{out}\approx-1/g_{m1}g_{m2}r_{o2}$ at its output.
It is usable as a regenerative current-threshold
detector/sense amplifier and as a negative-resistance
oscillator cell, but the all-saturated operating point
(4) with formal transresistance $\approx1/g_{m2}$ is
unstable for the usual $g_{m1}g_{m2}r_{o2}(R_{D1}\!\parallel\!r_{o1})\gg1$.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly identifies M2’s gate as tied to Vout, the positive-feedback loop through M1 and M2, and its consequences: negative input resistance, instability, and latching. This meets the golden solution’s full-credit rule.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in the figure.

answer.text:
The two devices are NMOS, sources and bodies to ground.
$$
M_{1}: G=X,\;D=V_{out},\;S=0\qquad 
M_{2}: G=V_{out},\;D=X,\;S=0
$$
i.e. the gate of each is the drain of the other.  $M_{1}$ is a
common-source device with load $R_{D1}$; the drain of $M_{2}$ is
loaded by the (high impedance) current source $I_{in}$.
It is a cross coupled, positive feedback, pair - in ordinary
sizes a latch, not a stable linear transimpedance amplifier.

Let $\beta_i=\mu_nC_{ox}(W/L)_i$, $V_{TH}$ the (common) threshold,
$\lambda =0$ for the essentials.  Gate currents are zero, so in
any internal d-c equilibrium

$$\;I_{in}=I_{D2}\;\qquad 
V_{out}=V_{DD}-I_{D1}R_{D1} \tag{1}$$

$$ 
I_{D1}= \tfrac{\beta_1}{2}(V_X-V_{TH})^{2}\;\;{\rm sat.},\qquad
I_{D2}= \beta_{2}\!\left[(V_{out}-V_{TH})V_X-\tfrac12V_X^{2}\right]\;\;{\rm lin.\;etc.}
$$

### The $I$--$V$ seen at $X$

Let $I_X=I_{D2}$ be the current the $M_1M_2R_{D1}$ network sinks
from node $X$, $V_{out}$ being allowed to follow $V_X$ through
$M_1,R_{D1}$.

* $V_X<V_{TH}$: $M_1$ off, $V_{out}=V_{DD}$, $M_2$ in the linear
region with $V_{GS2}=V_{DD}$,
$$
I_X=\beta_2\big[(V_{DD}-V_{TH})V_X-\tfrac12V_X^{2}\big],\qquad 
\frac{dI_X}{dV_X}>0 .
$$

* $V_X>V_{TH}$: $M_1$ turns on,
$$
V_{out}\approx V_{DD}-\frac{\beta_1R_{D1}}2\,(V_X-V_{TH})^{2}
\tag{2}$$
falls, hence $V_{GS2}=V_{out}$ falls.  With $M_2$ still
essentially linear,
$$
I_X=\beta_2\big[(V_{out}(V_X)-V_{TH})V_X-\tfrac12V_X^{2}\big].
$$
$I_X(V_X)$ rises, reaches a maximum, and then falls to
$\approx0$ when $V_{out}<V_{TH}$ turns $M_2$ off.  It is a
voltage controlled negative differential resistance
characteristic

```
 Ix ^          I_T+
    |           /\
    |          /  \   dIx/dVx < 0 : unstable
    |         /    \____  M2 off
    |        /
    +------------------------> Vx
                 VTH
```

A horizontal load line $I_X=I_{in}$ intersects the rising part
in a stable point, the falling part in an unstable point.
For $I_{in}$ larger than the peak there is no internal
intersection at all.

Indeed, about a both-on saturated point, with $C_X,C_{out}$
the node capacitances,

$$\begin{aligned}
C_X\dot v_x&=-g_{ds2}v_x-g_{m2}v_{out}\\
C_{out}\dot v_{out}&=-g_{m1}v_x-\big(R_{D1}^{-1}+g_{ds1}\big)v_{out}
\end{aligned}\qquad 
v_{out}=-g_{m1}(R_{D1}\!\parallel r_{o1})v_x $$

The (positive) loop gain round $v_x\to v_{out}\to i_{d2}\to v_x$ is

$$
\,T=g_{m1}(R_{D1}\!\parallel r_{o1})\;g_{m2}r_{o2}\,>0
$$

$v_x\uparrow\;\Rightarrow\;v_{out}\downarrow\;\Rightarrow\;
i_{d2}\downarrow\;\Rightarrow\;v_x\uparrow$ still more.
Formally

$$
\frac{v_{out}}{i_{in}}=
\frac{-\,g_{m1}(R_{D1}\!\parallel r_{o1})}
{\,r_{o2}^{-1}-g_{m1}g_{m2}(R_{D1}\!\parallel r_{o1})\,}
\approx\frac1{g_{m2}},\qquad
R_{X}\equiv\frac{v_x}{i_{in}}=
\frac{r_{o2}}{1-T}\approx
-\,\frac{1}{g_{m1}g_{m2}(R_{D1}\!\parallel r_{o1})}\;\;{\rm for}\;T\gg1,
$$

i.e. a negative resistance at $X$.  For $T<1$ this would be a
stable positive-feedback amplifier of enhanced gain $ \propto
1/(1-T)$; in practice $g_mr_o\gg1$ and $T\gg1$, the both-on
point, e.g.
$V_{out}=V_{TH}+\sqrt{2I_{in}/\beta_2}$,
$V_X=V_{TH}+\sqrt{2(V_{DD}-V_{out})/\beta_1R_{D1}}$, is a saddle,
unobservable in steady state.

### The two usable states

1. Output high.  $M_1$ (essentially) off, $M_2$ on, linear:
$$
V_{out}\approx V_{DD},\qquad 
I_{in}= \beta_2\big[(V_{DD}-V_{TH})V_X-\tfrac12V_X^{2}\big],
$$
$V_X$ small.  Stable while the loop gain on this branch is
$<1$.

2. Output low, railed.  $V_{out}$ has been driven below
$V_{TH}$, $M_2$ is off, $M_1$ is hard on.  In the ideal model
$V_X$ is driven to the compliance limit $V_{X,\max}$ of the
$I_{in}$ source ($\sim V_{DD}$ in practice), and, with $M_1$
in the linear region,
$$
\frac{V_{DD}-V_{out,L}}{R_{D1}}\approx
\beta_1\big[(V_{X,\max}-V_{TH})V_{out,L}-\tfrac12V_{out,L}^{2}\big]
\;\;\approx\;\;
\frac{V_{DD}}{1+\beta_1R_{D1}(V_{X,\max}-V_{TH})}\ll V_{DD}.
$$
The loop is opened by $M_2$ being off.

### Trip current

To first order regeneration starts when $V_X$ reaches
$V_{TH1}$ with $V_{out}\approx V_{DD}$, i.e. for $V_{DD}>2V_{TH}$

$$
\,I_{T+}\;\approx\;I_{D2}\big|_{V_{GS}=V_{DD},\,V_{DS}=V_{TH}}
      =\beta_{2}V_{TH}\Bigl(V_{DD}-\tfrac32V_{TH}\Bigr)\,  .
$$

Exactly, in the square law model, the trip is the peak of
$I_X(V_X)$, $dI_X/dV_X=0$, i.e. $T=1$ on the high branch:
with (2), in the linear-$M_2$/saturated-$M_1$ region,
$$
V_{out,T}-V_{TH}-V_{X,T}=R_{D1}\,\beta_1(V_{X,T}-V_{TH})V_{X,T},
\qquad 
I_{T+}= \beta_2\big[(V_{out,T}-V_{TH})V_{X,T}-\tfrac12V_{X,T}^{2}\big].
$$
Increasing $\beta_2$ raises $I_{T+}$; increasing $\beta_1$ or
$R_{D1}$ makes $V_{out}$ fall faster, strengthens the feedback
and lowers $I_{T+}$.  Once past the peak,
$v_x$ grows essentially exponentially: $M_1$ pulls $V_{out}$
down, $M_2$ sinks less and less of $I_{in}$, $V_X$ rises
further, until $M_2$ is off and $V_{out}$ is low.  Pulling
$V_X$ back down, by a reset device or by an $I_{in}$ that can
sink current, until $V_{out}(V_X)$ rises to $V_{TH2}$,
turns $M_2$ on and regenerates in the opposite direction.

In short: a regenerative NMOS latch / current-mode trip
circuit, presenting a negative resistance at $X$, with a
high output $\approx V_{DD}$ for $I_{in}<I_{T+}$ and a latched
low output for $I_{in}>I_{T+}$.  It is used, with an explicit
reset, as a current comparator, latch/sense element and
negative-resistance element; with only a unidirectional
ideal $I_{in}$ it trips once and must be reset externally.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly identifies that M2’s gate is tied to Vout, recognizes the positive-feedback loop, and explains its negative input resistance and regenerative latching behavior.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in the figure.

answer.text:
M1 and $M_{2}$ are NMOS devices with source and bulk to ground,
hence with no body effect.

$$\begin{aligned}
M_{1}:&\qquad G=X,\quad D=V_{out},\quad S=0\\
M_{2}:&\qquad G=V_{out},\quad D=X,\quad S=0
\end{aligned}$$

$M_{1}$ is a common source stage $X\to V_{out}$ with load $R_{D1}$.
$M_{2}$ is a common source stage $V_{out}\to X$ whose drain load
is, ideally, the input current source.  Two inverting stages are
connected in a ring: it is a regenerative, i.e. positive feedback,
circuit.

### DC, formal

Gate currents are zero, so at $X$ and at the output

$$ I_{D2}=I_{in},\qquad 
I_{D1}=\frac{V_{DD}-V_{out}}{R_{D1}} \tag{1}$$

with, in saturation and $\beta_i=\mu_nC_{ox}(W/L)_i$,

$$\begin{aligned}
I_{D2}&=\tfrac12\beta_2\,(V_{out}-V_{TH})^{2}(1+\lambda V_X)\\
I_{D1}&=\tfrac12\beta_1\,(V_{X}-V_{TH})^{2}(1+\lambda V_{out}) .
\end{aligned}$$

For $\lambda\approx0$

$$ V_{out}\approx V_{TH}+\sqrt{\frac{2I_{in}}{\beta_2}},\qquad
V_{X}\approx V_{TH}+\sqrt{\frac{2I_{D1}}{\beta_1}},\qquad
I_{D1}= \frac{V_{DD}-V_{out}}{R_{D1}} .$$

$M_{2}$ must take exactly $I_{in}$; $V_{out}$ is essentially the
$V_{GS2}$ needed to do so.  $M_{1}$ and $R_{D1}$ must then produce
that $V_{out}$, which fixes $V_X=V_{GS1}$.  Both saturated requires

$$V_{out}\ge V_X-V_{TH},\qquad V_X\ge V_{out}-V_{TH}.$$

### Small signal

Put $v_{gs1}=v_x$, $v_{gs2}=v_{out}$.  KCL at $X$ and at the output,
with $R'\equiv R_{D1}\parallel r_{o1}$, is

$$\begin{aligned}
i_{in}&=g_{m2}v_{out}+\frac{v_x}{r_{o2}} &&\text{at }X \tag{2}\\
0&=g_{m1}v_x+v_{out}\!\left(\frac1{R_{D1}}+\frac1{r_{o1}}\right)
   &&\text{at }V_{out} \tag{3}
\end{aligned}$$

From (3) the $M_{1}$ stage gain is

$$\frac{v_{out}}{v_x}=-g_{m1}R'=-g_{m1}(R_{D1}\parallel r_{o1}) .$$

Solving (2)-(3),

$$\,R_m\equiv\frac{v_{out}}{i_{in}}
      =\frac{1}{\,g_{m2}-\dfrac{1}{g_{m1}R'r_{o2}}\,}\,  \tag{4}$$

$$\,R_{in}\equiv\frac{v_x}{i_{in}}
      =\frac{1}{\,1/r_{o2}-g_{m1}g_{m2}R'\,}
      =-\frac{1}{g_{m1}g_{m2}R'-1/r_{o2}}\,  \tag{5}$$

i.e. for $r_o\to\infty$

$$\frac{v_{out}}{i_{in}}\approx\frac1{g_{m2}},\qquad
      \frac{v_x}{i_{in}}\approx-\frac{1}{g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{D1}}<0 .$$

The input resistance at $X$ is negative.  Physically, a larger
$I_{in}$ requires a larger $V_{GS2}=V_{out}$.  To obtain a larger
$V_{out}$, $M_{1}$ must conduct less through $R_{D1}$, so $V_X$
must fall: $dV_X/dI_{in}<0$.

The resistance at the output, $i_{in}=0$ (a.c.) and $R_{D1}$
included, is likewise

$$R_{out}=
\frac{1}{\;1/R_{D1}+1/r_{o1}-g_{m1}g_{m2}r_{o2}\;}
\approx -\frac{1}{g_{m1}g_{m2}r_{o2}}<0 .$$

### Loop gain and stability

Breaking the loop at the gate of $M_{2}$,

$$L = \bigl(g_{m1}R'\bigr)\bigl(g_{m2}r_{o2}\bigr)>0,$$

the product of the two (negative) stage gains.
With capacitances $C_X,C_{out}$ the linearised characteristic
equation is, in essence,
$(sC_X+1/r_{o2})(sC_{out}+1/R')-g_{m1}g_{m2}=0$.
Its determinant is negative, i.e. there is a right-half-plane
pole, when

$$L=g_{m1}g_{m2}(R_{D1}\parallel r_{o1})r_{o2}>1,$$

which is normally true, since $g_mr_o\gg1$.  Hence the
both-saturated operating point above is the metastable point
of a latch, not a stable linear operating point.  The circuit
regenerates to e.g. $V_{out}\approx V_{DD}$, $V_X\approx0$,
$M_{1}$ off, $M_{2}$ in triode sinking $I_{in}$; the opposite
state is reached with a real, supply-limited $I_{in}$ source
clamping $V_X$ high and $V_{out}$ low.

In short: formally a transimpedance $v_{out}/i_{in}\approx1/g_{m2}$
with a small negative input (and output) resistance
$-1/g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{D1}$.  With normal intrinsic gains
it is a positive-feedback latch / negative-resistance element,
useful for regeneration, hysteresis and oscillation, and usable
as a linear amplifier only if the loop gain is made $<1$, e.g.
by a sufficiently low shunt resistance at node $X$.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in the figure.

answer.text:
The circuit is a two stage shunt-shunt feedback
transimpedance amplifier.  $M_{1}$ is a common gate input
device, $M_{2}$ a common source gain device, $R_{F}$ returns
a current from the output to the input node.  $V_{b}$ is ac
ground.  Let the (small signal) voltage at the source of
$M_{1}$ be $v_{in}$, at $X$ be $v_{x}$, at the output $v_{out}$.
Body effect is absent for the symbols as drawn; for a common
substrate replace $g_{m1}$ by $g_{m1}+g_{mb1}$ in what follows.

In dc, with $I_{in}$ the dc value of the input source,

$$\begin{aligned}
v_{in0}&=V_{b}-V_{GS1}, \qquad v_{x0}=V_{GS2}\\
I_{D1}&=\frac{V_{DD}-v_{x0}}{R_{D1}},\qquad 
I_{D2}= \frac{V_{DD}-v_{out0}}{R_{D2}}+\frac{v_{in0}-v_{out0}}{R_{F}}\\
\frac{v_{in0}-v_{out0}}{R_{F}}&=I_{in0}+I_{D1}
\end{aligned}$$
i.e. $R_{F}$ also carries bias current.  Saturation requires
$v_{x}\ge V_{b}-V_{TH1}$ for $M_{1}$ and $v_{out}\ge v_{x}-V_{TH2}$
for $M_{2}$.

### Small signal forward path

$$\begin{aligned}
i_{d1}&=-g_{m1}v_{in}+\frac{v_{x}-v_{in}}{r_{o1}}\\
i_{d2}&=\phantom{-}g_{m2}v_{x}+\frac{v_{out}}{r_{o2}}
\end{aligned}$$

Node $X$: $v_{x}/R_{D1}+i_{d1}=0$, whence

$$
 \frac{v_{x}}{v_{in}}=A_{1}
      =\Bigl(g_{m1}+\frac1{r_{o1}}\Bigr)\bigl(R_{D1}\!\parallel\! r_{o1}\bigr)
      \approx g_{m1}\bigl(R_{D1}\!\parallel\! r_{o1}\bigr) \tag{1}
$$
the usual non-inverting CG gain.  The resistance looking
into the source of $M_{1}$ alone, i.e. with $R_{F}$ removed, is

$$
R_{in,CG}=\frac{v_{in}}{-i_{d1}}=\frac{R_{D1}+r_{o1}}{1+g_{m1}r_{o1}}
          =\frac{R_{D1}}{A_{1}}\approx\frac1{g_{m1}} . \tag{2}
$$

Node out, with $R_{2}=R_{D2}\parallel r_{o2}$,

$$
\frac{v_{out}}{R_{D2}}+i_{d2}+\frac{v_{out}-v_{in}}{R_{F}}=0
$$

$$
\,v_{out}= \bigl(R_{2}\!\parallel\! R_{F}\bigr)
        \left(\frac{v_{in}}{R_{F}}-g_{m2}v_{x}\right)\,
$$

i.e. the (loaded) voltage gain from the input node is

$$
 A_{v}\equiv\frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}}
      =\bigl(R_{2}\!\parallel\! R_{F}\bigr)\Bigl(\frac1{R_{F}}-g_{m2}A_{1}\Bigr)
      \approx -g_{m2}A_{1}\bigl(R_{2}\!\parallel\! R_{F}\bigr)
      \approx -g_{m1}g_{m2}(R_{D1}\!\parallel\! r_{o1})(R_{D2}\!\parallel\! r_{o2})  \tag{3}
$$
for $g_{m2}A_{1}R_{F}\gg1$ and $R_{F}\gg R_{2}$.  The $1/R_{F}$
term is the feedforward through $R_{F}$.  An increase in
$v_{in}$ raises $v_{x}$ and lowers $v_{out}$: the loop
through $R_{F}$ is negative.

### Closed loop transimpedance and input resistance

KCL at the input, with $i_{RF}$ taken from output to input
as drawn,

$$
I_{in}+i_{RF}=-i_{d1}=\frac{v_{in}}{R_{in,CG}},\qquad
i_{RF}=\frac{v_{out}-v_{in}}{R_{F}}
$$

so that

$$
 I_{in}= \frac{v_{in}}{R_{in,CG}}+\frac{v_{in}-v_{out}}{R_{F}}
       =v_{in}\!\left[\frac{A_{1}}{R_{D1}}+\frac{1-A_{v}}{R_{F}}\right]. \tag{4}
$$

Hence

$$
\,R_{in}\equiv\frac{v_{in}}{I_{in}}
      =\frac{1}{\,1/R_{in,CG}+ (1-A_{v})/R_{F}\,}
      =R_{in,CG}\;\Big\|\;\frac{R_{F}}{1-A_{v}}\,  \tag{5}
$$

and the transimpedance is

$$
\;
{\cal R}_{T}\equiv\frac{v_{out}}{I_{in}}=A_{v}R_{in}
      =\frac{A_{v}}{\,1/R_{in,CG}+(1-A_{v})/R_{F}\,}
      =\frac{-R_{F}}{\,1-\dfrac{1+R_{F}/R_{in,CG}}{A_{v}}\,}\;
\tag{6}
$$

With $|A_{v}|\gg 1+R_{F}/R_{in,CG}$, i.e. with effective loop
gain

$$
T_{eff}\approx\frac{|A_{v}|}{R_{F}/R_{in,CG}}
      \approx\frac{g_{m2}(R_{D1}\!\parallel\! r_{o1})(R_{D2}\!\parallel\! r_{o2})}{R_{F}}\gg1,
$$

$$\;{\cal R}_{T}\approx -R_{F},\qquad 
       R_{in}\approx\frac{R_{in,CG}}{1+T_{eff}}\approx
       \frac{1}{g_{m1}+ (1+|A_{v}|)/R_{F}}\;  $$

In this limit $v_{in}=I_{in}R_{in}$ is very small - a quasi
virtual ground - and from $I_{in}+i_{RF}=v_{in}/R_{in,CG}$

$$
i_{RF}\approx -I_{in},
$$

i.e. essentially all of $I_{in}$ flows (input to output) in
$R_{F}$, producing $v_{out}\approx-I_{in}R_{F}$; only the small
error current $v_{in}/R_{in,CG}$ enters $M_{1}$ and is amplified.
Increasing $R_{F}$ increases $|{\cal R}_{T}|$ but decreases
$T_{eff}$.

For $r_{o1},r_{o2}\to\infty$,
$A_{1}=g_{m1}R_{D1}$, $R_{in,CG}=1/g_{m1}$,
$A_{v}\approx -g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{D1}(R_{D2}\!\parallel\! R_{F})$.

### Output resistance

Put $I_{in}=0$ (input source open) and apply a test voltage
$v_{t}$ at the output.  Then $v_{in}=v_{t}R_{in,CG}/(R_{in,CG}+R_{F})$,
$v_{x}=A_{1}v_{in}$, and

$$
\;
R_{out}= \frac{1}{\,1/R_{2}+ \dfrac{1+g_{m2}A_{1}R_{in,CG}}{R_{F}+R_{in,CG}}\,}
       =R_{2}\;\Big\|\;\frac{R_{F}+R_{in,CG}}{1+g_{m2}R_{D1}}
       \approx (R_{D2}\!\parallel\! r_{o2})\;\Big\|\;\frac{R_{F}}{g_{m2}R_{D1}}\;
\tag{7}
$$
since $A_{1}R_{in,CG}=R_{D1}$.  Feedback lowers $R_{out}$ below
$R_{D2}\parallel r_{o2}$; with an external load replace
$R_{D2}$ by $R_{D2}\parallel R_{L}$ throughout.

In short: $M_{1}$ gives a $\approx1/g_{m1}$ input termination and
first voltage gain $g_{m1}R_{D1}$, $M_{2}$ gives the second,
inverting, gain, and shunt-shunt feedback through $R_{F}$ sets
$v_{out}/I_{in}\approx -R_{F}$, and further lowers both $R_{in}$
and $R_{out}$ by about the loop gain.  This is the standard
low-input-impedance TIA used e.g. at a photodiode input; the
poles at $X$ and at the output are inside the loop, so in
practice a small capacitor is usually placed across $R_{F}$
for stability.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly identifies M1 as the common-gate input device, M2 as the common-source stage driven by X, and RF as negative feedback from output to input forming a transimpedance amplifier. It also gives the expected −RF transimpedance and low input resistance.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in the figure.

answer.text:
The circuit is a two stage transimpedance amplifier
with shunt-shunt feedback.  $I_{in}$ is e.g. a photodiode
current.  Let $A$ be the input node, the source of $M_{1}$,
$v_{a}$ its small signal voltage, $v_{x}$ the voltage at $X$ and
$v_{o}$ the output voltage.  As drawn the bodies are tied to the
sources, so there is no body effect.  $V_{b}$ and $V_{DD}$ are ac
grounds.

$M_{1}$ is a common gate device, gate at the fixed bias $V_{b}$,
drain loaded by $R_{D1}$.  $M_{2}$ is a common source device,
gate at $X$, drain loaded by $R_{D2}$.  $R_{F}$ returns a current
proportional to $v_{o}$ to the input node $A$: output voltage
sampling, current mixing at the input, i.e. shunt-shunt
negative feedback.  An increase of $i_{in}$ raises $v_{a}$,
lowers $V_{GS1}$ and $I_{D1}$, raises $v_{x}$, raises $I_{D2}$ and
lowers $v_{o}$; the current returned through $R_{F}$ opposes
$i_{in}$.  $A$ is a low impedance, approximately virtual earth,
node.

In dc, with $M_{1,2}$ in saturation,
$$\begin{aligned}
V_{A}&=V_{b}-V_{GS1}, &
V_{X}&=V_{DD}-I_{D1}R_{D1}=V_{GS2},\\
V_{out}&=V_{DD}-I_{D2}R_{D2},
\end{aligned}\qquad 
\begin{array}{ll}
V_{X}\ge V_{b}-V_{TH1}& M_{1}{\rm \ sat.}\\
V_{out}\ge V_{X}-V_{TH2}& M_{2}{\rm \ sat.}
\end{array}
$$
$R_{D1}$ thus sets $V_{GS2}$ and hence $I_{D2}$ for a given
$I_{D1}$.  The usable $|i_{in}|$ is about the available output
swing divided by $R_{F}$.

### Small signal gain

Put $R_{1}'=R_{D1}\!\parallel\! r_{o1}$, $R_{2}'=R_{D2}\!\parallel\! r_{o2}$
($R_{2}'$ may include a load).  At $X$, $i_{d1}=-v_{x}/R_{D1}$ and

$$ 
\frac{v_{x}}{v_{a}}=
\frac{g_{m1}+r_{o1}^{-1}}{R_{D1}^{-1}+r_{o1}^{-1}}
\equiv A_{1}\approx g_{m1}R_{1}' >0
\tag{1}
$$
the usual CG voltage gain.  At the output, with
$i_{RF}=(v_{o}-v_{a})/R_{F}$ in the direction shown,

$$
\frac{v_{o}}{R_{D2}}+g_{m2}v_{x}+\frac{v_{o}}{r_{o2}}
      +\frac{v_{o}-v_{a}}{R_{F}}=0
$$
i.e.
$$
A_{v}\equiv\frac{v_{o}}{v_{a}}
      =-\,\bigl(g_{m2}A_{1}-R_{F}^{-1}\bigr)\,
        \bigl(R_{2}'\!\parallel\! R_{F}\bigr)
      \approx -g_{m2}R_{2}'A_{1}
      \approx -g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{1}'R_{2}'<0 .
\tag{2}
$$
The CG stage gives the low input impedance and isolates the
large input capacitance from the Miller effect of $M_{2}$;
$M_{2}$ supplies most of the loop gain.

KCL at $A$, the current into the source of $M_{1}$ being
$v_{x}/R_{D1}$,

$$
 i_{in}= \frac{v_{x}}{R_{D1}}+\frac{v_{a}-v_{o}}{R_{F}}
       =v_{a}\!\left[G_{in1}+\frac{1-A_{v}}{R_{F}}\right],
\qquad 
G_{in1}\equiv\frac{A_{1}}{R_{D1}}
      =\frac{1+g_{m1}r_{o1}}{R_{D1}+r_{o1}} .
\tag{3}
$$
$1/G_{in1}=(R_{D1}+r_{o1})/(1+g_{m1}r_{o1})\approx1/g_{m1}$ is the
resistance looking into the source of $M_{1}$ with $R_{F}$ removed.
Hence the closed loop transimpedance is

$$
\,R_{m}\equiv\frac{v_{o}}{i_{in}}
      =\frac{A_{v}}{\,G_{in1}+(1-A_{v})/R_{F}\,}
      \approx
      -\,\frac{R_{F}}
             {\,1+\dfrac{1+G_{in1}R_{F}}{|A_{v}|}\,}\,
\tag{4}
$$

with loop gain, in this notation,
$T\approx |A_{v}|/(1+G_{in1}R_{F})$.
For $T\gg1$, i.e. $g_{m1}g_{m2}R_{1}'R_{2}'\gg 1+g_{m1}R_{F}$,

$$
\,v_{o}/i_{in}\;\approx\;-R_{F}\,
$$

to an accuracy $\sim 1/T$, essentially independent of
$g_{m},R_{D},r_{o}$.  In particular $i_{RF}=(v_{o}-v_{a})/R_{F}
\approx -i_{in}$: incrementally almost all of $i_{in}$ flows
in $R_{F}$, the source current of $M_{1}$ changing very little.
The minus sign is the reference direction of $i_{RF}$ in the
figure.

### Input and output resistance

From (3)

$$
\,R_{in,cl}=\frac{v_{a}}{i_{in}}
   =\frac{1}{G_{in1}+(1-A_{v})/R_{F}}
   =\Bigl(\frac1{G_{in1}}\Bigr)\Big\|\frac{R_{F}}{1-A_{v}}
   \approx\frac{R_{F}}{|A_{v}|}\ll\frac1{g_{m1}}\,  .
\tag{5}
$$
Shunt feedback at the input lowers the already low CG input
resistance by $\sim 1+T$.

With $i_{in}$ open, a test voltage at the output gives, for
$r_{o}\to\infty$ for brevity,

$$
R_{out,cl}=
\left[\frac1{R_{D2}}+
\frac{g_{m1}\bigl(1+g_{m2}R_{D1}\bigr)}{1+g_{m1}R_{F}}
\right]^{-1}
\approx
\bigl(R_{D2}\!\parallel\! r_{o2}\bigr)\;\Big\|\;
\frac{R_{F}+1/g_{m1}}{1+g_{m2}R_{1}'}\;,
\tag{6}
$$
i.e. voltage sampling lowers the output resistance well below
$R_{D2}\!\parallel\! r_{o2}$.  Feedback also improves linearity
and desensitises $R_{m}$ to device parameters, at the cost of
gain set accurately, and essentially only, by $R_{F}$.

### Frequency response, trade offs

There are poles at $A$, at $X$ and at the output,
$$\omega_{a}\sim\frac1{R_{in}C_{in}},\qquad
  \omega_{x}\sim\frac1{R_{1}'C_{X}},\qquad
  \omega_{o}\sim\frac1{R_{2}'C_{o}},$$
$C_{in}$ being the photodiode plus $C_{gs1}$ capacitance,
$C_{X}$ containing $C_{gs2}$ and the Miller multiplied
$C_{gd2}$, $C_{o}$ the load capacitance.  Feedback moves the
input pole up by $\approx 1+T$, but $\omega_{x}$ and $\omega_{o}$
are inside the loop; if they approach the loop crossover the
response peaks and can become unstable.  In practice a small
$C_{F}$ is usually put across $R_{F}$ to compensate the
$C_{in}$-$R_{F}$ pole.

Increasing $R_{F}$ increases $|R_{m}|$ directly, but lowers
$T\propto R_{F}^{-1}$ for large $R_{F}$, lowers bandwidth,
and its thermal noise current $4kT/R_{F}$ is input referred
directly.  Larger $g_{m1}$ lowers $R_{in}$, input referred
noise and the error in (4), at the cost of power and $C_{in}$.
Larger $R_{D1}R_{D2}$ increase $|A_{v}|$ and $T$ but cost
headroom and lower $\omega_{x},\omega_{o}$.  This CG-CS
shunt-feedback form is the standard wideband optical receiver
front end: $R_{m}\approx-R_{F}$, very low $R_{in}$, low
$R_{out}$, bandwidth largely set by $R_{F}C_{in}$ and the
$X$ and output poles.  If $M_{1}$'s body is the common substrate,
replace $g_{m1}$ by $g_{m1}+g_{mb1}$ in $A_{1}$ and $G_{in1}$.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in the figure.

answer.text:
The circuit is a two stage, shunt-shunt feedback
transimpedance amplifier.  $I_{in}$ is injected into a low
impedance node, $R_{F}$ returns a current proportional to
$V_{out}$ to that node, and

$$R_{m}\equiv {V_{out}\over I_{in}}\approx -R_{F}\qquad 
{\rm for\; large\; loop\; gain}$$

$M_{1}$ is a common gate device, gate at a-c ground at $V_{b}$,
input at its source, output at its drain, node $X$.
$M_{2}$ is a common source device, gate at $X$, output at its
drain.  Hence from the input node, call its small signal
voltage $v_{i}$, to $X$ the gain is positive, from $X$ to
$V_{out}$ negative, and from $I_{in}$ to $V_{out}$ negative.
$R_{F}$ is voltage sampling at the output and current mixing
in shunt at the input: a voltage-shunt feedback amplifier
whose stabilized quantity is $V_{out}/I_{in}$.

### Bias

With $V_{I}$ the d-c voltage at the source of $M_{1}$,

$$\begin{aligned}
V_{GS1}&=V_{b}-V_{I}, & I_{D1}&=f(V_{GS1})\\
V_{X}&=V_{DD}-I_{D1}R_{D1}\\
V_{GS2}&=V_{X}, & I_{D2}&=f(V_{X})\\
V_{out}&=V_{DD}-I_{D2}R_{D2}\\
V_{I}-V_{out}&=(I_{D1}+I_{in,dc})R_{F}
\end{aligned}$$

the last being KCL at the input node; the d-c current of
$M_{1}$ returns through $R_{F}$ to the output.  Saturation
requires in particular
$V_{X}\ge V_{b}-V_{TH1}$ for $M_{1}$ and
$V_{out}\ge V_{X}-V_{TH2}$ for $M_{2}$.  The $R_{F}$ loop
stabilises this point: e.g. $V_{out}\uparrow\to$ more current
returned through $R_{F}$ to the input $\to I_{D1}\downarrow\to
V_{X}\uparrow\to I_{D2}\uparrow\to V_{out}\downarrow$.

### Small signal gain

Put $g_{m1e}=g_{m1}+g_{mb1}$ if the bulk of $M_{1}$ is at
a-c ground, $g_{m1}$ if bulk is tied to its source.
$V_{b}$ and $V_{DD}$ are a-c ground.  At node $X$,
$i_{d1}=-v_{x}/R_{D1}$ and
$i_{d1}=-g_{m1e}v_{i}+(v_{x}-v_{i})/r_{o1}$, i.e.

$$ 
{v_{x}\over v_{i}}\equiv A_{X}=
{(g_{m1e}r_{o1}+1)R_{D1}\over R_{D1}+r_{o1}}
\;\approx\;g_{m1e}\,(R_{D1}\!\parallel\! r_{o1})>0
$$
the familiar CG gain.  The resistance looking into the
source of $M_{1}$, with no $R_{F}$, is
$$
R_{C}={R_{D1}\over A_{X}}=
{R_{D1}+r_{o1}\over g_{m1e}r_{o1}+1}\approx {1\over g_{m1e}} .
$$

At the output, with $i_{RF}=(v_{out}-v_{i})/R_{F}$ in the
direction shown,
$$
{v_{out}\over v_{i}}\equiv A_{v}=
{-g_{m2}A_{X}+1/R_{F}\over 
1/R_{D2}+1/r_{o2}+1/R_{F}}
\;\approx\;-g_{m2}A_{X}\,
\bigl(R_{D2}\!\parallel\! r_{o2}\!\parallel\! R_{F}\bigr)<0 .
$$
The $1/R_{F}$ term is the small non-inverting feedthrough
through $R_{F}$.  Unloaded,
$|A_{v0}|\approx A_{1}A_{2}$ with
$A_{1}\approx g_{m1e}(R_{D1}\!\parallel\! r_{o1})$,
$A_{2}\approx g_{m2}(R_{D2}\!\parallel\! r_{o2})$.

KCL at the input,
$\,i_{in}=v_{x}/R_{D1}+(v_{i}-v_{out})/R_{F}$, gives
$$
{ i_{in}\over v_{i}}=
{A_{X}\over R_{D1}}+{1-A_{v}\over R_{F}},\qquad
R_{in}={v_{i}\over i_{in}}=
R_{C}\;\Big\|\;{R_{F}\over 1-A_{v}} 
$$
i.e. the CG resistance $R_{C}$ in parallel with $R_{F}$
Miller-shunted by the inverting gain to the output.
The (exact within this model) transresistance is
$R_{m}=A_{v}R_{in}$.

Define the effective loop gain for current return
$$
T\approx {|A_{v0}|R_{C}\over R_{F}}
      ={g_{m2}(R_{D2}\!\parallel\! r_{o2})R_{D1}\over R_{F}} .
$$
Then, for $g_{m}r_{o}\gg1$,
$$
\,R_{in}\approx {R_{C}\over 1+T}\approx
{{1/g_{m1e}}\over 1+T}\,,\qquad
\,R_{m}\approx -R_{F}\,{T\over 1+T}
      =-\Bigl[R_{F}\;\Big\|\;
        g_{m2}R_{D1}(R_{D2}\!\parallel\! r_{o2})\Bigr]\,  .
$$
For $T\gg1$, $R_{m}\to -R_{F}$, $R_{in}\to R_{F}/|A_{v0}|$,
$v_{i}$ is almost clamped, and essentially all of
$\Delta i_{in}$ flows (opposite to the arrow shown) through
$R_{F}$: $v_{out}\approx -i_{in}R_{F}$.  The sign is as
expected: $i_{in}\uparrow\to v_{i}\uparrow$ slightly $\to
I_{D1}\downarrow\to v_{X}\uparrow\to I_{D2}\uparrow\to
v_{out}\downarrow$, and $R_{F}$ returns this to the input,
closing a negative loop.  Feedback also improves linearity
by $\sim 1+T$.

At the output, with $I_{in}$ open,
$$
R_{out}=
\Bigl[{1\over R_{D2}\!\parallel\! r_{o2}}+
{1+g_{m2}R_{D1}\over R_{F}+R_{C}}\Bigr]^{-1}
\;\approx\;R_{D2}\!\parallel\! r_{o2}\;\;{\rm for}\;R_{F}\ {\rm large},
$$
in series with any external load $R_{L}\parallel R_{D2}$.

### Dynamics and tradeoffs

There are high impedance poles at $X$,
$\omega_{pX}\!\approx\!1/[(R_{D1}\!\parallel\! r_{o1})C_{X}]$
with $C_{X}$ including $C_{gs2}$ and Miller $C_{gd2}$, and at
the output,
$\omega_{po}\!\approx\!1/[(R_{D2}\!\parallel\! r_{o2})C_{out}]$,
plus the input pole at the very low $R_{in}$ with the
(source/photodiode) capacitance at the source of $M_{1}$ -
the reason for using a CG rather than a CS input.  Two
gain poles inside the $R_{F}$ loop readily give peaking in
$R_{m}(s)$; in practice a small $C_{F}$ across $R_{F}$ is
used for compensation.  Increasing $R_{F}$ raises the
ideal $|R_{m}|$ but lowers $T$, $R_{in}$ falls less, bandwidth
and phase margin suffer, and $4kT/R_{F}$ falls.  Increasing
$R_{D1},R_{D2}$ or $g_{m2}$ raises $A_{v0}$ and $T$ at the
cost of headroom and of the $X$ and output poles; increasing
$g_{m1e}$ lowers $R_{C}$, the input pole resistance and the
input referred noise.  Noise referred to the input is
dominated by $R_{F}$ and by $M_{1}$; noise of $M_{2},R_{D1},
R_{D2}$ is referred back divided by the first stage gain
$A_{X}$.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in the figure.

answer.text:
The circuit is a shunt-shunt feedback transimpedance
amplifier.  The signal is a current injected at the low
impedance node $X$ and the output is the voltage at $Y\equiv V_{out}$.

$M_{1}$ is an NMOS common-gate device, $V_{b}$ being a dc bias.
$M_{2}$ is a PMOS device with source to $V_{DD}$, gate to the
output and drain to the input node $X$.  The bodies are tied to
the sources, so to first order there is no body effect.
Call the unlabelled current sink at $X$, $I_{B}$.  $I_{1}$ is the
drain load/bias of $M_{1}$.

Intuitively $M_{2}$ is the feedback device.  It senses $v_{out}$
and returns a current $g_{m2}v_{out}$ to the input node.  In
equilibrium this returned current must cancel $i_{in}$, whence
$v_{out}\approx i_{in}/g_{m2}$.  $M_{1}$ and $M_{2}$ are also the
circuit known as a flipped voltage follower, used here as a
shunt regulator at the input.

### DC operating point

At the output node, with no dc load,

$$ I_{D1}=I_{1} $$

so $M_{1}$ is biased entirely by $I_{1}$.  Hence, $\lambda=0$
for brevity,

$$ V_{X}=V_{b}-V_{GS1},\qquad 
V_{GS1}=V_{THN}+\sqrt{\frac{2I_{1}}{\mu_nC_{ox}(W/L)_1}} $$

i.e. the input node is held about a $V_{GS}$ below $V_{b}$, like
a source follower, but with very low impedance, see below.
At $X$

$$ I_{D2}=I_{B}-I_{1}-I_{in,dc}>0 $$

sets the current, and therefore $g_{m2}$, of the feedback device,
and

$$ V_{out}=V_{DD}-|V_{GS2}|,\qquad 
|V_{GS2}|=|V_{THP}|+\sqrt{\frac{2I_{D2}}
{\mu_pC_{ox}(W/L)_2}}\;. $$

Saturation requires in particular

$$ V_{out}\ge V_{X}+V_{ov1}=V_{b}-V_{THN}\quad (M_{1}),\qquad
V_{X}\le V_{DD}-|V_{ov2}|\quad (M_{2}),\qquad 
V_{out}\le V_{DD}-V_{ov,I_{1}}\quad (I_{1}). $$

A positive $i_{in}$ steals current from $M_{2}$: $I_{D2}$ falls,
$|V_{GS2}|$ falls and $V_{out}$ rises.  The (class A) positive
swing is limited by $M_{2}$ turning off, $i_{in}^{+}<I_{D2}$.
A negative $i_{in}$ demands more $I_{D2}$, $V_{out}$ falls, and
is limited by $M_{1}$ entering the triode region at
$V_{out}\approx V_{b}-V_{THN}$.

### Small signal transresistance

Let $R_{1}$ be the (finite) impedance of $I_{1}$, $R_{B}$ that of
$I_{B}$, $r_{o1},r_{o2}$ the transistor output resistances, and
$v_{x}$ the small signal voltage at $X$.  At $Y$

$$ \frac{v_{out}}{R_{1}}-g_{m1}v_{x}+\frac{v_{out}-v_{x}}{r_{o1}}=0 $$

i.e. a common-gate voltage gain from $X$ to $Y$

$$ A\equiv\frac{v_{out}}{v_{x}}=
\frac{g_{m1}+r_{o1}^{-1}}{R_{1}^{-1}+r_{o1}^{-1}}
\approx g_{m1}\,(R_{1}\parallel r_{o1})\;, $$
$A=1+g_{m1}r_{o1}$ for an ideal $I_{1}$.  At $X$, KCL gives

$$ i_{in}=g_{m2}v_{out}+\frac{v_{out}}{R_{1}}
      +v_{x}\!\left(\frac1{r_{o2}}+\frac1{R_{B}}\right) 
      +\text{(terms in }v_{out}/R_{1}\text{ already included)} $$

in compact form, with $v_{x}=v_{out}/A$,

$$\,R_{m}\equiv\frac{v_{out}}{i_{in}}
      =\frac{1}{\,g_{m2}+R_{1}^{-1}+
        \dfrac{r_{o2}^{-1}+R_{B}^{-1}}{A}\,}\approx\frac1{g_{m2}}\,  $$

for $g_{m}r_{o}\gg1$.  The sign is positive.  The gain is set
not by a resistor but by the feedback transistor: to cancel
$i_{in}$ at $X$ the drain current of $M_{2}$ must change by
$i_{in}$, i.e. $g_{m2}v_{out}\approx i_{in}$.  E.g. $g_{m2}=1\,{\rm mS}$
gives $R_m\approx1\,{\rm k\Omega}=60\,{\rm dB\Omega}$, low, process
dependent, and usually followed by a voltage gain stage.

The input node is a virtual earth.  Indeed

$$ \,R_{in}\equiv\frac{v_{x}}{i_{in}}=\frac{R_{m}}{A}
      \approx\frac{1}{g_{m2}\,g_{m1}\,(R_{1}\parallel r_{o1})}\,  $$

for ideal bias sources $R_{in}\approx1/(g_{m1}g_{m2}r_{o1})$,
orders of magnitude below the $1/g_{m1}$ of a plain common
gate stage.  The large loop gain, about
$(g_{m1}r_{o1})(g_{m2}r_{o2})$ for ideal $I_{1}$ when the loop is
broken at the gate of $M_{2}$, is responsible.  A large
capacitance at the input, e.g. a photodiode, therefore sees
only a few to a few tens of ohms.

Shunt feedback at the output also makes the output resistance low.
Applying a test voltage at $V_{out}$ gives, to first order,

$$ R_{out}\approx R_{1}\parallel\frac1{g_{m2}}\approx\frac1{g_{m2}}\qquad(R_{1}\ {\rm large}) $$

essentially the same number as $R_{m}$.  With a load $R_{L}$,
replace $R_{1}$ by $R_{1}\parallel R_{L}$ above; $R_{m}\approx1/g_{m2}$
as long as $R_{L}\gg1/g_{m2}$.

### Frequency response and stability

Let $C_{X}$ be the total capacitance at $X$ (input device,
$C_{gs1}$, $C_{db2}$, etc.) and $C_{Y}$ that at $Y$ ($C_{db1}$,
$C_{gs2}$, load, etc.), neglecting $r_{o}$ and feedforward
capacitors.  KCL at the two nodes gives

$$ \frac{V_{out}}{I_{in}}(s)\approx
\frac{1/g_{m2}}
{1+s\dfrac{C_{Y}}{g_{m2}}+s^{2}\dfrac{C_{X}C_{Y}}{g_{m1}g_{m2}} } $$

a two pole response with

$$ \omega_{0}=\sqrt{\frac{g_{m1}g_{m2}}{C_{X}C_{Y}}},\qquad
Q=\sqrt{\frac{g_{m2}C_{X}}{g_{m1}C_{Y}}}\;. $$

Approximately the poles are at $g_{m2}/C_{Y}$ and $g_{m1}/C_{X}$
when well separated.  Large $C_{X}$ or small $C_{Y}$ makes
$Q$ large: gain peaking, ringing, and, with the extra phase of
$C_{gd2}$ bridging $X$ and $Y$ and other parasitics, possible
instability.  In practice $C_{Y}$ is often increased, at the
cost of bandwidth $\sim g_{m2}/C_{Y}$, to get $Q\lesssim0.7$,
or $g_{m1}$ is increased to push the input pole out.
Increasing $g_{m2}$ raises bandwidth and lowers $R_{in}$ and
$R_{out}$, but lowers $R_{m}=1/g_{m2}$ - the usual gain-bandwidth
trade-off of a shunt-feedback TIA.

In summary: $M_{1}$ is a common-gate input device biased at
$I_{1}$; $M_{2}$ provides local active shunt feedback from
output voltage to input current.  It presents
$R_{in}\approx1/(g_{m1}g_{m2}r_{o1})$, $R_{out}\approx1/g_{m2}$ and
$V_{out}/I_{in}\approx1/g_{m2}$, with a second order response
set by the input and output node capacitances.  It is widely
used as a very wideband, low input impedance front end, e.g.
for photodiodes, at the price of low, $g_{m}$-determined
transresistance and of noise injected directly at $X$ by
$M_{2}$ and the bias sources.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in the figure.

answer.text:
The (unlabelled) sink at the input node is called $I_{B}$ below.
$X$ is the input node, $v_{x}$ its small signal voltage.

$$ 
M_{1}:{\rm NMOS,\ CG},\qquad 
M_{2}:{\rm PMOS,\ source\ to\ }V_{DD}
$$

$M_{1}$ has fixed gate bias $V_{b}$, drain at $V_{out}$ loaded by
$I_{1}$.  The gate of $M_{2}$ is $V_{out}$ and its drain is $X$.
$M_{2}$ is a local shunt feedback device from the output node
to the input node.  The $M_{1}$-$M_{2}$ pair is the flipped-voltage-
follower form of a regulated common-gate stage. It is a
shunt-shunt feedback transimpedance stage.

### 1.  Bias

Gate currents are zero, hence from KCL at the output node, exactly,

$$ I_{D1}=I_{1}\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad I_{S1}=I_{1} $$

and at $X$

$$ I_{D2}=I_{B}-I_{1}-I_{in,Q}\;>\;0 $$

i.e. $M_{2}$ carries whatever current $M_{1}$ and $I_{B}$ do not.
In saturation, to first order,

$$\begin{aligned}
V_{GS1}&=V_{tn}+V_{ov1}, &
V_{ov1}&=\sqrt{\frac{2I_{1}}{\mu_nC_{ox}(W/L)_1}}\\
V_{SG2}&=|V_{tp}|+V_{ov2}, &
V_{ov2}&=\sqrt{\frac{2I_{D2}}{\mu_pC_{ox}(W/L)_2}}
\end{aligned}$$

so that

$$\;V_{XQ}=V_{b}-V_{GS1}\;,\qquad 
       \;V_{out,Q}=V_{DD}-V_{SG2}\;  $$

$V_{X}$ is, to first order, independent of $I_{in}$: it is a
regulated node.  Large signal,
$V_{out}=V_{DD}-|V_{tp}|-\sqrt{2(I_{B}-I_{1}-I_{in})/\beta_{p2}}$,
whose incremental slope is $1/g_{m2}$ below.
Saturation requires e.g.

$$V_{out}-V_X\ge V_{ov1}\;\;{\rm i.e.}\;\;V_{out}\ge V_b-V_{tn},
\qquad V_{DD}-V_X\ge V_{ov2},$$

plus compliance of $I_{1}$, $V_{DD}-V_{out}\ge V_{ov,I1}$, and of
$I_B$, $V_X\ge V_{ov,B}$.  $I_{D2}>0$ sets the maximum positive
$I_{in}$.

### 2.  Low frequency small signal

Let $\tilde g_{1}=g_{m1}+g_{mb1}$ - the $g_{mb1}$ term is absent
if the body of $M_{1}$ is tied to its source as drawn.  $M_{2}$
has body $=$ source, so no body effect.  Let $R_O$ be the
resistance from the output node to a.c. ground, i.e. the
resistance of $I_{1}$ in parallel with any load, and $R_B$ that
of $I_B$.

$$\begin{aligned}
i_{d1}&=-\tilde g_{1}v_x+\frac{v_{out}-v_x}{r_{o1}}\\
i_{sd2}&=-g_{m2}v_{out}-\frac{v_x}{r_{o2}}
\qquad\text{(current $M_{2}$ delivers to $X$)}
\end{aligned}$$

Output KCL, $i_{d1}+v_{out}/R_O=0$, gives the source-to-drain
gain of $M_{1}$

$$ 
A_{xo}\equiv\frac{v_{out}}{v_x}
      =\frac{\tilde g_{1}+1/r_{o1}}{1/R_O+1/r_{o1}}
      =(1+\tilde g_{1}r_{o1})\,\frac{R_O}{R_O+r_{o1}}
      \approx \tilde g_{1}\,(r_{o1}\!\parallel\! R_O)  .
$$

Input KCL, $i_{in}=v_x/R_B-i_{sd2}-i_{d1}$, gives

$$ i_{in}=v_x\!\left(\frac1{R_B}+\frac1{r_{o2}}\right)
      +v_{out}\!\left(g_{m2}+\frac1{R_O}\right) $$

whence the closed loop transimpedance

$$
\,R_m\equiv\frac{v_{out}}{i_{in}}
      =\frac{1}{\,g_{m2}+1/R_O+
        \dfrac{1/R_B+1/r_{o2}}{A_{xo}} }\, 
$$

For ideal $I_{1},I_B$, $R_O,R_B\to\infty$, $A_{xo}=1+\tilde g_{1}r_{o1}$,

$$
R_m=\frac{1+\tilde g_{1}r_{o1}}
         {\,1/r_{o2}+g_{m2}(1+\tilde g_{1}r_{o1})\,}
    =\frac{1}{g_{m2}+\dfrac{1}{r_{o2}(1+\tilde g_{1}r_{o1})}}
    \;\approx\;\frac1{g_{m2}}\;  .
$$

It is non-inverting and intrinsically low: an increment of
$i_{in}$ cannot go into $M_{1}$, whose current is fixed by
$I_{1}$, nor into $I_B$; it must be taken up by $M_{2}$,
$\Delta i_{sd2}=-i_{in}$, requiring $\Delta v_{out}=i_{in}/g_{m2}$.

Input resistance, at $X$,

$$
R_{in}= \frac{v_x}{i_{in}}=\frac{R_m}{A_{xo}}
     =\frac{1}{\,1/R_B+1/r_{o2}+(g_{m2}+1/R_O)A_{xo}\,}
$$

i.e. with ideal sources, looking into the transistors,

$$
\,R_{in,tr}= \frac{1}{1/r_{o2}+g_{m2}(1+\tilde g_{1}r_{o1})}
      \approx\frac{1}{g_{m2}\tilde g_{1}r_{o1}}\,,
\qquad R_{in}=R_B\parallel R_{in,tr}.
$$

This is the ordinary CG value $\sim1/\tilde g_{1}$ divided by
the loop gain, below.  $v_x=i_{in}R_{in}$ is a very good
virtual earth.

Output resistance.  Applying a test source at $V_{out}$ with
$i_{in}$ open gives, for ideal bias sources,

$$
R_{out,d}=
\frac{(1+\tilde g_{1}r_{o1})+r_{o1}/r_{o2}}
     {g_{m2}(1+\tilde g_{1}r_{o1})+1/r_{o2}}
\;\approx\;\frac1{g_{m2}},
\qquad
R_{out}=R_{out,d}\parallel r_{I1}\parallel R_L\approx\frac1{g_{m2}} .
$$

Thus the stage is low-impedance at both ports, with
$R_m\approx R_{out}\approx1/g_{m2}$ and $R_{in}\ll1/g_{m1}$.

Feedback view: breaking the loop at the gate of $M_{2}$,
the return gain is

$$ T_{0}\approx g_{m2}\,(r_{o1}\parallel R_O)\gg1, $$

the $M_{2}\!\to\!X\!\to\!M_{1}\!\to\!V_{out}$ loop.
$R_{in}\approx (1/\tilde g_{1})/(1+T_{0})$ and
$R_m\approx (r_{o1}\!\parallel\!R_O)/(1+T_0)\approx1/g_{m2}$,
the classic shunt-shunt results with feedback transconductance
$g_{m2}$.

### 3.  Frequency behaviour, limits

With $C_X$ the total capacitance at $X$ (photodiode/source
capacitance, $C_{gs1}$, $C_{db2}$) and $C_O$ that at the output
($C_{gs2}$, $C_{db1}$, $C_L$, $I_{1}$ parasitics), neglecting
$C_{gd1}$ feedforward and $r_{o2}$,

$$
R_m(s)\approx
\frac{R_{D}/(1+g_{m2}R_D)}
{1+s\,\dfrac{C_X/\tilde g_{1}+R_DC_O}{1+g_{m2}R_D}
   +s^{2}\dfrac{C_XR_DC_O}{\tilde g_{1}(1+g_{m2}R_D)}},
\qquad R_D=r_{o1}\!\parallel\! r_{I1}.
$$

For $g_{m2}R_D\gg1$,

$$ R_m(s)\approx\frac{1/g_{m2}}
{1+s\!\left(\frac{C_O}{g_{m2}}+\frac{C_X}{\tilde g_{1}g_{m2}R_D}\right)
 +s^{2}\frac{C_XC_O}{\tilde g_{1}g_{m2}}},\qquad
\omega_{0}\approx\sqrt{\frac{\tilde g_{1}g_{m2}}{C_XC_O}} .$$

Nominally the input pole is pushed to $\approx1/R_{in}C_X$
and the output pole to $\approx g_{m2}/C_O$, both very high,
which is why the circuit is used in front of a photodiode.
It is however a two-pole loop: for $C_X\gg C_O$,
$Q\approx\sqrt{(g_{m2}/\tilde g_{1})(C_X/C_O)}$ can exceed
unity, giving peaking/ringing unless $C_O$, $g_{m1}$ or
compensation is chosen accordingly.

In summary: $M_{1}$ is a current buffer with fixed current
$I_{1}$, $M_{2}$ supplies the signal current to the input node
under control of $V_{out}$, giving a very low $R_{in}\approx
1/(g_{m1}g_{m2}r_{o1})$, a low $R_{out}\approx1/g_{m2}$ and a
modest, well controlled transimpedance $v_{out}/i_{in}\approx
1/g_{m2}$, normally followed by a voltage-gain stage if large
transimpedance is required.

answers.question: Analyze the circuit shown in the figure.

answer.text:
The node at the source of $M_{1}$ is the input node.
Call it $X$, and call the (unlabelled) sink at $X$, $I_{B}$.

$M_{1}$ is an NMOS common gate device, $V_{G1}=V_{b}$,
drain at $V_{out}$, source at $X$.  $M_{2}$ is a PMOS
common source device, source at $V_{DD}$, gate at $V_{out}$,
drain at $X$.  $I_{1}$ is the (active) drain load of $M_{1}$.
$I_{in}$ is injected into $X$ and $V_{out}$ is taken out:
it is a current to voltage converter, i.e. a transimpedance
amplifier, with shunt-shunt feedback through $M_{2}$.

### DC bias

KCL at $V_{out}$, no d.c. load,

$$ I_{D1}=I_{1} $$

KCL at $X$, for $I_{in,dc}=0$,

$$ I_{B}=I_{D1}+I_{D2}\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad 
I_{D2}=I_{B}-I_{1}>0 $$

in the quiescent point.
Hence

$$\begin{aligned}
I_{1}&\approx \tfrac12\mu_nC_{ox}(W/L)_1
\bigl(V_b-V_X-V_{THN}\bigr)^{2}  \\
V_X &\approx V_b-V_{THN}-V_{ov1},\qquad 
V_{ov1}=\sqrt{\frac{2I_{1}}{\mu_nC_{ox}(W/L)_1}}
\end{aligned}$$

i.e. to first order $V_X$ is pinned by $V_b$ and $I_1$, and

$$ I_{D2}\approx \tfrac12\mu_pC_{ox}(W/L)_2
\bigl(V_{DD}-V_{out}-|V_{THP}|\bigr)^{2},\qquad
V_{out}\approx V_{DD}-|V_{THP}|-V_{ov2} .$$

Saturation requires, e.g.,
$V_{out}-V_X\ge V_{ov1}$ for $M_1$ and
$V_{DD}-V_X\ge V_{ov2}$ for $M_2$.

Signal intuition: $I_{D1}$ is fixed by $I_{1}$.  An extra
$i_{in}$ at $X$ cannot go into $M_{1}$ or into $I_{B}$; it
must be compensated by a change in $I_{D2}$,
$\Delta I_{D2}\approx -i_{in}$.  For the PMOS,
$\Delta I_{D2}=-g_{m2}\Delta V_{out}$, so
$\Delta V_{out}\approx i_{in}/g_{m2}$, positive.

### Small signal

Let $g_1=g_{m1}+g_{mb1}$; $M_1$ has body effect, body
to ground, $M_2$ has body to $V_{DD}$, no body effect.
$I_1,I_B$ are ideal, i.e. a.c. open.

Drain currents, into $X$ for $M_2$ and into the drain for $M_1$,

$$\begin{aligned}
i_{d1}&=-g_1v_x+\frac{v_{out}-v_x}{r_{o1}}\\
i_{d2}&=-g_{m2}v_{out}-\frac{v_x}{r_{o2}}\; .
\end{aligned}$$

At the (open) output node $i_{d1}=0$, whence

$$0=-g_1v_x+\frac{v_{out}-v_x}{r_{o1}},\qquad 
\frac{v_{out}}{v_x}=1+g_1r_{o1}\equiv A_v $$

the intrinsic common-gate voltage gain from $X$ to the
output. At $X$, $i_{in}+i_{d1}+i_{d2}=0$, i.e. with $i_{d1}=0$

$$ i_{in}=g_{m2}v_{out}+\frac{v_x}{r_{o2}} .$$

Hence the closed loop transresistance

$$
\,R_m\equiv\frac{v_{out}}{i_{in}}
      =\frac{1+g_1r_{o1}}{\,g_{m2}\bigl(1+g_1r_{o1}\bigr)+1/r_{o2}\,}
      =\frac{1}{g_{m2}}\;\Big\|\; \bigl(1+g_1r_{o1}\bigr)r_{o2}
      \;\approx\;\frac1{g_{m2}}\,  $$

in the usual case $g_{m2}(1+g_1r_{o1})r_{o2}\gg1$.
This is shunt-shunt feedback: $M_2$ samples $v_{out}$
and returns the current $g_{m2}v_{out}$ to the input node.
The feedback factor is $g_{m2}$, the open-loop
transresistance is $A_vr_{o2}$, the loop gain is
$g_{m2}A_vr_{o2}\gg1$, and $R_m\to1/g_{m2}$, set by
$M_2$ bias and size, essentially independent of $r_o$'s.

Input resistance, at $X$ with the output open,

$$
\,R_{in}\equiv\frac{v_x}{i_{in}}
      =\frac{1}{\,g_{m2}\bigl(1+g_1r_{o1}\bigr)+1/r_{o2}\,}
      \approx\frac{1}{g_{m2}(g_{m1}+g_{mb1})r_{o1}}\,  $$

very small, much smaller than $1/g_{m1}$.  $X$ is an
approximate virtual ground, $v_x=v_{out}/A_v$.  This is
the main attraction for e.g. a photodiode input: a large
input capacitance sees $R_{in}$ of tens of ohms.

Output resistance.  With $i_{in}$ open, applying $v_{test}$
at the output,

$$
R_{out}=
\frac{g_1+1/r_{o1}+1/r_{o2}}
     {\,g_{m2}\!\left(g_1+1/r_{o1}\right)+1/r_{o1}r_{o2}\,}
\;\approx\;\frac1{g_{m2}}\;,
$$

again lowered by the $M_2$--$M_1$ loop from the
$r_{o1},r_{o2}$ level to $\approx 1/g_{m2}$.  A finite
resistance $R_{I1}$ of $I_{1}$, or a load $R_L$, appears
in parallel with this and with $R_m$:
$R_m\approx (1/g_{m2})\|R_{I1}\|R_L\|A_vr_{o2}$.

In words: $M_1$ and $I_1$ give a large voltage gain
$A_v\approx (g_{m1}+g_{mb1})r_{o1}$ from the low
impedance input node to $V_{out}$; PMOS $M_2$ feeds
essentially all of a signal input current back as
$g_{m2}v_{out}$, fixing $v_{out}/i_{in}\approx1/g_{m2}$,
and dividing the input (and output) impedance by
roughly the loop gain.  Positive $i_{in}$ is limited
to about $I_{D2Q}$, when $M_2$ turns off; negative
$i_{in}$ is limited by $V_{out}$ falling to
$V_X+V_{ov1}$, putting $M_1$ in triode. ∎

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly identifies M1 as the common-gate NMOS and M2 as the PMOS feedback device driven by Vout, describes feedback to the input node, and derives very low input resistance with transimpedance and output resistance approximately 1/gm2.

answers.question: Does the circuit in the figure fail to oscillate if the three capacitors become arbitrarily large?

answer.text:
No. Increasing all three load capacitors only reduces the oscillation frequency.

Model each inverter near its switching point by a voltage gain $-A_0$ and output resistance $R_{\text{out}}$. The transfer function of one loaded stage is

$$ 
\frac{V_{out}}{V_{in}} = \frac{-A_0}{1 + s R_{\text{out}} C_L}  $$

For oscillation, the three inversions provide $180^\circ$, so each $RC$ pole must provide an additional $60^\circ$:

$$
\tan^{-1}\left(\omega_{\text{osc}} R_{\text{out}} C_L\right) = 60^\circ
\quad \Longrightarrow \quad
\omega_{\text{osc}} = \frac{\sqrt{3}}{R_{\text{out}} C_L}
$$

$$A(s)= -\,\frac{g_mr_o}{1+s r_oC_L}\equiv -\frac{A_0}{1+s/\omega_p},

\omega_p=\frac1{r_oC_L},\;\; A_0=g_mr_o .$$

$$(1+s/\omega_p)^{3}=-A_0^{3},$$

$$ \frac{s}{\omega_p}=-1+A_0e^{j\pi/3},\;-1+A_0e^{j\pi},\;-1+A_0e^{j5\pi/3} $$

so that a pair of poles is at

$$s=\omega_p\Bigl(-1+\frac{A_0}{2}\pm j\frac{\sqrt3}{2}A_0\Bigr).$$

They are in the right half plane iff

$$A_0=g_m r_o>2,$$

the usual Barkhausen condition for a 3-stage ring: at oscillation
each pole contributes $60^{\circ}$ of lag at $\omega_{osc}=\sqrt3\,\omega_p$,
where $|A|=A_0/2$.  A CMOS inverter biased at $V_M$, with both
devices saturated, has $(g_{mn}+g_{mp})(r_{on}\!\parallel\! r_{op})\gg2$.

scales all the ring poles toward the origin by $1/C_L$; it does
not move the right-half-plane pair into the left half plane.
In large-signal terms a transition simply takes
$\Delta t\sim C_LV_M/I_D$ to slew the next stage through its
threshold, and this transition propagates around the ring forever.

more slowly, e.g. in the linear model

oscillation.

Model an inverter about its switching point by its
small signal gain and its output pole,

$$

A_{0}=g_{m}r_{o},\qquad 
\omega_{p}=\frac{1}{r_{o}C_{L}} .
$$
