stages is

$$
L(s)=A(s)^{3}= \left[-\frac{A_{0}}{1+s/\omega_{p}}\right]^{3}.
$$

Each stage contributes $180^{\circ}$ from the inversion and
$-\tan^{-1}(\omega/\omega_{p})$ from the output pole. For a mode
of the ring the total phase around the loop must be $0\pmod{2\pi}$,
i.e. the three poles must supply $180^{\circ}$ in all, $60^{\circ}$
per stage:

$$
3\tan^{-1}\frac{\omega_{osc}}{\omega_{p}}=\pi
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad 
\tan^{-1}\frac{\omega_{osc}}{\omega_{p}}=60^{\circ},
$$

$$
\;\omega_{osc}= \sqrt{3}\,\omega_{p}= \frac{\sqrt{3}}{r_{o}C_{L}}\;
$$

At this frequency the magnitude contributed by one stage is

$$
|A(j\omega_{osc})|=
\frac{A_{0}}{\sqrt{1+(\omega_{osc}/\omega_{p})^{2}}}
= \frac{A_{0}}{\sqrt{1+3}}=\frac{A_{0}}{2},
$$

so that the loop magnitude at the phase condition is
$(A_{0}/2)^{3}$, independent of $C_{L}$.  Oscillation starts up
iff $A_{0}>2$, satisfied by a normal CMOS inverter, whatever
(finite) $C_{L}$ is.  Increasing $C_{L}$ moves $\omega_{p}$ down,
but $\omega_{osc}$ moves down in the same proportion, always
keeping $60^{\circ}$ of pole phase per stage and the same gain.

In large-signal terms there is no stable d-c point consistent
with an odd number of inversions in the loop; the common
threshold point is unstable for $A_{0}>2$.  A large $C_{L}$ merely
makes the nodes slew more slowly,
$T_{osc}\propto C_{L}V_{DD}/I_{D}\propto C_{L}$, so $f_{osc}\to0$ as
$C_{L}\to\infty$, but for any finite $C_{L}$ the circuit still
oscillates rail to rail.

$$

{\cal L}(\Delta f)\;\propto\;
\frac{1}{P}\left(\frac{f_{0}}{\Delta f}\right)^{2}
\;\propto\;
\frac{\;\overline{i_{n}^{2}}\;\Gamma_{rms}^{2}}
     {\,q_{\max }^{2}\,\Delta f^{2}},

because the transistors and the normalized waveform are
unchanged, whereas $q_{\max}$ doubles.  Hence
$$

   =\left(\frac{f_{0}'}{f_{0}}\right)^{2}
   =\frac1{4},
$$

answer.text:
Yes. In the ideal gate--delay model the period would simply
grow $\propto C_L$, but that model breaks down when the edge
at the $C_L$ node becomes much slower than the other delays.

Label the $C_L$ node $x$, and the other two nodes $y,z$.
For $C_L$ very large, $x$ moves on a time scale
$\sim R_{out}C_L$ much longer than the propagation time of the
other inverters. Hence, on the time scale of $x$, the other
inverters simply follow their static voltage transfer
characteristic $f(\cdot)$, which is decreasing, saturates at
the rails, and crosses $V_{in}=V_{out}$ at $V_M\approx V_{DD}/2$:

$$
y=f(x),\qquad z=f(y),\qquad 
\text{drive to }x = f(z)=f\!\bigl(f\!\bigl(f(x)\bigr)\bigr)\equiv F(x).
$$

The dynamics of the only slow node are first order,

$$
C_L\frac{dx}{dt}\;\propto\;F(x)-x .
$$

$F$ is again a decreasing inverter-like characteristic, with
a unique intersection with $F(x)=x$ at $x=V_M$. If $x<V_M$,
then $F(x)>x$ and the first inverter pulls $x$ up; if
$x>V_M$, then $F(x)<x$ and it pulls $x$ down. So $V_M$ is an
attracting fixed point, and a first-order system cannot
sustain a limit cycle. Any transient ringing decays.

In small-signal terms, each inverter is $-A_0/(1+s\tau_i)$,
and the closed-loop poles satisfy

$$
(1+s\tau_L)(1+s\tau_0)^2+A_0^{3}=0 .
$$

By Routh-Hurwitz this becomes stable for
$\tau_L/\tau_0 \gtrsim (1+A_0^{3})/2$, i.e. for sufficiently
large $C_L$. The large capacitor is dominant-pole
compensation for what is, at dc, a three-inversion negative
feedback loop: the excess phase can no longer reach
$180^\circ$ with loop gain $\ge 1$.

Thus for arbitrarily large $C_L$ the ring does not oscillate.
It settles with all three nodes at about the inverter
switching voltage $V_M$, all inverters on in their
high-gain region.

answer.text:
Yes. The naive delay argument, that a larger $C_L$ only makes
the period longer, assumes ideal logic gates. A real inverter is
a finite-gain amplifier with a finite output resistance.

Let $X$ be the node loaded by $C_L$, and let $C_p$ be the
ordinary parasitic capacitance at the other two nodes.
Near its switching voltage $V_M$ an inverter can be modelled as

$$ -\,\frac{A_0}{1+s/\omega_p}\qquad 
\omega_p=\frac1{R_oC_p}$$

for the two unloaded stages, and

$$ -\,\frac{A_0}{1+s/\omega_L}\qquad 
\omega_L=\frac1{R_oC_L}\ll \omega_p$$

for the stage driving $C_L$. $A_0$ is the low frequency
magnitude of the inverter gain.

The three inversions contribute $3\times180^{\circ}$ around
the loop. For oscillation the three $RC$ poles must supply
another $180^{\circ}$ at a frequency at which the loop gain
magnitude is at least unity.

The loaded pole can supply at most $90^{\circ}$. Hence the
other $180^{\circ}-90^{\circ}$ must come from the two fast
poles, requiring a frequency of order $\omega_p$ or higher:
for $\omega<\omega_p$ the total pole lag is
$<90^{\circ}+45^{\circ}+45^{\circ}=180^{\circ}$.

But at $\omega\gtrsim\omega_p$,

* the two fast stages have magnitudes $\lesssim A_0/\sqrt2$ each,
* the loaded stage has magnitude
  $$\frac{A_0}{\sqrt{1+(\omega/\omega_L)^2}}
   \approx A_0\frac{\omega_L}{\omega}
   \lesssim A_0\frac{\omega_L}{\omega_p}
   =A_0\frac{C_p}{C_L}.$$

Thus the loop gain magnitude at any frequency where the
phase condition can be met is at most

$$|L| \;\lesssim\; A_0^{3}\,\frac{C_p}{C_L}\,\frac12 .$$

For $C_L \gtrsim \tfrac12 A_0^{3}C_p$ this is $<1$, and for
still larger $C_L$ it tends to zero. Barkhausen's criterion
can never be satisfied.

In time-domain terms, $X$ then moves so slowly that
inverters 2 and 3 act as an essentially instantaneous
non-inverting buffer from $X$ back to the input of inverter 1.
Inverter 1 therefore has its output fed back to its own
input, a stable connection. The only dc solution,
$V_1=V_2=V_3=V_M$, becomes stable: perturbations decay
instead of growing into a limit cycle. The ring settles
with all inverters biased in their transition region,
drawing static current, and does not oscillate.

answer.text:
Yes. It does not merely oscillate more slowly; beyond a certain
$C_L$ oscillation is quenched altogether.

Linearise the inverters about their switching voltage $V_M$.
Let a stage have (magnitude of) low-frequency gain $A_v=g_mr_o$ and
output resistance $r_o$. Let $C_0$ be the normal node capacitance,
$\tau_0=r_oC_0$, and for the loaded node $\tau_L=r_o(C_L+C_0)\approx
r_oC_L$.

The closed-loop characteristic equation is

$$
\bigl(1+s\tau_L\bigr)\bigl(1+s\tau_0\bigr)^2 + A_v^{\,3}=0,
$$

i.e.

$$
a_3s^3+a_2s^2+a_1s+a_0=0
$$

with

$$
\begin{aligned}
a_3&=\tau_L\tau_0^2, &
a_2&=\tau_0^2+2\tau_L\tau_0,\\
a_1&=\tau_L+2\tau_0, &
a_0&=1+A_v^3 .
\end{aligned}
$$

By Routh–Hurwitz the $V_M$ equilibrium is stable iff
$a_2a_1>a_3a_0$. But as $\tau_L\to\infty$,

$$
\frac{a_2a_1}{a_3a_0}
\;\approx\;
\frac{(2\tau_L\tau_0)(\tau_L)}{\tau_L\tau_0^2(1+A_v^3)}
= \frac{2\tau_L}{\tau_0(1+A_v^3)}\;\longrightarrow\;\infty .
$$

So for sufficiently large $C_L$ (roughly $\tau_L/\tau_0\gtrsim A_v^3/2$)
all closed-loop poles move into the left half-plane: the metastable
point becomes *stable*.

Physically: with $C_L$ huge, node $B$ moves so slowly that the second
and third inverters follow it quasi-statically and stay in their
high-gain region. The loop then behaves like a single dominant-pole
stage in negative feedback, not like three rail-to-rail logic gates
chasing each other. A small rise of $B$ above $V_M$ is amplified
(non-inverted) through inverters 2 and 3 to the input of inverter 1,
which pulls $B$ back down, and vice versa — with no overshoot, because
the motion of $B$ is essentially first order.

Hence for arbitrarily large $C_L$ the circuit settles to

$$
V_A \approx V_B \approx V_C \approx V_M,
$$

with all inverters biased in their transition region, and does not
oscillate.

the $3\,{\rm dB}$ is bought with power; the oscillator FOM is
essentially unchanged.

answers.question: Determine the small-signal resistance seen looking into the supply node of the ring oscillator in the figure.

answer.text:
At the (unstable) d-c point of the ring all three
inverters are biased at $V_{in}=V_{out}$ with both devices
in saturation.  Let the $N$ and $P$ devices of an inverter
have $g_{mN},r_{oN}$ and $g_{mP},r_{oP}$, the three inverters
being identical.  Apply a test voltage $V_{X}$ at the common
supply terminal and let the current drawn be $I_{X}$.

The excitation $V_{X}$ is common to the three stages.
By the cyclic symmetry of the ring the small-signal voltages
at the three internal nodes must therefore be the same; call
it $V$.  For any one stage the gate and the drain of the
$N$ device are both at $V$, and the gate and the drain of
the $P$ device are both at $V$.  In the common-mode
excitation each transistor is diode connected.

Hence the current in one stage, from $V_{X}$ to ground, is,
through the $P$ device,

$$I_{1}=g_{mP}(V_{X}-V)+\frac{V_{X}-V}{r_{oP}}
      =\big(g_{mP}+g_{oP}\big)(V_{X}-V),$$

and through the $N$ device,

$$I_{1}=g_{mN}V+\frac{V}{r_{oN}}
      =\big(g_{mN}+g_{oN}\big)V,$$

with $g_{o}=1/r_{o}$.  Thus one inverter presents, between
supply and ground, the series resistance

$$R_{\text{stage}}=\frac{1}{g_{mP}+g_{oP}}+\frac{1}{g_{mN}+g_{oN}}
   =\left(\frac1{g_{mP}}\Big\Vert r_{oP}\right)
   +\left(\frac1{g_{mN}}\Big\Vert r_{oN}\right),$$

and

$$V = V_{X}\,
\frac{g_{mP}+g_{oP}}{g_{mN}+g_{oN}+g_{mP}+g_{oP}},\qquad
I_{1}= \frac{(g_{mN}+g_{oN})(g_{mP}+g_{oP})}
            {g_{mN}+g_{oN}+g_{mP}+g_{oP}}\,V_{X}.$$

The three stages are in parallel for $I_{X}=3I_{1}$, so

$$R_{X}=\frac{V_{X}}{I_{X}}
      =\frac13\left[
        \frac{1}{g_{mN}+g_{oN}}+
        \frac{1}{g_{mP}+g_{oP}}
        \right]
      =\frac13\Big[
        \big(\tfrac1{g_{mN}}\!\parallel r_{oN}\big)+
        \big(\tfrac1{g_{mP}}\!\parallel r_{oP}\big)
        \Big]
      \approx \frac{1}{3}\left(\frac1{g_{mN}}+\frac1{g_{mP}}\right),$$

the last form for $g_{m}r_{o}\gg1$.  For matched devices this is $\approx 2/3g_{m}$.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: The static gm-based derivation is internally consistent, but it ignores the oscillation-driven charging and discharging of the load capacitances, which sets the supply-node resistance.

answers.question: Determine the small-signal resistance seen looking into the supply node of the ring oscillator in the figure.

answer.text:
Let the (incremental) voltages at the three internal nodes
be $v_{1},v_{2},v_{3}$, the inverters being identical.  Bias the
ring at the (unstable) point at which

$$v_{in}=v_{out}=V_{M}\qquad\text{for every stage,}$$

so that every NMOS and every PMOS is in saturation, with
$g_{mn},r_{on}$ and $g_{mp},r_{op}$.

Apply a test voltage $v_{x}$ to the common supply rail and let
$i_{x}$ be the current it delivers. The excitation is common
to the three stages, and the circuit is invariant under a cyclic
permutation of the stages. Hence, for the linearised circuit,

$$v_{1}=v_{2}=v_{3}\equiv v .$$

Thus, for every stage, the gate and the drain of the NMOS are
at the same small-signal voltage $v$, and the gate and the drain
of the PMOS are also at $v$.  Each transistor is therefore
small-signal diode connected.

For the PMOS, looking from its source,

$$r_{p}= \frac{1}{g_{mp}+g_{op}}
      =\frac1{g_{mp}}\;\Big\|\;r_{op},$$

and for the NMOS, looking from its drain,

$$r_{n}= \frac{1}{g_{mn}+g_{on}}
      =\frac1{g_{mn}}\;\Big\|\;r_{on}.$$

In one stage the PMOS and NMOS diode resistances are in series
between the supply rail and ground, carrying the same current.
The resistance of one stage across the supply is therefore
$r_{p}+r_{n}$.  The three stages are in parallel across the
test source, so

$$
R_{X}= \frac{r_{p}+r_{n}}{3}
     =\frac13\left[
        \frac{1}{g_{mp}+1/r_{op}}+
        \frac{1}{g_{mn}+1/r_{on}}
        \right]
     =\frac13\left[
        \left(\frac1{g_{mp}}\Big\|r_{op}\right)+
        \left(\frac1{g_{mn}}\Big\|r_{on}\right)
        \right].
$$

For $g_{m}r_{o}\gg1$,

$$
R_{X}\;\approx\;\frac13\left(\frac1{g_{mn}}+\frac1{g_{mp}}\right),
$$

e.g. for $g_{mn}=g_{mp}=g_{m}$, $R_{X}\approx 2/3g_{m}$.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: The static gm-based derivation ignores the oscillation-driven charging and discharging of the load capacitances, which sets the supply resistance.

answers.question: Determine the small-signal resistance seen looking into the supply node of the ring oscillator in the figure.

answer.text:
Let the (small signal) outputs of the three inverters be
$V_{1},V_{2},V_{3}$, and apply a test voltage $V_{X}$ at the
common supply node, drawing $I_{X}$.

For the metastable bias point used in the small signal analysis
of the ring, $V_{in}=V_{out}$ for every stage and all of the
stages are identical, with $(g_{mN},r_{oN})$ for the NMOS and
$(g_{mP},r_{oP})$ for the PMOS device.  KCL at the three output
nodes gives, with $g_o\equiv 1/r_o$,

$$\begin{aligned}
(g_{mP}+g_{oP})V_X&=(g_{mP}+g_{mN})V_3+(g_{oP}+g_{oN})V_1\\
(g_{mP}+g_{oP})V_X&=(g_{mP}+g_{mN})V_1+(g_{oP}+g_{oN})V_2\\
(g_{mP}+g_{oP})V_X&=(g_{mP}+g_{mN})V_2+(g_{oP}+g_{oN})V_3 .
\end{aligned}$$

The circuit is cyclically symmetric, so the unique solution is

$$V_{1}=V_{2}=V_{3}\equiv V_{o} .$$

Hence the input of every inverter is tied, in the small signal
sense, to its own output: each inverter is two diode-connected
devices in series between $V_X$ and ground. The current in one
inverter is therefore

$$ I = (g_{mN}+g_{oN})V_{o}
     = (g_{mP}+g_{oP})(V_{X}-V_{o}) ,$$

i.e.

$$ I=\frac{V_{X}}
{\dfrac{1}{g_{mN}+g_{oN}}+\dfrac{1}{g_{mP}+g_{oP}}} .$$

There are three such branches in parallel, $I_{X}=3I$.  Thus

$$\;R_{X}=\frac{V_{X}}{I_{X}}
      =\frac13\left[
        \frac{1}{g_{mN}+g_{oN}}+\frac{1}{g_{mP}+g_{oP}}
        \right]\;$$

i.e.

$$ R_{X}= \frac{1}{3}\Big[\,\big(\tfrac1{g_{mN}}\parallel r_{oN}\big)
      +\big(\tfrac1{g_{mP}}\parallel r_{oP}\big)\Big]
      \;\approx\; \frac{1}{3}\left(\frac1{g_{mN}}+\frac1{g_{mP}}\right),
\qquad g_mr_o\gg1, $$

the resistance of one diode-connected NMOS in series with one
diode-connected PMOS, with three such branches in parallel.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: The derivation consistently analyzes a static metastable operating point and obtains a gm-based diode-connected resistance, but misses the dominant resistance from oscillation-driven charging and discharging of the load capacitances.

answers.question:
For the ring oscillator in the figure, somebody computes the small-signal resistance `RX`
seen looking into the supply node as

```text
RX ~= (1/3) (1/gmn + 1/gmp)
```

where `gmn` and `gmp` are the transconductances of the NMOS and PMOS devices in each
inverter, because each inverter behaves as two diode-connected devices in series.

If the circuit oscillates, does this answer change?

answer.text:
Yes, for the circuit in its steady oscillating state. The quoted
value is only the linearization about the unstable dc point.

At that (metastable) point,
$$V_1=V_2=V_3\approx V_{DD}/2 ,$$
all devices are saturated, and a common supply perturbation makes
the three internal nodes move in unison, $v_1=v_2=v_3$.  Hence, incrementally,
$v_g=v_d$ for every transistor: each branch looks like a PMOS diode
in series with an NMOS diode,
$$r_{\rm branch}\approx \frac1{g_{mp}}+\frac1{g_{mn}},\qquad 
R_X\approx \frac13\Bigl(\frac1{g_{mp}}+\frac1{g_{mn}}\Bigr)$$
with $r_o$'s neglected. But this point is unstable: the ring has
right-half-plane poles and noise there grows into a limit cycle.

In steady oscillation the node waveforms are large, rail-to-rail,
delayed/inverted copies of one another ( $120^{\circ}$ apart at the
fundamental), not equal voltages.  Thus for a given inverter
$v_g\ne v_d$; it is not two diode-connected devices. Its transistors
cycle through off, saturation and triode, so $g_{mn},g_{mp}$ are
periodic functions of time, often zero.  Most of the time one device
in each supply-to-ground branch is off, so there is no static diode
path from $V_{DD}$ to ground; supply current flows mainly in pulses
that charge the node capacitances, plus short-circuit current during
transitions.

Hence $R_X$ of the oscillating circuit is not the constant
$\tfrac13(1/g_{mn}+1/g_{mp})$.  Instantaneously it is time-varying,
and a slowly measured value is governed by the average dynamic
current, e.g. $\bar I_{DD}\approx 3 f_{\rm osc}C_LV_{DD}$, i.e. by
$f_{\rm osc}(V_{DD})$, not by the transconductances at the metastable point.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: It identifies the capacitive charging mechanism and gives the equivalent average-current expression, but does not establish that the resulting resistance remains on the order of the MOS on-resistance or inverse transconductance. Its emphasis on devices being off could also suggest a misleadingly higher resistance.

answers.question:
For the ring oscillator in the figure, somebody computes the small-signal resistance `RX`
seen looking into the supply node as

```text
RX ~= (1/3) (1/gmn + 1/gmp)
```

where `gmn` and `gmp` are the transconductances of the NMOS and PMOS devices in each
inverter, because each inverter behaves as two diode-connected devices in series.

If the circuit oscillates, does this answer change?

answer.text:
No, in the ideal matched small--signal sense. The mistake is to
think of the diode connection as applying to the oscillation
signal itself. It applies to the signal produced at the internal
nodes by a supply perturbation.

Apply a test increment $v_x$ at the common supply and let
$v_1,v_2,v_3$ be the increments it produces at the three inverter
outputs. The test source drives the three stages identically, so
it excites only the common mode of the ring. By the cyclic
symmetry of the three identical stages the response to $v_x$ must
satisfy

$$
v_1=v_2=v_3\equiv v .
$$

Hence, for this supply-produced increment, the gate of every
transistor does move by exactly the same amount as its drain:
the NMOS and PMOS of a stage do act, for the common mode, as two
diode-connected devices in series between $v_x$ and ground.
KCL at one output node, with no gate current, gives, including
$r_o$,

$$
\big(g_{mp}+g_{dp}\big)(v_x-v)=\big(g_{mn}+g_{dn}\big)v ,
$$

so the current drawn by one stage from the supply is

$$
i_{\text{stage}}=\big(g_{mp}+g_{dp}\big)(v_x-v)
      =\frac{v_x}{\dfrac1{g_{mn}+g_{dn}}+\dfrac1{g_{mp}+g_{dp}}}.
$$

Three stages in parallel therefore give

$$
R_X=\frac13\left[
\frac1{g_{mn}+g_{dn}}+\frac1{g_{mp}+g_{dp}}
\right]
\;\approx\;
\frac13\left(\frac1{g_{mn}}+\frac1{g_{mp}}\right),
$$

as quoted.

The oscillation itself is the other, differential, mode of the
ring: successively $120^{\circ}$ apart,

$$
o_1+o_2+o_3=0\qquad 
\big(o_i\ \text{the oscillatory part of }v_i\big).
$$

Its first-order contribution to the total supply current is
proportional to $\sum_i o_i$ (each $o_i$ enters once as a drain
voltage and once as the next stage's gate voltage), hence it
cancels; and a purely common supply excitation has no component
along this sum-zero mode. The common-mode (supply) and
differential-mode (oscillation) motions are orthogonal, so the
oscillatory mode neither is excited by $v_x$ nor contributes to
$i_x$ to first order. That pole of the differential mode is
cancelled at the supply port.

So $R_X$ is unchanged by the presence of the (linearised)
oscillation; the diode-connected picture is correct only for the
common-mode increment produced by the supply test signal, not for
the $120^{\circ}$ oscillation signal itself.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: It reaches the broad conclusion that oscillation does not make RX much larger, but it asserts the static diode-connected model still applies. It misses the required dynamic charging mechanism and the argument that RX remains on the order of the MOS on-resistance.

answers.question:
For the ring oscillator in the figure, somebody computes the small-signal resistance `RX`
seen looking into the supply node as

```text
RX ~= (1/3) (1/gmn + 1/gmp)
```

where `gmn` and `gmp` are the transconductances of the NMOS and PMOS devices in each
inverter, because each inverter behaves as two diode-connected devices in series.

If the circuit oscillates, does this answer change?

answer.text:
Yes -- in the sense that the quoted number is not the
impedance of the oscillating circuit.  It is the impedance
linearised about a point at which the circuit does not stay.

Let the internal nodes be $A,B,C$.  The (unstable) d-c solution is

$$
A=B=C=V_M\approx V_{DD}/2 ,
$$

with every device saturated with the $g_{mn},g_{mp}$ used above.
For a symmetric supply perturbation the symmetry gives
$\delta A=\delta B=\delta C$, so for every stage incrementally
$\delta v_{in}=\delta v_{out}$: the stage momentarily looks like a
PMOS diode in series with an NMOS diode between $V_{DD}$ and ground.
Three such stages in parallel give

$$
R_X \approx \frac13\Bigl(\frac1{g_{mn}}+\frac1{g_{mp}}\Bigr).
$$

That operating point has loop gain $>1$ and is unstable.  In
oscillation $A,B,C$ are large, roughly rail-to-rail waveforms shifted
by $T_{osc}/3$; in particular $v_{in}\ne v_{out}$ for a stage except at
the brief crossing instants.  There is no fixed $Q$ point about which
to linearise:

* $g_{mn}$ and $g_{mp}$ are not constants; over a period each device
goes through cut-off, triode and saturation.
* In a non-switching inverter one device is essentially off, so there
is no diode-connected d-c path from $V_{DD}$ to ground.
* The supply current is not a static crowbar current; it consists
mainly of pulses charging the node capacitances.  Only the stage
actually switching draws appreciable through-current, and only
briefly.

Hence there is no time-invariant small-signal $R_X$ of the quoted
form; the incremental supply conductance is periodic in time,
depending on the phase of the oscillation at which the perturbation
is applied, with mixing to $f_{test}\pm nf_{osc}$.

A slow, period-averaged measurement gives instead

$$
\bar I_{DD}\approx 3C_L V_{DD} f_{osc}(V_{DD}),\qquad
R_{X,\text{avg}}=\left(\frac{d\bar I_{DD}}{dV_{DD}}\right)^{-1}
 =\frac{1}{3C_L\!\left[f_{osc}+V_{DD}\,df_{osc}/dV_{DD}\right]},
$$

which is in general quite different from
$\tfrac13\bigl(1/g_{mn}+1/g_{mp}\bigr)$ evaluated at the metastable
point.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: It correctly identifies capacitive charging as the source of oscillating supply current and gives an averaged-current expression. But it does not show that the resulting resistance remains on the order of the MOS on-resistance or inverse transconductance, and its claim that it is generally quite different from the static estimate misses the key conclusion.

answers.question: In the circuit shown in the figure, what happens to the initial voltage gain as the width of M7 increases?

answer.text:
This is the StrongARM latch. In reset, $CK=0$, $S_{1}-S_{4}$
precharge $P,Q,X,Y$ to $V_{DD}$ and $M_{7}$ is off.  When $CK$
goes high $S_{1}-S_{4}$ turn off and $X$ and $Y$ are discharged
through $M_{3,4}$ and the input pair $M_{1,2}$.

Before the cross-coupled $M_{5,6}$ turn on, the latch is
essentially an integrator. With $C_X=C_Y=C$ and
$I_{D1}\approx I_{D2}\approx I_{7}/2$,

$$
V_X \approx V_{DD}-\frac{I_{D1}}{C}t ,\qquad 
V_Y \approx V_{DD}-\frac{I_{D2}}{C}t .
$$

Regeneration starts at $t=t_0$, when $V_X,V_Y$ have fallen by
about $|V_{TH,P}|$, so that $M_{5,6}$ turn on:

$$
t_0 \approx \frac{C|V_{TH,P}|}{I_{D1,2}} .
$$

The differential voltage already developed at that moment is

$$
\Delta V_{XY}(t_0)=\frac{I_{D1}-I_{D2}}{C}t_0
      \approx \frac{g_{m1,2}V_{id}}{C}t_0 ,
$$

so the ``initial'' gain, i.e. the gain just before regeneration,
is

$$
A_{v,i}\equiv \frac{\Delta V_{XY}(t_0)}{V_{id}}
      \approx \frac{g_{m1,2}}{I_{D1,2}}|V_{TH,P}|
      =\frac{2|V_{TH,P}|}{V_{OV1,2}} .
$$

$M_7$ is not biased with a fixed current; its gate is the
digital clock. Increasing $W_7$ lowers its on resistance,
pulls the common source node of $M_{1,2}$ down, and therefore
increases $I_7$ and $I_{D1,2}$, i.e. increases $V_{OV1,2}$.
Although $g_{m1,2}$ grows, it grows only as $\sqrt{I_{D1,2}}$,
whereas $t_0$ shrinks as $1/I_{D1,2}$. Hence

$$
A_{v,i}\propto \frac{g_{m1,2}}{I_{D1,2}}\propto \frac{1}{\sqrt{I_{D1,2}}}
$$

decreases. The latch regenerates faster, but with a smaller
initial differential voltage, so the input-referred contribution
of $M_{3}$-$M_{6}$ becomes larger.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly concludes that initial gain decreases: a wider M7 raises tail current, while input-pair gm grows sublinearly, so gm/ICM falls. The integration-time explanation is consistent with the golden solution.

answers.question: In the circuit shown in the figure, what happens to the initial voltage gain as the width of M7 increases?

answer.text:
At the rising edge of $CK$, $S_{1}-S_{4}$ turn off and $M_{7}$
turns on. The nodes $X$ and $Y$, precharged to $V_{DD}$, begin
to discharge through $M_{3,4}$, $M_{1,2}$ and $M_{7}$.

Until $V_X,V_Y$ have fallen by about $|V_{thp}|$, $M_{5,6}$ are
still off and there is no regeneration. In this interval a
differential output is built up only by integration of the
input-pair current difference on $C_X=C_Y=C$:

\[
\Delta V_{XY}\approx \frac{g_{m1,2}\,\Delta V_{in}}{C}\,t_0
\]

where $t_0$ is the time for $X,Y$ to fall by $|V_{thp}|$,

\[
t_0 \approx \frac{C|V_{thp}|}{I_{D1,2}} .
\]

Hence the voltage gain present at the start of regeneration is

\[
A_{v0}\equiv \frac{\Delta V_{XY}}{\Delta V_{in}}
      \approx g_{m1,2}\frac{|V_{thp}|}{I_{D1,2}}
      =\frac{g_{m1,2}}{I_{D1,2}}|V_{thp}|
      \approx \frac{2|V_{thp}|}{V_{ov1,2}} .
\]

Increasing $W_7$ lowers the on-resistance of the tail switch
and increases $I_{D1,2}$ -- the common-source node of $M_{1,2}$
is pulled lower and $V_{ov1,2}$ rises. Although $g_{m1,2}$
increases, it increases only sub-linearly with current,
$\propto\!\sqrt{I_{D1,2}}$, while the integration time $t_0$
falls as $1/I_{D1,2}$.

Thus

\[
A_{v0}\propto \frac{g_{m1,2}}{I_{D1,2}}
\]

decreases with increasing $W_7$, roughly as $W_7^{-1/2}$ while
$M_7$ limits the current, levelling off when $I_{D1,2}$ becomes
limited by $M_{1,2}$ themselves.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly concludes that the initial gain decreases as M7 widens, and explains that increased tail current raises gm sublinearly while shortening the integration time, reducing the relevant gm/current gain factor. The exact threshold approximation is not essential.

answers.question: In the circuit shown in the figure, what happens to the initial voltage gain as the width of M7 increases?

answer.text:
At the beginning of the evaluate phase $CK$ is high,
$S_{1}-S_{4}$ are off, and $X$ and $Y$ have been precharged to
$V_{DD}$. The cross-coupled PMOS devices $M_{5},M_{6}$ are still off.
$X$ and $Y$ are discharged by the currents of $M_{1}$ and $M_{2}$,
through $M_{3}$ and $M_{4}$, until $V_X$ or $V_Y$ has fallen by
$|V_{th,p}|$ and regeneration by $M_{3}-M_{6}$ begins.

Let $I_D$ be the quiescent current in each input branch and
$\Delta I_D$ its input-induced difference. During this initial,
pre-regenerative interval

$$
\Delta I_D \approx g_{m1,2}\,\Delta V_{in},
\qquad 
t_{r}\approx \frac{C_{X,Y}|V_{th,p}|}{I_D},
$$

where $t_r$ is the time for $X,Y$ to fall by $|V_{th,p}|$.
Hence the differential voltage developed at $X,Y$ when
regeneration starts is

$$
\Delta V_{XY}(t_r)\approx \frac{\Delta I_D}{C_{X,Y}}t_r
      =\frac{g_{m1,2}}{I_D}|V_{th,p}|\,\Delta V_{in},
$$

so that the initial voltage gain is

$$
A_{v,i}\equiv \frac{\Delta V_{XY}(t_r)}{\Delta V_{in}}
      \approx \frac{g_{m1,2}}{I_D}|V_{th,p}|
      =\frac{2|V_{th,p}|}{V_{ov1,2}} ,
$$

apart from a similar term due to the unequal turn-on times
of $M_3$ and $M_4$, also proportional to $g_{m1,2}/I_D$.

Increasing $W_7$ lowers the impedance from the common-source
node of $M_1,M_2$ to ground. That node is pulled lower,
$V_{ov1,2}$ and $I_D$ increase, and $X,Y$ discharge faster, i.e.
$t_r$ decreases. Although $g_{m1,2}$ increases, $g_{m1,2}/I_D
=2/V_{ov1,2}$ decreases.

Therefore the initial, pre-regenerative voltage gain decreases
— the latch decides faster, but with less initial amplification.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly predicts that the initial gain decreases as M7 widens, and explains that increased tail/branch current makes gm/ID decrease. The integration-time derivation is consistent with the essential mechanism; formula details do not change the conclusion.

answers.question: In the figure, what happens to the initial voltage gain if we increase the capacitance at nodes P and Q?

answer.text:
During reset $CK=0$, $S_{1}-S_{4}$ are on and

$$V_X=V_Y=V_P=V_Q=V_{DD}\qquad M_3,M_4,M_5,M_6\;{\rm off} .$$

When $CK$ goes high $M_{1},M_{2}$ first discharge $P$ and $Q$.
For $V_{in1}>V_{in2}$, $I_{D1}>I_{D2}$ and $P$ falls faster than
$Q$.  $M_{3}$ and $M_{4}$ do not conduct until their sources have
fallen about a threshold below their gates, e.g.

$$t_{3}\approx \frac{C_{P}V_{THN}}{I_{D1}},\qquad 
       t_{4}\approx \frac{C_{P}V_{THN}}{I_{D2}}\; .$$

Hence the two sides of the NMOS latch turn on at different times,

$$\Delta t=t_{4}-t_{3}\approx 
C_{P}V_{THN}\!\left(\frac1{I_{D2}}-\frac1{I_{D1}}\right)
\approx C_{P}V_{THN}\frac{\,I_{D1}-I_{D2}\,}{I_{D}^{2}}
\approx C_{P}V_{THN}\frac{g_{m1,2}V_{id}}{I_{D}^{2}}\propto C_{P} .$$

During $\Delta t$ essentially only the early side, say $M_{3}$,
discharges the output capacitance $C_{X}$, while $V_{Y}$ stays near
$V_{DD}$.  The differential voltage seeded at $X\!-\!Y$ before
$M_{5},M_{6}$ start regeneration is therefore

$$\Delta V_{XY,0}\approx \frac{I_{D}\Delta t}{C_{X}}
      \approx \frac{C_{P}}{C_{X}}\,V_{THN}\,\frac{\Delta I_{D}}{I_{D}},$$

i.e.

$$A_{0}\equiv\frac{\Delta V_{XY,0}}{V_{id}}
      \approx \frac{C_{P}}{C_{X}}\frac{g_{m1,2}V_{THN}}{I_{D}}\;,$$

increases, roughly in proportion to $C_{P}=C_{Q}$.  The price is
a longer discharge time $t_{3,4}\propto C_{P}$, i.e. a slower
comparator.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: The answer incorrectly concludes that the initial gain increases with capacitance, and bases this on a timing-skew mechanism rather than the gain accumulated across P and Q. It correctly notes that larger capacitance slows discharge, but misses that the longer amplification time cancels the reduced differential-voltage slope, leaving the initial gain essentially unchanged.

answers.question: In the figure, what happens to the initial voltage gain if we increase the capacitance at nodes P and Q?

answer.text:
This is a StrongARM dynamic latch. During reset $CK=0$,
$S_{1}$-$S_{4}$ precharge $X,Y,P,Q$ to $V_{DD}$, so $M_{3}$-$M_{6}$ are off.
When $CK$ goes high, the tail device $M_{7}$ turns on and the
precharge devices turn off.

### Initial phase

At first $M_{3}$ and $M_{4}$ remain off, so $X$ and $Y$ stay at
$V_{DD}$ while $I_{D1}$ and $I_{D2}$ discharge the capacitances
at $P$ and $Q$, $C_{P}=C_{Q}$.

$M_{3},M_{4}$ begin to conduct when $V_{P,Q}$ has fallen by about
a threshold voltage below $V_{DD}$:

$$
V_{DD}-V_{P}(t_{1}) \approx V_{THN}
\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad
t_{1}\approx \frac{C_{P}V_{THN}}{I_{D1,2}} .
$$

The differential voltage developed at $P,Q$ up to that moment is

$$
\Delta V_{PQ}(t_{1})
   =\frac{I_{D1}-I_{D2}}{C_{P}}\,t_{1}
   =\frac{g_{m1,2}\,\Delta V_{in}}{C_{P}}\,t_{1}.
$$

Substituting $t_{1}$,

$$
\;\Delta V_{PQ}(t_{1})
      \approx \frac{g_{m1,2}}{I_{D1,2}}\,V_{THN}\;\Delta V_{in}\;
$$

so the initial (pre-regeneration) voltage gain is

$$
A_{\text{init}}=\frac{\Delta V_{PQ}}{\Delta V_{in}}
\approx \frac{g_{m1,2}V_{THN}}{I_{D1,2}}
\approx \frac{2V_{THN}}{V_{OV1}},
$$

which, to first order, does **not** contain $C_{P}$.

### Intuition

Increasing $C_{P,Q}$ makes $P$ and $Q$ discharge more slowly,
$\,dV_{P}/dt = I_{D}/C_{P}$, so the differential voltage at any
given instant is smaller. But it takes proportionally longer
for $V_{P,Q}$ to fall by $V_{THN}$ and turn on $M_{3},M_{4}$.
The longer integration time exactly compensates for the
smaller $dV/dt$, leaving the seed voltage handed to the
regenerative $X$–$Y$ latch unchanged.

The penalty is speed: the initial delay $t_{1}\propto C_{P,Q}$
increases (the benefit is reduced kickback to the input, since
the same charge disturbance now produces a smaller $\Delta V = \Delta Q/C_{P,Q}$).

answers.question: If we increase the widths of M5 and M6 in the figure, does the speed improve or degrade?

answer.text:
The $M_{3}$-$M_{6}$ cross-coupled pair is the regenerative latch
at nodes $X$ and $Y$. $S_{3},S_{4}$ precharge $X$ and $Y$ to $V_{DD}$
when $CK$ is low.

When $CK$ goes high, the decision is made in two phases:

1. **Initial discharge:** $X$ and $Y$ are discharged through
$M_{3},M_{4}$-$M_{1},M_{2}$-$M_{7}$. Since initially
$V_{X}=V_{Y}=V_{DD}$, $M_{5}$ and $M_{6}$ have $V_{SG}\approx 0$ and are
**off**. They turn on only after $X$ (or $Y$) has fallen by about
$|V_{THP}|$. The time for this is roughly
$$
t_{0}\;\approx\;\frac{C_{X,Y}\,|V_{THP}|}{I_{tail}/2}
$$
During this entire phase $M_{5},M_{6}$ contribute nothing except
capacitance at $X$ and $Y$: their drain junction capacitance and
the gate capacitance of the opposite device. Increasing $W_{5,6}$
increases $C_{X,Y}$ and hence increases $t_{0}$.

2. **Regeneration:** Once $M_{5},M_{6}$ turn on, the latch
regenerates with a time constant
$$
\tau_{reg}\;\approx\;\frac{C_{X,Y}}{g_{m3,4}+g_{m5,6}}
$$
Increasing $W_{5,6}$ increases $g_{m5,6}$, but it increases
$C_{X,Y}$ due to $M_{5,6}$ in almost the same proportion — $g_{m}/C$
of the device itself is essentially its intrinsic speed. So
$\tau_{reg}$ improves negligibly, if at all.

Hence the added $g_m$ in regeneration does not compensate for
the extra load during the initial discharge phase, during which
$M_{5},M_{6}$ are inactive. The total decision time increases:

**Increasing $W_{5}$ and $W_{6}$ degrades the speed** (which is why the PMOS latch devices are typically kept small).

The decision time is degraded.

With $CK$ low, $X$ and $Y$ are precharged to $V_{DD}$, so $M_{5}$
and $M_{6}$ are off.  When $CK$ goes high, $X$ and $Y$ are first
discharged through $M_{3}$-$M_{1}$ and $M_{4}$-$M_{2}$.  Only after
one node has fallen by about $|V_{THP}|$ does the pMOS latch begin
to act.

The delay is approximately

$$
t_{d}\;\approx\;
\underbrace{\frac{C_{XY}|V_{THP}|}{I_{D1,2}}}_{\text{initial discharge}}
\;+\;
\underbrace{\frac{C_{XY}}{g_{m3,4}+g_{m5,6}}
\ln\!\frac{V_{DD}/2}{\Delta V_{0}}}_{\text{regeneration}}\qquad 
\Delta V_{0}\approx \frac{\Delta I_D}{I_{D}}\,|V_{THP}|
$$

Increasing $W_{5,6}$

* does **not** increase the discharge current in the first phase,
  since $M_{5,6}$ are off, but it increases $C_{XY}$ by the drain
  junction capacitance of one device and the gate capacitance of
  the cross-coupled device.  Hence the first term, and the time to
  develop $\Delta V_0$ and to turn on the pMOS latch, increase.
  $\Delta V_0$ itself is essentially unchanged.

* in regeneration the current through $M_{5,6}$ is initially fixed
  by $M_{1,2,7}$, not by $W_{5,6}$.  At fixed current
  $g_m\propto\sqrt{W}$, while the parasitic capacitance
  $\propto W$.  Thus $g_{m5,6}/C_{XY}$ does not improve; it
  typically falls, so the regeneration time constant
  $C_{XY}/(g_{m3,4}+g_{m5,6})$ also increases.

Hence both the signal-development time and the regeneration time
grow.  $M_{5,6}$ are normally kept small — just large enough to
complete the pull-up and hold the final state.

answers.question: If we increase the widths of M5 and M6 in the figure, does the speed improve or degrade?

answer.text:
The circuit is a StrongARM dynamic latch. Its delay is
essentially

$$t_{d}\approx t_{dis}+t_{reg}\ln\frac{\Delta V_{logic}}{\Delta V_{0}} $$

and increasing $W_{5,6}$ hurts both terms.

**1. Discharge before regeneration**

When $CK$ rises, $X$ and $Y$ are initially at $V_{DD}$ and
$M_{5},M_{6}$ are off. $C_{X,Y}$ must first be discharged
through $M_{3,4}$-$M_{1,2}$ by about $|V_{THP}|$ before the
PMOS latch even turns on:

$$t_{dis}\approx \frac{C_{X,Y}\,|V_{THP}|}{I_{SS}/2}$$

$I_{SS}$ is set by $M_{1},M_{2},M_{7}$, not by $M_{5},M_{6}$.
Widening $M_{5},M_{6}$ only adds their gate capacitance to the
opposite output node and their drain capacitance to their own
output node, i.e. $C_{X,Y}\uparrow$. Hence $t_{dis}\uparrow$,
while the differential voltage built up in this phase,
$\Delta V_{0}\approx |V_{THP}|\,\Delta I_{in}/I_{SS}$, is
unchanged.

**2. Regeneration**

Once both cross-coupled pairs are on,

$$\Delta V_{out}(t)\approx \Delta V_{0}\,
e^{\,t/\tau_{reg}},\qquad 
\tau_{reg}\approx\frac{C_{X,Y}}{g_{m3,4}+g_{m5,6}} .$$

At the start of regeneration the branch current is about
$I_{SS}/2$, so $g_{m5,6}\propto\sqrt{W_{5,6}}$, whereas the
capacitance contributed by $M_{5,6}$ is $\propto W_{5,6}$.
Thus $C_{X,Y}/(g_{mn}+g_{mp})$ does not fall; for the
self-loaded nodes shown it rises. The larger PMOS therefore
gives no regeneration advantage to compensate for the
slower initial discharge. It also makes the $S_{3},S_{4}$
precharge of $X,Y$ slower.

In short, wider $M_{5},M_{6}$ increase the load at $X$ and $Y$
without increasing the discharging current: the comparator
decision time increases, i.e. the speed degrades (the only
benefit being somewhat smaller $M_{5,6}$ mismatch).

answer.text:
The four $CK,\overline{CK}$ devices are not signal devices.
They are switches in series with the signal devices,
e.g. for node $X$

$$V_{DD}-P_{Z}-P_{\overline{CK}}-X-N_{CK}-M_{1,Z}-GND$$

and similarly for node $Y$.  $X$ and $Y$ are dynamic nodes.
In one half cycle, e.g.,

* $CK=1$ : the left hand clocked inverter is on, $X=\bar Z$,
  $Y$ is floating;
* $CK=0$ : the right hand clocked inverter is on, $Y=\bar X$,
  $Z=\bar Y$ through ${\rm Inv_{3}}$, $X$ is floating,

so that $Z$ toggles once per clock period.  The clock
period must satisfy, roughly,
$T_{CK}/2>t_{X}$ and $T_{CK}/2>t_{Y}+t_{{\rm Inv_{3}}}$.

The current that must charge or discharge $X$, resp. $Y$,
is the current of the series stack.  It is essentially set
by the unchanged data devices, the upper $p$ device and
$M_{1}$, whose gates are $Z$, resp. $X$.  Making the clock
device wider decreases only the $R_{ck}$ part of
$R_{data}+R_{ck}$, a decrease which rapidly saturates at
$R_{data}$.

What does increase, essentially in proportion to $W_{ck}$,
is

* the drain junction, and gate overlap, capacitance of the
clock devices directly on the dynamic nodes $X$ and $Y$,
* the source junction capacitance on the internal stack
nodes between the data and the clock devices, with its
associated Elmore delay and charge sharing, and
* the gate capacitance put on $CK$ and $\overline{CK}$,
slowing the clock edges themselves for any finite clock
driver resistance.

In Elmore form, e.g. for a pull up of $X$,

$$
\tau_X\;\approx\;R_{data}C_{mid}
+\bigl(R_{data}+R_{ck}\bigr)
\Bigl(C_{g,next}+C_{db,ck}\Bigr) \qquad 
R_{ck}\propto W_{ck}^{-1},\;\; C_{db,ck},C_{mid}\propto W_{ck}
$$

and analogously for $Y$.  The $R_{ck}C_{g,next}$ term saved
by a wider clock device is more than paid for by the
$R_{data}C_{db,ck}$ and $R_{data}C_{mid}$ terms added, and by
the slower $CK/\overline{CK}$ edge.  The slower slew at
$Y$ in addition increases the delay of ${\rm Inv_{3}}$ in
the loop.

Hence the $X$ and $Y$ transitions, and with them the maximum
toggle rate, get slower.  Clock devices in such TSPC/C$^{2}$MOS
stages should be kept small; widening them degrades speed,
while increasing clock power.

answer.text:
The two clocked inverters alternately drive the dynamic
nodes $X$ and $Y$.  During one clock phase $X=\overline Z$ must be
established, and during the next $Y=\overline X$, so that
${\rm Inv}_3$ can change $Z$.  The maximum clock frequency is
therefore set by the time needed to charge or discharge $X$ and $Y$.

For example, discharge of $Y$ takes place through the right-hand
clocked NMOS and the right-hand $M_1$.  The transistor $M_1$ is
already on, with its gate at $X$, and for most of the transition it
is saturated; it essentially fixes the discharge current.  The
same is true of the upper PMOS device on a charging transition.
The clocked device is merely the series switch that completes the
path, with a small $V_{DS}$.

Hence widening a clocked transistor

* lowers its series resistance, but does not appreciably increase
the current delivered to $X$ or $Y$, since that current is limited
by the data transistor in series with it;
* puts its drain junction and gate-drain capacitance directly on
$X$ or $Y$, increasing $C_X$ and $C_Y$ roughly in proportion to $W$;
* increases the capacitance of the internal stack node, worsening
charge sharing, and increases the load on $CK$ and $\overline{CK}$,
slowing the clock edges and increasing clock feedthrough to $X$
and $Y$.

To first order the delay is

$$
t_p \;\approx\; \frac{C_{X,Y}\,\Delta V}{I_{\text{data,sat}}}\,,
$$

with $I_{\text{data,sat}}$ essentially unchanged while
$C_{X,Y}$ grows.  The stage delay therefore increases and the
maximum operating frequency decreases.  Clocked devices in such
C$^2$MOS stages are kept small; drive strength is obtained by
widening the data devices, whose drain capacitances are not
directly on $X$ and $Y$.

answer.text:
The two clocked inverters form two $C^{2}{\rm MOS}$ latches in a
loop with ${\rm Inv_{3}}$.

$$ Z\to X\qquad {\rm on}\;CK ,\qquad 
   X\to Y\to Z\qquad {\rm on}\;\overline{CK}$$

so $Z$ toggles once per clock period.  $X$ and $Y$ are
dynamic nodes: in one half cycle they must be completely
charged or discharged, in the other they float.

Widening only the $CK,\overline{CK}$ devices

* does almost nothing for the current that charges $X$ or $Y$.
  That current is set by the signal devices in series with
  them, the $Z$-driven and the $X$-driven $p$ device and $M_{1}$,
  whose sizes are unchanged.  The clock device, with its gate
  at the rail, is essentially a switch already.

* does increase, $\propto W_{ck}$, the capacitance that those
  signal devices have to drive:
  $$C_{X}=C_{g,{\rm next}}+C_{d,ckp}+C_{d,ckn},\qquad
    C_{Y}=C_{g,{\rm Inv_{3}}}+C_{d,ckp}+C_{d,ckn} .$$
  In Elmore terms the term $R_{\rm in}C_{d,ck}$ in
  $(R_{\rm in}+R_{ck})(C_{L}+C_{d,ck})$ grows linearly with
  $W_{ck}$ and outweighs the $1/W_{ck}$ decrease of $R_{ck}$.

* increases, $\propto W_{ck}$, the diffusion capacitance of the
  internal source nodes of the clock devices.  Those nodes must
  be pre-positioned by the signal device alone while the latch
  is opaque, and they charge-share with $X$ or $Y$ when the
  clock turns on.

* increases the load $C_{g,ck}$ on $CK$ and $\overline{CK}$,
  slowing the clock edges themselves, and increases clock
  feedthrough to the floating nodes $X$ and $Y$.

Hence, with $I_{\rm drive}$ essentially fixed,
$t_{X,Y}\approx C_{X,Y}\Delta V/I_{\rm drive}$ increases.
The half-cycle delays increase and the maximum toggle
frequency decreases: the speed degrades.

answers.question: Does the structure in the figure provide quadrature outputs?

answer.text:
The two clocked stacks are dynamic inverters.

* $CK=1,\;\overline{CK}=0$ : the left hand stack is on,
the right hand stack is off
$$
X=\bar Z\qquad Y,\;Z\;\;{\rm hold}
$$

* $CK=0,\;\overline{CK}=1$ : the left hand stack is off,
the right hand stack is on
$$
Y=\bar X\qquad Z=\bar Y=X\qquad X\;\;{\rm holds}
$$

$Z=\bar Y$ is fed back to the input of the first stack.
Hence $X$ can change only on a rising $CK$ edge and
$Z$ can change only on the following falling $CK$ edge, and
both toggle once per $CK$ period.  E.g. in steady state, with
$T$ the $CK$ period,

$$\begin{array}{c|cccc}
      &0\!-\!T/2&T/2\!-\!T&T\!-\!3T/2&3T/2\!-\!2T\\ \hline
CK &1&0&1&0\\
X  &1&1&0&0\\
Z  &0&1&1&0\\
Y=\bar Z&1&0&0&1
\end{array}$$

i.e. $X$ and $Z$ are $f_{CK}/2$ square waves of $50\%$ duty
cycle, displaced in time by $T/2$.  The output period is
$2T$, so $T/2$ is a quarter of an output period:

$$
\Delta\phi = \frac{T/2}{2T}\,2\pi = \frac{\pi}{2}\;,
$$

$X$ and $Z$ - $Y=\bar Z$ is the complement of $Z$ - are in
quadrature.  Exact $90^{\circ}$ requires a $50\%$ duty cycle
$CK$. ∎

answer.text:
The two clocked inverters are $C^{2}$MOS latches.

* On the left the clock devices are on for $CK=1$. Hence,
for $CK=1$,
$$
X=\overline Z
$$
and for $CK=0$, $X$ is held on its node capacitance.

* On the right the clock devices are on for $CK=0$. Hence,
for $CK=0$,
$$
Y=\overline X\qquad\Longrightarrow\qquad Z=\overline Y = X\;{\rm in\;this\;phase}
$$
and for $CK=1$, $Y$, and therefore $Z$, is held.

Thus the left latch is a master transparent on $CK$ high and
the right latch is a slave transparent on $CK$ low, connected
as a toggle flip-flop, $D=\overline Q$.  Starting e.g. from
$(X,Z)=(1,0)$, in successive half clock periods

$$
\begin{array}{c|ccccccccc}
      &0&1&2&3&4&5&6&7&8\\ \hline
CK    &1&0&1&0&1&0&1&0&1\\
X     &1&1&0&0&1&1&0&0&1\\
Z     &0&1&1&0&0&1&1&0&0
\end{array}
$$

i.e.

$$
(X,Z):\;(1,0)\to(1,1)\to(0,1)\to(0,0)\to(1,0)\cdots
$$

$X$ changes only on the rising edge of $CK$ and $Z$ only on
the falling edge. Both $X$ and $Z$ therefore have period
$2T_{CK}$, $50\%$ duty cycle, and the transitions of $Z$ lag
those of $X$ by $T_{CK}/2$, one quarter of the output period
$2T_{CK}$.

Hence, for a $50\%$-duty-cycle clock, $X$ and $Z$ are
divide-by-two outputs in quadrature, $90^{\circ}$ apart at
$f_{CK}/2$. $Y=\overline Z$ is the complementary $Q$ phase.
In practice $X$ is a dynamic node and should be brought out
through a buffer matched to ${\rm Inv_3}$.

* The left latch is on for $CK=1,\;\overline{CK}=0$ and
holds $X$ for $CK=0$.

$ {\rm Inv_3}$ makes the d-c feedback to the left latch

$$
X^+ = \bar Z = Y ,\qquad Y^+=Y .
$$
$X$ can change only at the rising clock edge.

For $CK=0$ the right latch is an inverter, the left latch holds:
$$
Y^+ = \bar X ,\qquad Z^+ = \bar Y^+ = X .
$$
$Y$ (and $Z$) can change only at the falling clock edge.

divide-by-two signal.  $X$ also toggles once per clock
period, i.e. it is also at $f_{CK}/2$, with $50\%$ duty
cycle for a $50\%$ clock.  In successive $CK$ half-cycles,
e.g.,

$$\begin{array}{c|cccccc}
CK & 1&0&1&0&1&0\\ \hline
X  & 0&0&1&1&0&0\\
Y  & 0&1&1&0&0&1\\
Z  & 1&0&0&1&1&0
\end{array}$$

edge.  The separation is $T_{CK}/2$, whereas the output
period is $2T_{CK}$.  That is $T_{out}/4$, i.e. $90^{\circ}$,
between the master output $X$ and the slave output $Y$
(or $Z$).  In principle $X$ and $Y$ are the quadrature
divided outputs, assuming a $50\%$ duty-cycle clock.

answers.question: In the circuit shown in the figure, does the speed improve or degrade if we increase the widths of the clocked transistors?

answer.text:
The two stacked inverters are alternately enabled
$C^{2}$MOS inverters.  With the static inverter in the loop
the circuit is a $\div 2$ circuit.

```
                A                B
  F  ---[inv CK]-----[inv CKbar]-----o--[inv]--- F
```

$A$ and $B$ are dynamic nodes.  Each must be evaluated,
and hold its value on its capacitance, in one half clock
period.  Let, in one inverter, $X_{P}$ and $X_{N}$ be the
nodes between the clock transistor and the signal
transistor on the $p$ and on the $n$ side.

When, e.g., the first inverter is on with $A=V_{DD}$, its
signal $n$-device is off and its clock $n$-device has pulled
$X_{N}$ to ground.  $CK$ now goes low, the first inverter is
turned off and $A$ is left floating at $V_{DD}$.  The second
inverter evaluates, $B$ changes, the static inverter changes
$F$, i.e. the input of the first inverter changes, turning
its signal $n$-device on.  The charge stored on $C_{A}$ is
now shared with the charge on $C_{X_{N}}$, which is at
ground:

$$ 
A:\;V_{DD}\;\longrightarrow\;
V_{DD}\,{C_{A}\over C_{A}+C_{X_{N}}}\qquad 
\Delta V = V_{DD}\,{C_{X_{N}}\over C_{A}+C_{X_{N}}}
$$

and analogously on the $p$ side, and at $B$ in the other
half cycle.  The corrupted $A$ is the input of the second,
now evaluating, inverter: its pull-down overdrive is
reduced, its pull-up may even turn on slightly, and it
switches much more slowly.  $A$ is floating, so the lost
voltage is never restored in that half cycle.

Now

$$
C_{X}\;\approx\;C_{db,\,{\rm clock}}+C_{sb,\,{\rm signal}}\;\propto\;W_{\rm clock}
$$

so widening the clock devices increases $C_{X}$ and
increases the charge-sharing droop on the dynamic nodes
$A$ and $B$.  The series resistance $R_{ck}C_{X}$ is
essentially independent of $W_{ck}$, the resistance
benefit on charging $C_{A,B}$ is limited by the unchanged
signal device in series, and the larger $C_{g,ck}$ in
addition loads $CK,\overline{CK}$.

Hence, counter to first intuition, widening the clocked
transistors lowers the maximum toggle frequency, and can
cause failure to divide.  The clock devices should be no
wider than necessary.

answers.question: In the circuit shown in the figure, does the speed improve or degrade if we increase the widths of the clocked transistors?

answer.text:
The circuit is a dynamic $\div 2$: two clocked inverters in a loop with the output inverter. Their outputs are dynamic nodes — when a clocked inverter is off, its output level exists only as charge on the node capacitance, with no keeper to restore it.

Widening the four $CK/\overline{CK}$ devices gives very little extra drive, because each is in series with an unchanged signal transistor: $R_{on}$ quickly becomes dominated by the signal device. What widening does increase, roughly proportionally to $W$, is:

1. **The diffusion capacitance at the internal stack nodes** (between each clock transistor and its signal transistor), and
2. **The gate load on $CK/\overline{CK}$**, slowing the clock edges themselves.

The first effect is fatal here because of charge sharing. Consider the NMOS side of a clocked inverter while it is on with its output high: the signal NMOS is off, the clock NMOS is on, so the internal stack node is pulled to ground. The inverter then turns off, and — through the feedback loop — its input toggles. The signal NMOS now turns on and connects that grounded internal node to the dynamic output node, which is supposed to be holding a "1". The output droops to

$$V_{DD}\,\frac{C_{out}}{C_{out}+C_{stack}}, \qquad \Delta V = V_{DD}\,\frac{C_{stack}}{C_{out}+C_{stack}}.$$

The PMOS side does the complementary damage to a stored "0". Since $C_{stack}\propto W_{clock}$, a wider clock device produces a larger droop every half-cycle. That reduced level is what drives the next stage for the rest of the phase: lower overdrive, slower discharge/charge, and, if the droop is large enough, the complementary device of the next inverter begins to turn on and fights the transition. The level cannot be restored until the next active phase.

So beyond the small width needed to make the clock device's resistance a minor part of the stack resistance, **increasing the clocked-transistor widths degrades the maximum operating speed** — and can eventually cause outright failure. In high-speed dynamic dividers the clocked devices are therefore kept small.

That matches the golden solution’s explicit full-credit rule for improvement followed by a charge-sharing limit, even though it overstates the severity of the swing loss.

answers.question: In the circuit shown in the figure, does the speed improve or degrade if we increase the widths of the clocked transistors?

answer.text:
The circuit is the $C^{2}MOS$ divide-by-two. The first
clocked inverter is on for $CK=1$, the second for $CK=0$,
and the static inverter closes the loop. Hence the outputs
of the two clocked inverters, say $X$ and $Y$, are not driven
for alternate half cycles. They are dynamic nodes: the
value is stored only on their capacitance.

Call $X_{1}$ the internal node between the upper clocked
$PMOS$ and the upper data $PMOS$ of the first latch, and
$X_{2}$ the corresponding node in the lower branch. When
the latch has been on, $X_{1}$ is pulled to $V_{DD}$ by the
clock device and $X_{2}$ to ground, irrespective of the
data. When the latch turns off $X_{1},X_{2}$ and $X$ float.

During the off half cycle the other latch and the feedback
inverter change the data input of the off latch. The data
device therefore turns on and connects the floating output
$X$ to an internal node which is at the opposite rail.
E.g. with $X$ stored at $V_{DD}$, the NMOS data device turns
on and connects $X$ to $X_{2}=0$. Charge is shared between
$C_{X}$ and $C_{int}$, the capacitance at $X_{2}$:

$$
\Delta V_{X}\;\approx\;V_{DD}\,
\frac{C_{int}}{C_{int}+C_{X}}\;,
$$

and analogously for a stored $0$ through the PMOS side.
The same occurs at $Y$ in the other half cycle.

$C_{int}$ is essentially the drain junction and overlap
capacitance of the clocked device. Increasing $W_{ck}$

* increases $C_{int}\propto W_{ck}$, hence increases
$\Delta V_{X},\Delta V_{Y}$;
* therefore leaves the still-active downstream latch with a
degraded input, $V_{DD}-\Delta V$ instead of $V_{DD}$. Its
drive current $\propto (V_{DD}-\Delta V-|V_{th}|)^{2}$ falls
rapidly, and for large $\Delta V$ it can even be spuriously
switched within the same half cycle;
* increases the capacitance that must be restored through
the data device when the latch turns on again;
* increases the gate load on $CK$ and $\overline{CK}$, slowing
the clock edges, to which $C^{2}MOS$ delay is very sensitive.

The reduction in the series resistance of the clock device,
$\propto 1/W_{ck}$, is more than outweighed by these effects.
The maximum clock frequency at which the circuit still
divides correctly therefore decreases. In practice the
clocked devices are kept near minimum size.

answers.question: Analyze the arrangement in the figure.

answer.text:
Label the nodes as

```
        CK      Inv1    CK      Inv2    Inv3
  E o---/ ------o-->o---/ ------>o----->o---o
  ^             A      B         C      D     |
  |___________________________________________|
```

$E$ is taken as the output. In the ideal model an
inverter whose input is disconnected holds its input
voltage on the parasitic capacitance at that input.
$CK$ and $\overline{CK}$ are assumed never to be closed
simultaneously.

Let $Q_n$ be the value of $E$ during the $n$-th interval
for which $CK=1$.

### $CK=1,\ \overline{CK}=0$

The left switch is closed and the middle switch is open.
Hence

\[
A=E,\qquad B=\bar A=\bar E .
\]

Node $C$ is floating. It holds its previous value, and the
two inverters to the right give

\[
D=\bar C,\qquad E=\bar D=C .
\]

Thus nothing changes at the output during this phase. What
is important is that the present output $Q_n$ is written onto
the capacitance at $A$:

\[
A_n = Q_n .
\]

### $CK=0,\ \overline{CK}=1$

Now the left switch is open and the middle switch is
closed. Node $A$ floats, so it retains $A_n=Q_n$. Therefore

\[
B=\bar A_n=\bar Q_n,\qquad C=B=\bar Q_n,
\]
\[
D=\bar C,\qquad E=\bar D=C=\bar Q_n .
\]

The output therefore changes once, just after $CK$ goes
low, to $\bar Q_n$.

At the end of this phase $C=\bar Q_n$ is stored on the
capacitance at the input of the second inverter. In the
next $CK=1$ phase that stored value becomes the new
output. Consequently

\[
\,Q_{n+1}=\bar Q_n\,.
\]

For example, starting with $Q=0$:

| phase | $CK$ | stored $A$ | stored $C$ | $E$ |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---:|
| 1 | 1 | 0 | 0 | 0 |
|   | 0 | 0 | 1 | 1 |
| 2 | 1 | 1 | 1 | 1 |
|   | 0 | 1 | 0 | 0 |
| 3 | 1 | 0 | 0 | 0 |

The output therefore stays constant for one full clock
period, then changes for the next full period:

```
CK : _/‾‾\__/‾‾\__/‾‾\__/‾‾\_
E  : ‾‾0‾‾|‾‾‾1‾‾‾|‾‾‾0‾‾‾|‾
            toggles only on CK falling
```

## Conclusion

The circuit is a **dynamic toggle flip-flop, i.e. a
divide-by-two circuit**:

\[
f_E=\frac{f_{CK}}{2}.
\]

It is not a static latch. Although three inverters are
connected in a ring, the ring is never closed all at once;
the two floating nodes alternately store the bit. The odd
number of inversions around the ring makes the recirculated
bit come back inverted after every clock cycle.

Practical consequences:

- $CK$ and $\overline{CK}$ must not both be on: that would
  close the three-inverter ring and produce a ring oscillator,
  destroying the stored state. A small both-off dead time is
  normally used.
- The storage is dynamic. Leakage on nodes $A$ and $C$
  limits how long a phase may last, so there is a minimum
  clock frequency and the clock cannot simply be stopped.
- The half-period must allow settling through the switch
  plus the inverter chain, which sets the maximum clock
  frequency.
- There is no data input and no defined starting phase:
  on power-up the divider may start in either of its two
  phase states.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly identifies a dynamic-latch toggle divider and explains that the output toggles once per input-clock period, giving half the input frequency. The extra implementation details are not needed for full credit.

answers.question: Analyze the arrangement in the figure.

answer.text:
Label the nodes as

```
        CK          Inv1     CK         Inv2      Inv3
 Q o---/ ---o A ----|>o----o B ---/ ---o C ----|>o---o D ---|>o---o Q
 ^                                                                     |
 +---------------------------------------------------------------------+
```

A switch is closed when its control is high. $CK$ and
$\overline{CK}$ are assumed non-overlapping, so the two switches are
never closed together. The storage elements are the input
capacitances of $Inv_{1}$ and $Inv_{2}$ at nodes $A$ and $C$; the circuit
is dynamic.

### $\overline{CK}$ phase: $CK$ open, $\overline{CK}$ closed

Node $A$ is floating and retains its previous value. Let it be $X$.
Then

$$B=\bar X,\qquad C=B=\bar X,\qquad D=X,\qquad Q=\bar D=\bar X .$$

So during this phase the (held) value at $A$ propagates through the
three inverters, and $Q$ is set to $\bar A$.

### $CK$ phase: $CK$ closed, $\overline{CK}$ open

Now $C$ is floating and retains its value, while $Q$ drives $A$:

$$A=Q,\qquad Q=C\;\;(\text{through }Inv_{2},Inv_{3}),$$

so $Q$ itself does not change in this phase; it merely writes its
value into $A$.

### One full clock cycle

Suppose in a $\overline{CK}$ phase $A=X$, so $Q=\bar X$.
In the next $CK$ phase $A\leftarrow Q=\bar X$.
In the next $\overline{CK}$ phase this new $A$ is held, so

$$Q_{\text{new}}=\overline{A}=\overline{\bar X}=X=\bar Q_{\text{old}}.$$

Thus $Q$ inverts once per complete $CK$ period. E.g., starting
with $A=0$:

| phase | $\overline{CK}$ | $CK$ | $\overline{CK}$ | $CK$ | $\overline{CK}$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| $A$ | 0 | 1 | 1 | 0 | 0 |
| $Q$ | 1 | 1 | 0 | 0 | 1 |

Hence this is a toggle (T) flip-flop, i.e. a divide-by-two:

$$f_Q=\frac{f_{CK}}{2},$$

with $Q$ changing in the $\overline{CK}$ phase (on the falling edge of
$CK$) and a 50% duty cycle. Every node in the loop is in fact a
$f_{CK}/2$ waveform, phase-shifted according to which phase updates it.

At first glance the three inverters in a loop might suggest a ring
oscillator. That does not happen in normal operation because the loop
is never closed: one switch is always open. It is essentially two
dynamic latching stages in a loop with an odd number (three) of
inversions, so the recirculated bit returns inverted. (With an even
number it would recirculate unchanged and act as a dynamic memory.)

Practical caveats:

* $CK$ and $\overline{CK}$ must be non-overlapping. If both switches
  conduct substantially, the three inverters form a closed ring and
  tend to oscillate with period $\approx 6t_{pd}$, producing spurious
  toggles.
* Storage at $A$ and $C$ is only on parasitic/gate capacitance, so the
  circuit is dynamic: there is a minimum clock frequency set by
  leakage, and the state is lost if the clock stops with a node left
  floating.
* Each phase must be long enough to charge the dynamic node and settle
  the inverter chain; this sets the maximum clock frequency.
* There is no reset, so the phase of the divided output at power-up is
  indeterminate.

It is a very compact, fast dynamic $\div 2$ counter, widely useful as
the first divider stage in clock-generation/PLL prescalers.

answers.question: Analyze the arrangement in the figure.

answer.text:
Label the output of the right-most inverter as $Q$, and the other nodes as

- $A$: input of $\text{Inv}_1$
- $B$: output of $\text{Inv}_1$
- $C$: input of the middle inverter

so that

$$
B=\overline A,\qquad Q = C\ \text{(through two inverters)} .
$$

The two switches are driven by complementary, ideally non-overlapping, clocks: when $CK$ is high the left switch is closed and the $\overline{CK}$ switch is open, and vice-versa. The crucial point is that the loop is **never closed in the d-c sense**. The parasitic/gate capacitances at $A$ and $C$ act as dynamic storage elements.

### Phase 1: $CK=1,\ \overline{CK}=0$

The left switch is closed, the right switch is open.

$$
A = Q,\qquad B=\overline A = \overline Q .
$$

Node $C$ is floating, but its capacitance retains the value it had in the previous phase, so $Q$ (driven through the last two inverters from $C$) is held unchanged. In this phase the first inverter *samples* $Q$ and prepares $\overline Q$ at $B$.

### Phase 2: $CK=0,\ \overline{CK}=1$

The left switch opens, the right switch closes. Node $A$ is now floating, but retains the sampled value of $Q$, so $\text{Inv}_1$ keeps driving

$$
B = \overline{Q_{\text{old}}}.
$$

With the $\overline{CK}$ switch closed,

$$
C = B = \overline{Q_{\text{old}}},\qquad 
Q_{\text{new}} = C = \overline{Q_{\text{old}}}.
$$

Hence, once per full clock period,

$$
\boxed{\,Q^{+} = \overline{Q}\,}
$$

i.e. the circuit is a **toggle (T) flip-flop with $T\equiv1$**, or equivalently a **divide-by-2 counter**.

A typical sequence, starting from $Q=0$, is

| phase | $A$ | $B$ | $C$ | $Q$ |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| $CK$ | 0 | 1 | (held 0) | 0 |
| $\overline{CK}$ | (held 0) | 1 | 1 | **1** |
| $CK$ | 1 | 0 | (held 1) | 1 |
| $\overline{CK}$ | (held 1) | 0 | 0 | **0** |

So $Q$ toggles on every $\overline{CK}$ phase, stays constant in between, and therefore has period $2T_{CK}$ (frequency $f_{CK}/2$) with approximately 50% duty cycle. The output of the middle inverter provides $\overline Q$.

### Interpretation and limitations

- Structurally it is two dynamic latches in a loop: an inverting master latch ($CK$ switch + $\text{Inv}_1$) followed by a non-inverting slave latch ($\overline{CK}$ switch + two inverters), with the slave output fed back to the master input. The odd number of inversions in the loop produces toggling rather than storage because the loop is broken in time by the two clock phases.
- The clocks must be essentially non-overlapping ("break-before-make"). If both switches were closed simultaneously, the three inverters would form an odd ring with no stable state — it could oscillate or settle unpredictably.
- It is a **dynamic** circuit: nodes $A$ and $C$ are floating for half a cycle. Leakage, charge sharing, and clock feedthrough corrupt the stored charge if the clock is too slow, so there is a minimum operating frequency, and the state is lost if the clock stops. Conversely, each phase must be long enough for the switch plus inverter delay(s) to settle, setting the maximum frequency.
- The initial state after power-up is arbitrary, but from then on the toggling is deterministic (no reset is provided).

In short: despite looking like an unstable 3-inverter ring, the complementary clocked switches turn it into a well-defined dynamic master–slave toggle flip-flop — the classic $\div 2$ prescaler/counter stage.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly identifies the arrangement as a dynamic-latch divide-by-two and explains its alternating sample/hold, toggle behavior, and half-frequency output, satisfying the golden solution’s full-credit rule.

answers.question: How does the red inverter in the figure affect the performance?

answer.text:
The circuit is a dynamic master–slave divide-by-two. Let

- $Q$ be the node at the far left (the output of the last black inverter, fed back to the input), and
- $X$ be the output of $\text{Inv}_1$.

The red inverter is an **unclocked feed-forward inverter in parallel with the clocked master latch** ($\text{CK}$ switch $+\ \text{Inv}_1$). It is not a keeper: a keeper would feed $X$ back to the input of $\text{Inv}_1$, whereas this device feeds $Q$ forward to $X$ at all times.

**When $CK$ is on ($\overline{CK}$ off)** the master is transparent and the slave holds $Q$. The input of $\text{Inv}_1$ is then $Q$ (through the closed switch), so the red inverter and $\text{Inv}_1$ do exactly the same job, in parallel:

$$X=\bar Q .$$

Two things help speed. First, the red path bypasses the series resistance of the $\text{CK}$ switch, so $X$ starts moving as soon as $Q$ moves instead of waiting for the input node of $\text{Inv}_1$ to charge through the switch. Second, once $\text{Inv}_1$ turns on, two inverters drive the capacitance at $X$ instead of one. The master therefore settles in well under a half clock period, and the maximum toggle frequency of the divider goes up. In fact the red inverter even starts pre-driving $X$ toward its *next* value during the preceding $\overline{CK}$ phase, so part of the master delay is hidden.

**When $CK$ is off ($\overline{CK}$ on)** the master is supposed to be in hold and completely isolated from the slave. $\text{Inv}_1$ holds $X=\bar Q_{\text{old}}$ from the charge stored on its input node, the slave makes $Q_{\text{new}}=X=\bar Q_{\text{old}}$, and the divider has toggled. But the red inverter is still connected, and it now *disagrees* with $\text{Inv}_1$:

$$\text{Inv}_1:\; X=\bar Q_{\text{old}}=Q_{\text{new}},\qquad 
\text{red}:\; X=\bar Q_{\text{new}}=Q_{\text{old}} .$$

So during the whole hold phase the red inverter fights $\text{Inv}_1$ for node $X$: there is contention (crowbar) current, the swing and noise margin at $X$ are degraded, and the red device’s gate capacitance loads $Q$ while its drain capacitance loads $X$, slowing the slave a little and raising power. Worse, $X\!\to\!$Inv$_2\!\to\!$Inv$_3\!\to\!Q\!\to\!$red$\!\to\!X$ is a closed loop of three inverters. If the $\overline{CK}$ phase lasts longer than the delay around that loop, $X$ is dragged across the slave’s threshold, $Q$ flips back, then flips again — the loop ring-oscillates and the $\div2$ action is lost. Correct operation at high speed relies on the clock phase ending before that unwanted second toggle gets around the loop.

**Net effect:** the operating window is shifted *up* in frequency. $f_{\max}$ increases (the reason the device is added in RF prescalers, where the clock is always present and fast), but a substantial $f_{\min}$ appears, well above the leakage-limited minimum of the plain dynamic divider: the circuit misbehaves at low clock rates, oscillates if the clock stops with $CK$ low, and burns extra power in contention. The red inverter is therefore sized as a compromise — strong enough to start $X$ swinging quickly, weak/delayed enough not to overpower $\text{Inv}_1$ and corrupt $X$ within one half-cycle.

gpt_6_luna_max.rationale: Correctly identifies the red inverter as an unclocked feedforward path that bypasses part of the first latch and improves high-speed operation, while also recognizing the low-frequency regenerative-loop/contention problem that raises the minimum usable clock frequency.

answers.question: How does the red inverter in the figure affect the performance?

answer.text:
The black circuit is a dynamic recirculating flip-flop.
The state is held, in alternate clock phases, as charge on
the input capacitance of ${\rm Inv}_1$ and on the input
capacitance of the following inverter.  It therefore has a
minimum clock frequency set by leakage.

The red inverter is meant to be the back-to-back keeper
for ${\rm Inv}_1$, but as drawn it is not connected directly
across ${\rm Inv}_1$: its loop contains the $CK$ switch.

* $CK$ off, $\overline{CK}$ on: this is the phase in which
the input node of ${\rm Inv}_1$ is floating and needs to be
held.  The $CK$ switch is open, so the keeper loop is open.
That node still floats and still leaks.  The circuit is not
made static, and $f_{\min }$ and clock-stop behaviour are
unchanged.

* $CK$ on: the keeper loop is closed, but the input of
${\rm Inv}_1$ is then already driven through $CK$ by the
recirculating signal.  The keeper is redundant.

Worse, in the $\overline{CK}$ phase the output of the red
inverter is tied to the recirculating node.  When the right
hand inverters try to toggle that node to its new value,
the red inverter, fed from the old output of ${\rm Inv}_1$,
tries to hold it at its old value.  The right-most inverter
must overpower the red inverter on every toggle.  The red
inverter also loads the output of ${\rm Inv}_1$ and the
recirculating node.

Hence, as drawn, the red inverter gives no static-holding
benefit, but increases clock-to-output delay and contention
power, lowers $f_{\max }$, and, if it is not much weaker than
the right-most inverter, can prevent the circuit from
toggling at all.  A useful keeper must be connected directly
across ${\rm Inv}_1$, on the ${\rm Inv}_1$ side of the $CK$
switch, and made deliberately weak.

It also says the minimum-frequency limit is unchanged and predicts reduced maximum speed, contrary to the key effects. answers.question: How does the red inverter in the figure affect the performance?

answer.text:
The black circuit is a dynamic toggle flip-flop. The values at
the inputs of the inverters are stored only on gate capacitance
while $CK$ or $\overline{CK}$ is off, so it will not retain its
state for a long, or stopped, clock period.

The red inverter is a feedback, or keeper, inverter around
${\rm Inv_1}$.  It cross-couples the first stage:

* it regeneratively holds the state of ${\rm Inv_1}$, so leakage
at the dynamic node no longer destroys the stored bit.  In
principle the stage now works down to dc, with much better
immunity to leakage and noise.

* on every change of state the new value must fight the keeper.
The driver, here the last inverter through the $CK$ switch,
must overpower the red inverter, and the red inverter loads
the output of ${\rm Inv_1}$.

Hence retention is gained at the expense of speed and power:
larger clock-to-output delay, contention current during
switching, increased power, and a lower maximum toggle
frequency.  The red inverter must therefore be made very weak
-- small $W/L$, long channel -- compared with ${\rm Inv_1}$ and
with the inverter driving it.  Made full strength, it will
seriously slow, and can even prevent, the divide-by-two
action.
